en: The Great Dharma Torch Dhvasani Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of Central India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Prologue.
Chapter Two: Subduing Māra. Chapter One: The Prologue. Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions.
They have all attained mastery, with their minds well-liberated and their wisdom well-liberated;
they are able to subdue themselves like great dragons,
having accomplished what was to be done and laid down the heavy burden.
Having attained their own benefit and exhausted all fetters of existence,
they accord with the true teaching and are fully endowed with liberation;
they are able to enter the stage of universal sovereignty.
Their names were the Venerable Subhūti,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa,
and the Venerable Śāriputra.
Āyuṣmat Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
with such śrāvakas of great majestic power and supernormal faculties as these serving as his leaders;
at that time, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, [approached].
Accompanied by ten billion Brahmā assemblies and immeasurable devas of the Brahma-palaces,
each with their respective retinues, they all gathered together.
At that time, there were also the various deva hosts of Ābhāsvara Heaven.
As well as the hosts of the Parīttābha devas,
the Abhāsvara devas,
and the Apramāṇābha devas.
The assembly of the Abhirati devas,
up to the assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa devas—
such immeasurable billions of deva assemblies as these.
Each of them, together with their retinues, also assembled there.

At that time, there was also the celestial host of the Lord of Merchants; this Lord of Merchants was the eldest among the five hundred bodhisattva sons of Māra, and in other sūtras he is called the "Guide."
The assembly of the Tuṣita Heaven;
Śakra Devānām Indra and the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
and so on, up to the assembly of the Cāturmahārājika Heaven.
In this manner, immeasurable multitudes of devas,
each with their own retinues, also all gathered there.
At that time, the assembly of devas all had this thought:
"I wish that the World-Honored One would, according to our needs, expound for us a single Dharma-gate;
would it not be well for us to hear it?
Having formed this thought, he proceeded to where the Buddha was.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew and stood to one side.
At that time, the devaputra Subhavyūha adjusted his robes before the Buddha.
He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
joined his palms together at the level of his head, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
out of compassion for all sentient beings,
I now wish to question the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the World-Honored One.
How do sentient beings come to understand the Dharma and Vinaya?
By training in accordance with the Buddha’s virtues and practicing in conformity with the World-Honored One’s teachings according to the Dharma.
World-Honored One,
how do sentient beings attain freedom from indolence and diligently cultivate the sūtras,
upholding both their words and their meanings?
One contemplates in accordance with the meaning and the Dharma,
and through swift recitation, gains power by means of the Dharma,
O Blessed One.
How do sentient beings enter the dharma-gate of the fundamental wisdom of all syllables?
Having dwelled in this dharma-gate, they are able to discern and know;
because of this knowledge, [they attain liberation].
By entering the first gate of contemplation, one attains the meaning of all dharmas;
even up to the attainment of entry into the profound dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination,
one shall fully awaken to and know them all.
World-Honored One,
how is it that sentient beings do not give rise to weariness,
nor produce a distracted mind?
“World-Honored One, he understands that the objects of his own mind are mere mental projections;
he skillfully knows the supreme Dharma and is able to enter into it accordingly.”
Now, desiring to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Tathāgatagarbha and attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata,
I venture to entreat the Tathāgata to proclaim such a profound sūtra as this gateway of dhāraṇīs.
For what reason?
World-Honored One,
it is difficult to obtain a human body.
Although one has obtained a human body, its lifespan is further shortened;
within this brief life there are three additional evils.
What are these three?
First, their mental nature is stubborn and corrupt, such that they do not accept wholesome words.
Second, they constantly harbor stinginess and envy, fearing that others may surpass them.
Third, even if they know someone is superior to themselves, they feel ashamed to consult or inquire of them.
These are called the three evils.
For this reason,
I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, regarding the dharani scriptures.
World-Honored One,
the Tathāgata has previously preached immeasurable billions of sūtras,
some of which were spoken in response to questions.
Or, without being asked, they say of themselves:
"World-Honored One,
we at this time..."
I see that an assembly of nine nayutas of devas has already gathered before the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
therefore, I now inquire about the sūtras within the Tathāgata’s ultimate Dharma of dhāraṇīs.
World-Honored One,
if there are those who can study this supreme gateway of dhāraṇīs,
all other qualities of the Buddha-dharma will naturally increase without requiring great effort.
At that time, having received such a question from the devaputra Subhavyūha,
the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda,"

Did you see how the Devaputra Subhatejas, through his eloquence regarding the meaning of the Dharma, even inquired of the Tathāgata concerning the appearance in the world [of Buddhas] and the causes and conditions for attaining the state of a Tathāgata;
did he not first inquire about this sūtra, the dharma-gate of this dhāraṇī?
Ānanda, this Devaputra Śubhatejas has already,
in the past, [served] fourteen billion Tathāgatas.
Question: Regarding this dhāraṇī sūtra, Ānanda,
I shall now explain for you the initial questions posed by the devaputra Bhadratejas to the Buddha, as well as the names of the dhāraṇīs.
Listen attentively,
Ānanda. This is the devaputra Śubhatejas.
In a former time, he was born into a great brahmin family as the son of that brahmin;
he was endowed with majestic virtue, and his household was wealthy and abundant.
He was constantly surrounded and protected by various devas;
he was intelligent and possessed great wisdom, being extensively versed in non-Buddhist treatises and fully understanding both the words and meanings of the four Vedas.
Having already recited it myself, I am further able to teach others.
At first, I questioned that Buddha regarding this *dhāraṇī*,
which skillfully masters the initial dharma-gates of treatises and subdues all heterodox arguments.
Furthermore, he is able to establish the fundamental roots of all syllables and skillfully explain the various meanings of their distinct differences.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
we wish to hear the name of that Buddha;
he is the Devaputra Good Radiance."
I wish to hear from whom I first heard this dhāraṇī sūtra in past lives,
as well as the merits and supramundane beneficial deeds of those noble disciples and their followers.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of the Adornment of Great Power.
Having entered this samādhi, he—
All realms of the past appeared before him.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat and adjusted his robes.
Baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee on the ground,
he joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One."
"Since the distant past, I have never before seen a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha enter this samādhi.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "So it is, so it is."
I have never before entered such a samādhi.
Why is this, Ānanda?
This samādhi cannot be entered by those in other lower stages,
nor is it entered for the sake of any other sūtras.
Why is this so? Ānanda,
all the Tathāgatas of the past...
There is not one who, without first entering this samādhi, subsequently preached this dhāraṇī sūtra;
furthermore, it was originally the question posed by this Devaputra Good Splendor (Suvikrānta-prabha) to the Buddha.
Therefore, Ānanda,
you should listen attentively to the name of that Buddha and the name of that sutra.
"I shall now explain these two kinds for you.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
Now is precisely the right time.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will,
for our sake, explain the name of the Buddha and the sutra spoken by the Devaputra Subhavyūha as he questioned you.
May the World-Honored One also speak of this deity’s merit of eloquence so that we may hear it.
Now this entire assembly of devas and humans all rejoice and desire to hear;
so too do these hosts of Brahmās and sons of gods.
"Listen with a single-minded desire to hear and listen well in this way.
He further addressed Ānanda: "Listen attentively, receive this with care, and reflect upon it well;
I shall now explain it."
Ānanda spoke again:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will explain it for me."
"I shall listen and receive it.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"I recall the past, immeasurable and boundless."
At that time, there was an eon named Bhadra-deva.
During that eon, there was a universal monarch (cakravartin).
He was known as Jihuang (Fire-Light).
He ruled over the four quarters of the world,
being fully endowed with the practice of the precepts and governing according to the Dharma.
The King’s principal consort gave birth to a son,
whom they named Fangguang (Radiant Light).
Ānanda, that youth Emitting Light at that time was none other than a bodhisattva in his final birth.
Having lived for more than two thousand years since his birth,
he finally left the household life to practice the Way;
gradually proceeding to the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained perfect and complete awakening.
Having attained Buddhahood, he was still named Emitting Light (Prabhāsa).
That Buddha’s retinue of disciples consisted of nine hundred billion nayutas of śrāvaka assemblies,
all of whom were great arhats.
Furthermore, Ānanda, there was an assembly of one hundred million great bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Tathāgata Emitting Light sat amidst that great assembly.
For the sake of all bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,
he has preached this profound sūtra of dhāraṇī;
yet, as for this gateway of dhāraṇī...
It is then able to comprehensively encompass all other sūtras.
For anyone who receives and maintains this dhāraṇī,
all matters concerning the bodhi of all Buddhas [will be accomplished].
Although they have not heard or seen [this teaching], they understand it naturally and clearly, and thus they are called Dharma Masters. Ānanda,
at that time, those assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—
He addressed the Buddha Emitting Light, saying,
"World-Honored One,
as for what is called the 'gate of dhāraṇī'..."
What is the meaning [of this]?
What is a *dhāraṇī*?
For what reason is it further called a "gate" (*mukha*)?
At that time, the Buddha Emitting Light addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas,
saying: "O māṇavas,
listen attentively, listen attentively!"
I shall explain this for you:
just as this great earth, being established, is able to sustain the production of all manner of jewels,
and can also produce all varieties of medicinal herbs, grasses, shrubs, forests, flowers, and fruits.
It sustains them all.
Furthermore, it can sustain all small and great mountains, as well as all ponds, rivers, and even the great oceans.
Moreover, it can also sustain the various classes of beings born from the four modes of birth—those with two legs, those with four legs, humans, deer, birds, and beasts.
This dhāraṇī is also like this,
O young brahmins.
As for what is called a "gate":
This is the Tathāgata.
The gateway of the Tathāgatagarbha gives birth to the inconceivable treasure-trove of all dharmas.
Thus it is, O māṇava.
Within this wondrous Dharma-gate of the dhāraṇī, all sūtras,
all chapters and phrases,
and all analytical meanings are produced.
Because it encompasses all the pāramitās,
it is called a "gate," O māṇava.
Furthermore, as for *dhāraṇī*,
because it is able to sustain all phenomena (*dharma*),
it is also called "ground" (*bhūmi*).
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, when that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Emitting Light spoke this Dharma..."
The sound shook the world and reached up to the Brahma palaces.
At that time, throughout the realm of Yama and all the places of suffering— the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals—
all who heard this thundering sound cried out in great distress.
Furthermore, Ānanda, it was heard in the Brahma palace that at that time,
Mahābrahmā and the assembly of Brahmās, having heard the cry, [acted accordingly].
They all went to the place where the Buddha Emitting Light was and asked him about the causes and conditions:
"World-Honored One..."
"From where did that cry just now come from?
Ānanda, it was because that Tathāgata was about to speak."
Even as he smiled,
he first employed his supernormal powers to cause all the Brahmā deities to see the sentient beings suffering within the various evil realms of hell.
Thereupon he spoke:
"The various Brahmā deities are none other than these very beings in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals."
Oppressed by hunger and thirst, they experience great suffering;
driven by this agony, they raise this cry.
Thereupon, Brahmā again addressed the Buddha:
Excellent, World-Honored One!
By the power of the Buddha,
may these sentient beings briefly eliminate all their sufferings and experience a short time of peace and happiness.
At that time, the Buddha Emitting Light immediately emitted a single ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows,
which illuminated throughout the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and the domain of Yama, reaching all sentient beings in those evil states.
All suffering and affliction were extinguished;
all the hells were transformed into gardens and ponds,
and these ponds were filled with exquisite water.
In the pond there were various flowers,
namely the utpala flower and the padma flower.
The *kumuda* flowers and *puṇḍarīka* flowers [are there],
and the waters of the ponds are fragrant, sweet, cool, and refreshing.
Furthermore, after the Tathāgata Prabhāsa has entered parinirvāṇa,
the Dharma shall remain for half an eon;
the same shall apply to the gardens and ponds.
Ānanda, at that time, Brahmā questioned that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what cause and condition [is this]?"
The Tathāgata smiled and again emitted this light from his white tuft of hair.
The Buddha addressed Brahmā:

"I have recollected the past karmic conditions of all sentient beings in these hells, among the hungry ghosts, the animals, and the realm of Yama, and how they have received these retributive fruits."
Furthermore, because of my original vow,
I smile. Moreover,
it is because I know that these sentient beings have fallen into the three evil realms due to the causal conditions of their past karmic transgressions.
I also know the amount of karma and the timing for the exhaustion of suffering;
therefore, I emit light as a skillful means. When I emit this light, [it serves this purpose].
All those sentient beings suffering from pain,
having their bodies and minds illuminated by the light, attained peace and security,
and each thought to themselves:
This is the light of the Buddha.
By recollecting the Tathāgata, their evil karma is extinguished;
furthermore, by virtue of the World-Honored One’s power of compassion, they are freed from all suffering and affliction.
Having sought their end, they pass away and are reborn among humans or in the heavens;
by these causes and conditions, the great hells are transformed into gardens and ponds.
The water was clear and cool, and exquisite flowers were scattered everywhere. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Brahmā, saying:
"Brahmā, you should carefully contemplate the inconceivable skillful means of the Tathāgata."
By means of his supernormal powers, he emits rare and wondrous light that is able to extinguish all suffering in the three evil realms,
O Brahmā.
The words spoken by the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, are vast and universal because they have issued from the Tathāgata; therefore,
he is named the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas again addressed the Buddha Emitting Light, saying:"
World-Honored One,
as the Tathāgata previously spoke of dhāraṇīs,
within these dhāraṇī-gates there are various phrases and meanings.
The Tathāgata has not yet spoken of this;
I now inquire about it.
I only pray that you will explain it so that we may understand.
Ānanda, at that time, that Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas,
saying: "Māṇava!"
"Do you wish to hear the meanings of the various phrases of the dhāraṇī-gate?
The bodhisattvas replied,
"So be it, World-Honored One."
"We wish to hear it.
The Buddha said, "Māṇava."
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall speak for you.
The bodhisattvas said:
World-Honored One,
I now focus my mind with single-minded devotion;
I only pray that you will skillfully explain it for me.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Māṇava,
within this single dharma-phrase of the dhāraṇī..."
This definitively establishes the meaning that subsumes immeasurable billions of sūtras;
one should know that what is spoken by the Tathāgata through his single power is without limit.
"You all have also acquired many kinds of Dharma gates.
If you were now able to receive them according to your capacity,
I could likewise explain many more to you."
Furthermore, Māṇava,
if the Tathāgata were to speak with all his might,
even those of little wisdom would be unable to receive it.
How much less could other sentient beings possibly proclaim it? Why is this?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess immeasurable power of majestic virtue.
Māṇava, there is immeasurable progress through diligent practice,
just as a skilled archer reflects within his own mind.
"If I were to discharge it now, it would surely pierce through the Brahma palace.
Having thought thus, he took up his bow and drew an arrow, shooting it upward into the void;
yet that discharged arrow could not even reach the realm of the earth and wind deities.
How could it possibly reach as far as the Brahma palaces of the higher realms? Why is this?
Because the minds of these ignorant people lack self-restraint and moderation.
Māṇava, all sentient beings are likewise;
they cannot know even a small fraction of the Tathāgata’s power of wisdom.
How could one possibly measure the realm of the Tathāgata?
Why is this? Because the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is [incomprehensible].
Because his immeasurable power and function are difficult to fathom,
you should simply listen to what the Tathāgata says with this single power.
Māṇava, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable power;
were the Tathāgata to exhaust his strength in speaking, [he could not fully describe it].
All sentient beings would be unable to receive it,
nor would they be able to uphold it. Why is this?
Māṇava, these sentient beings are deluded and ignorant;
the powers of all Tathāgatas are immeasurable and innumerable, equal to space itself.
Because one cannot practice within this Dharma.
Furthermore, māṇava,
I shall now [explain] for you.
To further illustrate this meaning through an analogy:
just as this great earth cannot be measured from east, west, south, or north,
so it is with the māṇava.
The powers of the Tathāgata have been perfumed by immeasurable merits and roots of goodness throughout countless eons;
for this reason, [they are so].
It cannot be known;
it cannot be measured.
You should know this.
Within this single phrase-gate of the sūtra,
one is able to comprehensively encompass the meanings of the phrases of immeasurable sūtras.
At that time, those bodhisattvas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that immeasurable sūtras further enter into the meaning of this single phrase?
The Buddha said:
Māṇava, the meaning of a single phrase is what is called the phrase of the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one enters into the presence of the Prajñāpāramitā,
this is called "entering all. This constitutes the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, being fully endowed with the non-empty Dharma, complete and without deficiency.
If one contemplates with single-mindedness and maintains uninterrupted mindfulness,
then in the mere time it takes to raise a hand,
one immediately attains the meaning of immeasurable and boundless pāramitās.
This phrase of wisdom is the fundamental phrase of the dhāraṇī.
I now wish to explain the limit and the further shore of the dhāraṇī.
This will cause them to enter this gateway of dhāraṇī.
This is the initial point of entry that does not sever the root.
You should be reverent and cautious, and do not give rise to a distracted mind.
Listen with a single mind, attend correctly, and sever all webs of doubt;
Ānanda, I shall speak for you.
At that time, after that Buddha had spoken thus,
there was among that assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Dīpaprabha.
He was originally of the Brahmin caste and also constantly followed that Tathāgata Emitting Light;
then that bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
it was previously stated that from within a single fundamental syllable of a dhāraṇī, immeasurable billions of sūtras can be produced;
their meaning is thus roughly manifest.
"Bhagavān, I do not yet know what this 'gate of one phrase' is.
I only pray that you will analyze and explain it for me."
At that time, the Buddha Emitting Light addressed the Bodhisattva Lamp-Light, saying:
"Māṇava, you should know this."
I shall now further illustrate the meaning of this dhāraṇī by means of a simile.
Why is this? Because this gateway of the dhāraṇī reaches the very limit and the further shore.
This is realized and known only by the supreme, most excellent, and inconceivable wisdom of all Buddhas;
it cannot be known by ordinary people of little wisdom who are shrouded in ignorance.
If an ordinary person were to know [this],
it would be impossible,
just as it is with ordinary people.
They know only that the daytime portion is day and the nighttime portion is night. Why is this?
Because they perceive the light of the sun and moon.
"O Māṇava, by seeing the sunlight one knows it is day;
by seeing the moonlight one knows it is night."
"What do you think?
Can the wisdom of that ordinary person be said to be real?
"No, World-Honored One."
Why is this? Because what is seen by the eye is not wisdom.
The Buddha said, "It is so."
Māṇava, because of the illumination from external light,
these ordinary worldlings speak of "seeing" as "knowledge."
The wisdom of the Tathāgatas is not like that;
it is only after investigation that they speak of wisdom, O māṇava.
Therefore, the Tathāgatas, having realized the true dharma as being like a track in the sky through their own realized wisdom,
subsequently gather others and instruct them so that they may know it.
Furthermore, māṇava,
have you ever heard this?
This fundamental meaning consists of forty phrases in total.
Regarding the first phrase therein, its name is "A.
One should know that this phrase subsumes the remaining thirty-nine phrases, all of which enter into "A."
Māṇava, once all such phrases have been subsumed within the letter "A," then all worldly speech and its underlying meanings are likewise included.
Furthermore, medicinal herbs, forests, trees, and even all forms of vocal activity— including instructions, sounds, names, explanations, characteristics, and all such various categories—
are likewise included therein. Moreover,
all species of sentient beings are also included.
There are those with feet and those without feet; those with two feet, four feet, and even many feet;
birds that fly and beasts that run, as well as those born from wombs or eggs, and all species belonging to water and land.
Having included all humans and non-humans among all people,
whatever vocal actions,
skillful means, speech, and sounds there may be—
Furthermore, all things— including syllables, whether coarse or subtle, extensive or concise, and their explanations—
arise from the fundamental source of syllables within the Mātṛkā-piṭaka;
the fundamental source of syllables is the primary basis.
This is indeed included within the Mātṛkā-piṭaka. O young men (māṇava),
it is like the Nāga King Anavatapta,
who in the mere blink of an eye can raise clouds that cover seven thousand yojanas and send down fine rain throughout Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, it is like the great lake where those dragons dwell, from which four rivers flow out,
circulating through the four directions and entering the four oceans.
As for all other small rivers, ponds, pools, ditches, and canals,
he is able to fill them all with moisture as required.
Thus it is, O māṇava.
Within these two dharma-gates of this dhāraṇī,
there are immeasurable billions of sūtras;
the meaning of even a single phrase therein is likewise so.
"You should listen and receive this; having heard it, you should uphold it.
Proclaim it to others everywhere and do not harbor secrecy or stinginess.
You all should know this."
Within this meaning, the two characters "Ē" and "A" must always be maintained in continuous succession;
one should constantly and uninterruptedly keep the Tathāgata in mind,
as they are also complete in terms of linguistic expression and doctrinal significance.

One should further understand that these various pāramitās are fulfilled because the skillful means of teaching the meaning are uninterrupted, and because the realization of the meaning is increasingly clarified.
Although the great darkness within his body was completely dispersed and extinguished without remainder,
because he did not sever such skillful means, he caused the Buddha-dharma to increase,
attained the opening of the *dhāraṇī* gates, and [achieved] further progress.
Do not harbor other thoughts, do not perform other deeds;
contemplate only this meaning and do not abandon this faith.
Sit alone in contemplation, observing, examining, and discerning it.
Whether right or wrong, one should engage in skillful consultation with those who are learned;
the Tathāgata’s Dharma-teaching arises from the void,
and one should accordingly follow the Tathāgata’s instructions.
Furthermore, māṇava,
I shall employ various similes and skillful means for you to demonstrate this single-syllable dharma-gate of the dhāraṇī.
It is like lighting a small amount of grass for illumination before many torches have been set up;
it is like holding a single torch before a thousand lamps have been suspended. Why is this so?
I fear that you may feel alarm and dread; therefore,
I shall now provide further analogies for this single gateway, O māṇava.
Suppose, for example, there were a person who went into the great ocean and took up a single drop of water.
What do you think?
Is this person of little wisdom?
"Do you know whether that ocean water has diminished or not?
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, māṇava.
What you have heard is like a single drop of water mentioned before."
"O Māṇava, I have not yet spoken [the Dharma] as if water had not been drawn;
you all should listen according to your capacity."
I shall speak for you;
once you have heard it,
fortify your mind as if donning great armor.
Thereafter, one is able to enter the gateway of a single phrase;
having attained thorough understanding without doubt, the mind is not startled or terrified.
This is called the armor of the mind being firm, stable, and immovable.
Just as those sense faculties are established upon the four great elements,
so too should you enter into faith in the sequence of skillful means within the Tathāgata’s teaching;
it should be exactly like this.
Ānanda, at that time,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Lamp-Light again addressed the Tathāgata Emitting Light, saying:
"World-Honored One..."
The two characters "A" and "Ka" have a single meaning.
Since their meaning is one, they cannot be made into two.
The Tathāgata has taught this meaning regarding these two characters in a state where there is no distinction.

“If his body sores were such as these, would he be worthy of offerings?

"I pray that you will seek it quickly.

Abhaya replied,

what could that blind man possibly say?
Māṇava, I have already informed you previously;
now I shall again provide an illustration.
"You should know that these are the subtle and secret words of the Tathāgata’s skillful means.

those various sentient beings who commit evil deeds.

amidst such various sufferings and afflictions,

by means of these causes and conditions, the characteristics of the aggregates no longer appear.
It also constitutes the tongue faculty.

General characteristics and specific characteristics;

Chapter Eight: The Four Foundations of Mindfulness. From the *Mahādharmapradīpa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, Chapter Eight, "The Four Foundations of Mindfulness":
Ānanda, at that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Emitting Light...
Having spoken this Dharma,
he rose calmly from his lion throne and,
with the Buddha-eye, surveyed the ten directions.
Returning to his original seat, he sat cross-legged and entered the Lion’s Vigorous Display Samādhi.
He emitted a great radiance that illuminated all infinite and boundless worlds throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Great Brahma Kings of all the infinite and boundless worlds in the ten directions,
as well as the gods of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita,
and Brahmakāyika assemblies, all had this thought:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!

"We, the assembly of devas,

If this single-phrase gate were to be explained in full:
Suppose there were all the sounds and various musical instruments within the trichiliocosm—
namely, the sounds of the Four Heavenly Kings and the sounds of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The sounds of the Yāma Heaven,
the Tuṣita Heaven,
and the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
The sounds of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven,
and even all the sounds within the palaces of the Māra kings—
all these are the sounds of the Dharma; yet even to expound this single phrase would not be sufficient to exhaust them.
Why is this? Because, Brahmā,
a single gateway reveals the profound, vast, and great treasury of the Buddha.
This Tathāgatagarbha is vast, immeasurable, boundless, and limitless, such that it cannot be exhausted.
Were it to be proclaimed,
it would cause the bodies and minds of all sentient beings to become pure, peaceful, secure, and happy.
That which was previously unattained is now entirely attained;
all this is due to the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Chapter Eleven: The Teaching of the Three Vehicles. From the *Mahādharanī-sūtra*, Chapter Eleven: The Teaching of the Three Vehicles. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
At that time, the Tathāgata Prabhāsa addressed a brahmin youth named Viśākha in the midst of the great assembly,
saying: "You, Viśākha."
If a śrāvaka wishes to teach and transform others,
how can they cause others to rejoice?
First, they should purify their own actions of body, speech, and mind.
One should vow to apply diligent effort in skillfully studying the meaning of the Dharma,
constantly engage in much reflection to achieve wisdom,
and only thereafter teach others.
This causes them to give rise to joy and increases their wholesome qualities.
Were it not otherwise,
one would be unable to cause others to analyze and explain those meanings.
One should dwell thus, be mindful thus, and train thus. Why is this?
For if one lacks wisdom, one is not training well.
If one does not even know it oneself, how much less can one teach others? Viśākhā,
it is like a hornless bull in the world that has no capacity for fighting.
Since they neither protect themselves nor protect others,
why is this? It is because they lack the implements for combat.
In this way, Viśākhā, if śramaṇas,
brāhmaṇas, or any other sentient beings do not apply themselves diligently to study,
they will be unable to contemplate the meaning.
It is not as good as practicing what one preaches;
one is unable to engage in discussion or discourse with others. Why is this?
Because they lack wisdom,
they possess only arrogance and increase their sense of "mine," whereby the wholesome dharmas of both themselves and others are entirely diminished.
Therefore, those who possess wisdom do not give rise to arrogance;
the mind of "mine" does not exist, and the notion of a self does not arise.
Furthermore, they are without attachment and do not crave their own bodies.
Why is this? Because one who has seen the Noble Truths does not give rise to afflictions;
because evil poison has been extinguished, there is no contention.
Because he is free from enemies, he has no sense of "mine";
because he does not praise himself, he eliminates the afflictions of desire;
and by not dwelling on other matters, he contemplates only causes and conditions.
Furthermore, they teach others to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination and all arising and ceasing.
Viśākha, this is what is called a practitioner of the Śrāvaka path.
One should skillfully guard one's own actions of body, speech, and mind,
and is also able to teach others to remain far removed from these three faults.
Furthermore, Viśākhā:
The pratyekabuddha is not like this;
he has no thought of preaching,
but merely awakens by himself and is unable to teach others.
Why is this? Because such a person has severed their great vows and profound practices;
they delight only in quiescence and have no aspiration for transformation-birth.
They are entirely unable to proclaim the various dharmas;
nor can they speak of the retribution of good and evil karma,
nor indeed of anything from the faults and afflictions of birth and death to the peace and bliss of nirvāṇa— nothing at all is spoken.
Observing only the minds of others to discern their inclinations and desires,
one immediately manifests universal supernatural transformations with sovereign ease and unimpeded mastery,
causing others to attain faith and understanding.
Acting as a field of merit for all beings, they generate great virtue;
according to their aspirations, these are immediately fulfilled,
surpassing even the śrāvakas.
Vaiśākha, because he has attained the power of mastery over the supernormal faculties,
that man as well has practiced fewness of desires and contentment for a long time in the distant past.
Now, acting in this way, with such karma and such vows,
by virtue of his original vow, he takes but a small portion within the Buddha-dharma, manifesting only supernatural powers to benefit others as appropriate.
In reality, however, they are unable to preach the Dharma to deliver others or cause them to rejoice. Viśākhā,
such persons merely awaken to that Dharma for themselves.
Therefore, they are unable to preach the Dharma or provide instruction;
nevertheless, they likewise possess such skillful means as to compassionately manifest supernatural powers for the sake of sentient beings and bring forth roots of goodness.
If there were no Buddha in the world, he would remain within the mundane realm;
but since a Buddha has appeared in the world, he has entered parinirvāṇa.
When this person emerged, there was no teacher to instruct him.
Relying solely on one's own power to leave the household life and practice,
one realizes awakening through internal reflection;
for this reason, such a person excels the field of merit of the śrāvakas.
Vesākha, this is the practice and activity of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, Vesākha:
To transform sentient beings?

I shall now briefly explain the bodhisattva’s training rules; as for the training rules of the bodhisattvas themselves, one first contemplates all the tainted phenomena (*āsrava-dharma*) that exist in the world.
He then saw that all conditioned phenomena arise from conditions, do not abide for even a moment, perish from instant to instant, and are by nature empty and quiescent.
Having known this, he desired to cause all beings to experience joy.
One should first practice the six pāramitās oneself,
and also transform sentient beings so that they practice the six pāramitās,
causing them to abandon stinginess and attachment.
If that person has nothing to give, the bodhisattva provides for them,
instructing and encouraging them to practice giving so that their hearts may rejoice;
furthermore, he consoles and instructs them by means of upholding the precepts.
In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should always diligently practice the various pāramitās, such as patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Having caused sentient beings to thus train in the bodhisattva practices,
they themselves experience joy in body and mind,
and they also cause sentient beings to experience joy in body and mind.
And that bodhisattva does not relinquish such a mind of diligent exertion until the end of life.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva...
By virtue of his great compassion and the power of his diligence,
immeasurable sentient beings aspire to follow his teachings,
each thinking to themselves: [I shall learn from him].
"When shall we attain such conduct? Viśākhā,
even the gods on high still delight in the conduct of that man."
How much more so for human beings!
Therefore, you all should diligently train in the conduct of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).

Chapter Twelve: The Collection of the Three Dharmas. At that time, the Tathāgata Emitting Light again addressed Viśākha, saying:
Vaiśākha, if you reflect upon the meaning of the three stores of karma as I have explained them.
Then one will be able to enter all dharma-gates,
Viśākha. If a person aspires to accomplish this dharma, [they shall succeed].
One should apply oneself with diligent vigor. Why is this?
For those who are indolent shall ultimately never arrive.
Why is this? Because such a person is unable to fully cherish and delight in this true Dharma;
therefore, one should rely upon a virtuous friend and diligently study with a profound mind.
Viśākhā, it is like a wondrous jewel,
such as a crystal bead or a lapis lazuli bead.
Furthermore, by placing other pure jewels at the edge of the pond water,
they cause the water to take on the same color as those jewels. Why is this?
By the power of the purity of this precious gem,
its radiance reflects afar, causing that water to follow the color of the gem;
and so it is, in every way.
Viśākhā, it is the same for all sentient beings when they associate with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Furthermore, whatever other objects are cast into that water will also take on the color of a jewel.
The majestic radiance of this jewel can transform other colors;
nothing outside of this jewel has the power to transform them. Vaiśākha.
Now, these three kinds of the treasury of skillful means and karma are likewise so:
whether one studies them oneself or teaches others to study them,
no one among gods or humans can destroy them.
Viśākhā, these three collections are the verbal teachings of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;
they comprise all utterances, speech, sounds, eloquence, and the resolution of difficult meanings through debate.
Furthermore, all parables arise from these three collections of the teachings. Viśākha,
if a person upholds the meaning of these three collections, [they shall attain liberation].
They will never be destroyed by the heterodox arguments of those outside the path.
Even if the entire Jambudvīpa were filled with immeasurable multitudes of people,
all of whom were clever heterodox masters of great treatises.
Vaiśākha, everyone came to pose various difficult questions,
yet in the end they were unable to defeat him.
Setting aside the masters of treatises who fill Jambudvīpa,
even if all the sentient beings filling these four continents were capable of engaging in debate and posing challenging questions;
Nor can it be bent.
Furthermore, Viśākhā,
setting aside the four continents.
Suppose that all sentient beings filling the trichiliocosm were each great masters of discourse,
capable of receiving and upholding all the Buddha’s scriptures as well as the texts of the non-Buddhists.
They all came at once to pose difficult questions,
yet he was able to answer them all without any impediment. Why was this?
Because within the Buddha-dharma one has previously studied these three skillful means through the scriptures,
for this reason, Viśākhā,
there are certain Dharma masters.
Whether one is a layperson or a monastic,
if they are able to receive and uphold these three Dharma-treasuries,
they will be able to answer all questions and challenges as they wish.
For what reason?
Because this Dharma is the very root of immeasurable and boundless wisdom, Viśākhā.
This Dharma is rare and inconceivable;
it is called the Sūtra Difficult for All the World to Destroy.
I have now briefly explained it, yet even you do not understand it.
How much more so, Viśākhā,
for one who has long practiced wisdom and skillful means.
One is thus able to discern this treasury of the three types of karma.
Why is this? Because the wisdom of the Buddha is profound, while the minds of the great masses of sentient beings are small and cannot contain it.
If one can understand and know such great wisdom,
then one will be able to sever the immeasurable nets of doubt of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Viśākhā:
If a person, though able to uphold these three types of teachings on the treasury of karma,
does not know the skillful means,
they will be unable to know the skillful means for entering [the path].
"How can this be explained?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Emitting Light..."
When he had spoken thus,
Viśākhā again addressed the Tathāgata Prabhāsaṃkrama, saying:
"World-Honored One,..."
Regarding these three fundamental storehouses of karma,
how are they produced, from where do they come, and to where do they go?
The Buddha said:
Viśākhā, I shall question you in return;
answer as you see fit.
Viśākha, what do you think?
From what does such an element of wind arise?
Is it large or small? Is it narrow or wide?
Is it long or short? Is it coarse or fine?
From where does it come, and to what place does it go?
Can one know their clan, family, village, hamlet, city, and country;
even down to the specific boundaries of such places of birth, their physical dimensions and proportions,
and their past and future bases of existence?
Viśākhā said, "No,
World-Honored One.
Such a wind cannot be known, because it has no location."
"He cannot be seen, because he is without marks;
even his family name, clan, and place of birth are all unknowable,
World-Honored One."
Such winds arise from space;
they have no basis for abiding and no location,
pervading all places.
In this way, Viśākhā,
wind emerges from space without a specific location;
its family lineage, place of birth, and true origin are actually unknowable.
It is so, it is so. The skillful means of the teachings on the treasury of the three types of karma are likewise thus:
they have no location and come from nowhere.
Furthermore, it neither goes anywhere, nor arises, nor ceases.
Why is this? Because the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable and can be known only by the wisdom of a Buddha.
Māṇava, this treasury of the three types of karma is truly unknowable;
there is ultimately no one who can reach its limits or determine its measure.
Whether for one kalpa or less than a kalpa;
whether for a hundred kalpas or a hundred thousand kalpas;
or even for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.
Even throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable eons,
they cannot be known; only the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, is able to know these three kinds of karmic treasuries.
I have spoken according to their respective faculties and dispositions.
Māṇava, for this reason, you all should know this.
These three types of verbal teachings have no place of abiding and no limit. Why is this?
Because the Bodhi of all Buddhas has no place of abiding and no point of reliance.
Even the essential nature of the causes and conditions of karmic actions comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
If one can know this, [one attains liberation].
He immediately knew that the treasury of karma has no place of abiding and is immeasurable and boundless.
At that time, the brahmin Viśākha again addressed the Buddha Emitting Light, saying:
"World-Honored One..."
"What is the condition of karma?
The Buddha said to Viśākhā:
'What do you think?'"
"What is it called when one first enters the womb?
Vaiśākha replied, "World-Honored One," [and continued:
"World-Honored One."
This is called the water element named *kāra-lā*.
The Buddha said:
What is this *kalala* called after the first seven days have passed?
It is called the *arbuda*.
The Buddha asked again:
After seven days have passed in that Arbuda hell, what is it called next?
It is called Nirarbuda.
The Buddha asked again:
After seven days have passed, what is this *peḷāsi* called?
It is called a *gaṇa*.
The Buddha asked again:
"World-Honored One, after this *kalala* has passed seven days, what is it called next?
"It is called the *arbuda*."
After the stages of Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava,
and so forth have passed,
it is called "reception" (vedanā).
The Buddha said,
"Viśākhā, you should know that this sensation is fundamentally without reality and exists only as a false illusion."
It arises through the combination of false causes and conditions; because of this,
all the limbs and members of the body are produced.
That is to say, because the five blisters arise, the skin and flesh arise;
because the skin and flesh arise, the tendons and bones arise;
because the tendons and bones arise, the marrow and brain arise.
Because the marrow and brain arise, the hair of the head and body arises.
Because the hair of the head and body arises, the nails and teeth arise.
Because the nails and teeth arise, all the limbs, members, and joints of the body arise.
In this way, all the limbs, members,
and joints of the body come from nowhere and have no place of abiding;
they exist entirely through the combination of causes and conditions.
Thus, these five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements—
their characteristics, forms, colors, sizes,
and dimensions— all likewise come from nowhere and have no place of abiding.
If that were truly existent, there would have to be going and coming;
yet, in all such cases, there is no place of abiding and nothing can be known.
Since it has no name, it does not exist.
How can it be explained, Viśākhā?
It is through the conjunction of the causes and conditions of the father and mother.
At that time, the link of consciousness (vijñāna) enters the womb and develops into the kalala stage.
Regarding that which is called a "womb," Vasiṣṭha, it is like this:
when those parents are not in union, [the embryo does not form].
In this case, there would be no kalala,
nor even skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, or any of the constituent parts of the body.

How could there be physical form, shape, length, shortness, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, dwelling places, and coming and going?
Furthermore, if this consciousness did not unite with even a single drop of seminal essence within the womb, [how could these things exist]?
Furthermore, entities such as shape and color cannot be established.
Moreover, if one does not harmonize with the twelve links of dependent origination,
even old age and death cannot arise.
If there were no arising or ceasing, how could there be names or descriptions?
Thus it is, Viśākhā.
It is solely by the power of the continuous succession of the twelve links of dependent origination that form,
sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise in combination.
Thus it is, Viśākhā.
These three kinds of verbal teachings, skillful means,
and the treasury of karma have no location and no limits;
they neither come nor go.
You should know that this dharma is without arising and without cessation;
it has no root and is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, Viśākhā:
One should know that these are the three kinds of treasuries of the skillful means of verbal instruction.
What are the names of these three treasuries?
The first is the treasury of human verbal instruction.
Second is the treasury of the teachings spoken by devas;
third is the treasury of the teachings spoken by those who are neither humans nor devas, O Brahmin.
Regarding what is called "human verbal instruction":
all of these, by way of the characteristic of speech,
should be known as human verbal instruction.
Viśākhā, that which is called the teaching of the devas involves seeing and hearing because their modes of activity differ.
Having understood through such contemplative skillful means that one generates such a mind exactly as it is and not otherwise,
one is able to attain meditative concentration, the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of the minds of others.
All this arises from the power of collecting the mind through single-minded mindfulness;
thus, such pure wisdom is produced.
This is called the supreme, pure teaching of the celestial deities.
Vaiśākha, that which is called the "Teaching-Treasury of neither humans nor devas" refers to the threefold teaching born of great compassion and encompassing all beings.
It gives rise to the paths of the three vehicles and all dharmas;
therefore, it is called a "treasury" (garbha).
This teaching is a skillful means based on the fruit of great compassion.
He contemplates all places throughout the realms of evil destinies,
seeing that all sentient beings there possess nothing but manifold sufferings;
with single-minded resolve, he seeks to rescue them, free from any other thought.
Therefore, it is called "Great Compassion.
Because it benefits others,
it is called "instruction."
Viśākhā, these dwelling places born from the treasury of the three karmas are constantly and single-mindedly contemplated by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as their protection and sustenance.
13. Chapter on the Characteristics of the Dharma Master. *Mahādharmolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, Chapter Thirteen: "Characteristics of the Dharma Master.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, there is yet another power of empowerment that arises from constant diligence.
What is meant by the diligence born from the cause of the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-bala*)?
If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who wish to attain the eloquence (*pratibhāna*) of the Tathāgata in its full perfection:
All this is brought about by a diligent mind and ardent exertion;
thus, in a single moment, one can expound hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sūtra passages and verses without end.
Why is this? Because they have skillfully accomplished verbal karma,
they obtain unimpeded eloquence through the power of empowerment.
Because of this eloquence, in all questions and answers,
one is inexhaustible and never interrupted,
like a steep cliff from which a torrential stream rushes downward.
Although one may wish to stop it, it can never be brought to an end.
When that stream flows downward, even a small amount of water is difficult to block;
how much more so, then, a great river?
In this way, Viśākhā,
if there is a Dharma teacher who [is proficient] in these three types of scriptural collections of verbal instruction,
One should cultivate eloquence for even a single day,
whether by hearing, reciting,
or reflecting upon it.
Because of that diligence, he expounds the teaching as appropriate without ceasing;
how then could any other challenges or difficulties ever obstruct him?
Viśākhā, it is impossible that a spring’s flow should enter a river but not reach the ocean.
If a person has long cultivated diligence,
it is impossible for them to become weary or abandon this dhāraṇī.
I have now spoken but a little,
like taking a single minute drop from the great ocean;
how could it possibly diminish it?
I now proclaim this dharma-gate of the great dhāraṇī of diligence and eloquence;
even a small portion of it shall not diminish. Thus, Viśākha.
You should know that you have attained the eloquence of those three treasuries of karma,
which can illuminate the very foundations of all dharmas and is inexhaustible in response to all challenges and inquiries.
Why is this? Because this Dharma-gate is boundless.
Furthermore, Viśākhā:
Those who have attained this treasury of eloquence through the empowerment of such diligence,
when faced with difficult questioning or the insults of others,
should give rise to joy and cultivate a mind of great compassion.
One does not see insults nor observe self and other;
there is no sense of "mine" and no fear. Why is this?
Vaiśākha, because all internal and external fears and evils have been entirely extinguished and non-existent,
this is the accomplishment of the oral karma of a Dharma teacher.
Furthermore, Viśākhā,
if a Dharma teacher is seated on a throne preaching the Dharma,
there may be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās [who approach].
Surrounded by the fourfold assembly—
some of whom had studied for a long time and some who had only recently heard the teaching.
Whether they possess faith or lack it,
among those sentient beings, if they behold a woman of upright and beautiful appearance,
they may give rise to a mind of defiled attachment and lose their mindfulness of the Dharma.
At that time, the Dharma teacher should skillfully observe and,
through skillful means, subdue that person,
clearly demonstrating the characteristics of their transgressions so that they may attain awakening.
Give rise to a sense of shame and remorse within yourself so as not to cause him anger. Why is this?
If he gives way to resentment, he will give rise to unwholesome states of mind.
Such a person may at times insult and humiliate the Dharma Master,
slander the scriptures, and obstruct the Buddha-dharma;
thus their transgressions and afflictions will increase further.
Therefore, Viśākhā,
if any Dharma masters wish to perform acts of reprimand and subjugation,
they should first eliminate desire, hatred, delusion, and pride within themselves.
Only then does one instruct and reprove others so that they may eliminate and sever [the afflictions].
It is impossible for one who has not severed them themselves to cause others to eliminate them.
Therefore, a Dharma Master must first practice it himself and only then guide others.
He should not first seize upon the faults of others while neglecting his own virtues. Why is this?
Viśākhā, all sentient beings have deep and thick bonds of desire;
when objects of greed appear before them, they disregard their own selves.
If one abandons skillful means and first resorts to reprimand,
it only increases the defilement of anger, like fire consuming fuel;
when hatred is intense, delusion increases all the more.
The afflictions of the three poisons arise simultaneously;
yet when these three poisons erupt intensely within sentient beings,
they do not hear external words, do not remember their own affairs, and remain entirely ignorant of both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Even if they should hear it for a moment, they are unable to receive it,
Viśākhā; for when those sentient beings are possessed by the three poisons, [they cannot understand].
It is like a blind person who cannot distinguish whether a road is level or rugged;
it is like a deaf person who cannot hear whether a sound is coarse or subtle;
and it is like a drunken person who cannot discern the directions of east, west, south, and north.

Just as one possessed by a ghost does not find peace in their place and speaks wildly and recklessly, so too it is with all sentient beings whose hearts are scorched by the fire of poison; they likewise remain unaware of good and evil.
Viśākhā, when the afflictions of sentient beings are thus rampant,
the Dharma master should preach for them the remedial methods, such as the contemplation of impurity.
May they swiftly attain untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and burn away the fetters of the three poisons within those sentient beings. Thus, Viśākha.
This is one who is a Dharma teacher of great wisdom and eloquence,
capable of skillfully guiding the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
and upāsikās, causing them all to rejoice.
It extinguishes the diseases of affliction of those sentient beings.
Furthermore, Viśākhā, when any Dharma masters wish to preach the Dharma,
they should first observe the faculties and dispositions of the assembly.
Thereafter, one should preach according to what is required.
If one knows that sentient beings will derive benefit from hearing about generosity,
the Dharma-preacher should first speak on generosity to cause them to rejoice.
One should know that at such a time, one ought not to further expound other dharma-gates.
Alternatively, if there are those who desire to uphold the precepts,
the Dharma Master should then expound the precepts for them.
Nor should one preach other profound dharmas to them.
Such sentient beings may at times delight in practicing patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Up to the point where they desire to hear various Dharma gates,
he explains them all for them so that they may quickly attain understanding, Viśākhā.
In this way, the Dharma-preacher should apply themselves with diligent vigor and skillful means to preach the Dharma. Why is this?
For if one wishes to attain Buddhahood, it is essential to do so throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas.
One should practice with courageous diligence and exert oneself in asceticism, even to the point of sacrificing one's body, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and brain,
as described in other sūtras. Furthermore,
Dharma masters should not engage in contentious debate.
Now, contentious debate is the very root of ignorance and affliction; therefore,
the Dharma Master should apply himself with diligent vigor.
One should swiftly extinguish ignorance and also exhort others to abandon it. Viśākhā,
these Dharma masters must first be fully endowed with the aforementioned virtues.
Thereafter, he teaches by means of various skillful methods for the sake of the assembly. Viśākhā,
the Dharma teacher should always reflect in this manner.
The place where I now sit is precisely the Tathāgata’s lion throne;
you should remain patient and silent— why do you suddenly give rise to anger?
"Following whatever questions and difficulties those sentient beings may raise,
I shall explain them all so that they may be filled with joy.
Having formed this thought, [he proceeded].
All contentious debates and the minds of "self" and "other" will naturally be extinguished.
Furthermore, Viśākhā,
as for the Dharma master:
One should always maintain compassion, speak with kindness, and remain humble to protect the minds of the assembly.
Why is this? For if one harbors anger or envy and dwells on thoughts of victory and defeat, one will incur a grave and heavy offense.
Preaching the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness accomplishes great merit;
it enables the Buddha-dharma to abide long in the world.
In whatever place one is born, [one shall...]
They shall constantly encounter all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of holy sages,
and be able to receive and purify the various offerings of the world,
even when provided with a lofty and grand lion throne of jewels.
Furthermore, even if one were to present tens of millions of priceless, renowned robes to the Dharma Master,
how could one ever repay that Dharma Master’s kindness and virtue?
Although the Dharma Master accepts these things, he should feel deep shame and remorse, and must not give rise to a mind of greed.
One should give rise to compassion and must not harbor arrogance;
one must not allow the roots of goodness of the donors to be extinguished,
but should cause all sentient beings to attain joy.
Furthermore, Viśākha,

Chapter Seventeen: The Accomplishment of Patience; Chapter Eighteen: Realizing Nirvāṇa. Chapter Sixteen: The Accomplishment of Wisdom. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
At that time, there was among that assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Candana,

it gives rise to neither attachment nor doubt.

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhāsa-garbha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candana, saying:
Excellent, excellent,
Candana! It is so, it is so.
Candana, it is not only you who do not give rise to doubt regarding this Dharma;
indeed, within this Dharma there is nothing to be doubted.
Candana, you should know that within this Dharma there is no such thing as an external phenomenon.
This dharma is likewise not found within those external dharmas.
I shall now explain it;
listen with a sincere mind.
If Dharma masters attain the meaning of these three kinds of karmic treasuries,
they will be able to understand the various distinctions among the minds of all sentient beings,
and they will also be able to understand the differences between the wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions of sentient beings.
However, when that Dharma master wishes to preach the Dharma,

and only then preach for them.
Candana, you should know that there are some bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess the power of supernatural faculties but lack the power of wisdom.
There are those who possess the power of wisdom but lack the power of supernormal faculties;
there are those who have attained both the power of supernormal faculties and the power of wisdom;
and there are those who have attained the power of supernormal faculties but lack the power of wisdom.
Furthermore, those who possess wisdom but lack the power of supernormal faculties (abhijñā) will not swiftly emerge from birth and death. However,
if they attain both supernormal faculties and the power of wisdom, [they shall do so].
At a later time, he will be able to bear a heavy burden,
O Māṇava; for he is one capable of bearing a great and heavy burden.
