they too come to listen to the Dharma, Candanana.
When such a great assembly has gathered,
that bodhisattva-mahāsattva,
within these three gateways to the treasury of karma—
One should understand the various causes and conditions, the various sentient beings, the various mental activities, the various karmic actions, and the various modes of body, speech, and mind.
If that Dharma master understands these three types of gateways to the treasury of skillful means, [he shall attain mastery].
He immediately knows the mental activities and inclinations of sentient beings;
knowing that those sentient beings have various doubts and various questions,
he is able to answer them in various ways.
If he does not ask,
the Dharma Master should immediately know whether his mind is one of faith or lack of faith.
From the initial thought up to the many thoughts,
the Dharma Master should fully understand them in their proper sequence.
Having understood them, he should resolve them so as not to allow for dispute or contention.
The Dharma Master should thus preach to sentient beings, either in brief or in detail, as appropriate to their needs.
First, the Dharma Master must personally cultivate the power of wisdom and the power of diligence.
When training for oneself,
one should remain mindful of abandoning sleep and indolence.
Having trained in this way, [one should proceed].
He causes those countless hundreds of thousands of millions of devas and humans to be humbled by his intelligence and majestic power,
and only then does he preach for them.
Furthermore, māṇavas,
once you have accomplished the power of wisdom and the power of diligence,
you should further train in the mind of great diligence.
For what reason?
If one cannot cause the minds of human beings to submit,
how could one transform the various devas of the desire and form realms?
Māṇavas, you should simply reflect for yourselves;
do not say that the Tathāgata gives rise to stinginess regarding all dharmas.
Furthermore, do not think that I harbor a mind of contempt toward sentient beings.
Even the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not deceive or treat with arrogance those in the animal realm,
let alone a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
It is for the sake of sentient beings that the Tathāgata appears in the world,
whether for the duration of one kalpa, less than one kalpa,
or for immeasurable kalpas.
He was born among them for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas. O māṇava,
if there were currently any bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who delighted in hearing the true Dharma, yet the Tathāgata were to be parsimonious and not preach it to them, [he would have been born here].
That is impossible.
Listen attentively;
I shall provide an analogy.
Māṇava, it is as if there were an elder who had an only son;
his family was abundant in wealth, treasures, and various servants.
Then those parents strictly commanded their household members to attend upon and guard them so as not to allow them to be harmed,
ensuring they were free from all illness and suffering, and neither cold nor heat, hunger nor thirst.
May they be kept far away from all hardships such as water and fire, and from all unfavorable circumstances;
may they also be provided with every kind of medicine, food, drink, clothing, dwellings, and bedding.
There was no lack of any necessary provision;
for the sake of this child, a wet nurse was provided,
and superior delicacies and fine flavors were always abundant.
In this way, Māṇava, the Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha acts as the father of the Bodhisattva,
constantly instructing the Bodhisattva to practice the six pāramitās.
One should nurture, protect, and guard the bodhicitta so that it does not decline or perish. Why is this?
In order to increase the bodhicitta,
one causes the mind to be free from stinginess, anger, and indolence,
and so forth, until the mind no longer regresses or deteriorates.
Why is this? Because they do not regress,
they will swiftly achieve the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, the Tathāgata constantly instructs bodhisattvas;
he is the father of bodhisattvas and is also called their guide.
Because they are able to never retreat from the path to enlightenment,
they are called "Guiding Teachers.
Furthermore, because they do not sever the path to enlightenment.
He was also named the Guide.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candana..."
Having heard what the Buddha had said, he immediately questioned that Radiant Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
within this assembly of immeasurable billions, [who is it?]"
"Is there any bodhisattva who has attained this Dharma?
The Buddha said, "Candana."
For what reason do you now harbor such profound anxiety?
Because the assembly of bodhisattvas has questioned the Tathāgata repeatedly regarding these bodhisattvas who all dwell within the profound and secret Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Their faith is as firm and solid as a vajra.
How can one say that this assembly of bodhisattvas has not attained such a profound Dharma?
Candana spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
among this assembly of billions of bodhisattvas, is there such a dharma as that which the Buddha has spoken?
The Buddha said:
Māṇava, do you yourself harbor such doubts in your own mind that you ask me this: "Do these bodhisattvas possess such qualities? Māṇava?
"You possess a sincere heart toward the Tathāgata;
why then do you pose such a question:
'Is there this Dharma within this great assembly or not?'"
Because you have doubts, I shall now further provide an analogy.
For example, there was a great minister of King Jyotiṣprabha who,
in the midst of a great assembly, spoke these words:
I now know with certainty that this King Jyotiṣpāla was able to practice giving, even to the point of relinquishing his own cherished body and life;
subsequently, this person [will appear] amidst the great assembly.
Again he spoke these words:
"This King Jyotiṣpāla is so greedy and stingy in his accumulation that he cannot give away even the smallest portion, O māṇava."
You are just like this: at first you said,
"I believe the Tathāgata, the Arhat,
the Samyaksaṃbuddha," but now you cannot believe the Dharma I have taught, nor do you rejoice in it or practice accordingly.
Thus, his previous words were inconsistent with his own actions;
he merely asked me repeatedly about the three baskets of the teachings,
yet he did not understand my intellectual power, my diligence, or any of my various accomplishments.
Māṇava, there are those who,
upon hearing the exposition of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and unimpeded eloquence,
are immediately able to believe and understand them.
Other sentient beings, being of little learning and meager wisdom, are unable to inquire about such matters;
thus, these sentient beings are difficult to conceive of and difficult to enter.
Yet, if they are able to have faith and understanding, and to contemplate and discern the various powers, fearlessnesses, and eloquence of the Tathāgata—
This is impossible.
Why is that? O Māṇava.
This karma is difficult to enter;
one must practice the various pāramitās and so forth for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas before one can then believe and understand such powers and fearlessnesses.
Māṇava, if there are sentient beings who do not give rise to faith upon hearing the aforementioned accounts of various meritorious deeds,
I shall likewise constantly teach them how to gather themselves in and never abandon them.
Therefore, you all should constantly practice and study this.

Chapter Seventeen: The Accomplishment of Patience. From the *Mahādharanī-dharmolkā-sūtra*, Chapter Seventeen: The Accomplishment of Patience. At that time, the Bodhisattva Candana again addressed the Buddha Emitting Light, saying:
"Bhagavān,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplish the power of patience?
How does he train in performing deeds for the benefit of all sentient beings, like a Buddha-Tathāgata?"
Abiding in his own patience, he was unshakable amidst all the hundreds of thousands of difficult questions posed by those heterodox teachers and their assemblies.
The Buddha said, "Māṇava,"
You ask about the power of patience.
There are many kinds of the power of patience;
which power of patience do you ask me about?
That is to say, there is the patience of the Tathāgatas,
the patience of the Bodhisattvas,
and the patience of the Arhats.
There is the patience of an anāgāmin;
there is the patience of a sakṛdāgāmin;
there is the patience of a srotāpanna.
There is the stage of patience of the eight persons;
there is the patience of those who practice by way of faith;
and there is also the patience of the non-Buddhist seers possessing the five supernatural powers.
Māṇava, there are now such various gateways of patience as these;
among them, which patience do you inquire about?
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candana said,
“World-Honored One,
I shall inquire herein concerning the patience of a bodhisattva.”
"Bhagavān,
what kind of patience must a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain in order to be able to fulfill all the Buddha-dharmas?"
Is it not because the Bodhisattva’s power of patience,
having relied upon the Tathāgata’s great power of patience,
is able to fully realize all Buddha-dharmas?
The Buddha said, "Māṇava,
it is indeed by relying on the Tathāgata’s power of patience that one accomplishes the Buddha-dharma."
Nevertheless, Māṇava, one does not thereby accomplish all the Buddha-dharmas.
Listen attentively to what that patience accomplishes.
I shall now speak.
Māṇava, you should know that all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are fully endowed with the power of patience.
There are four kinds of impartial mind.
What are the four?
They are as follows: the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
If a mind of anger arises, one should become aware of it immediately;
having become aware of it, one is then able to apply the antidote and sever it. O Māṇava!
You should know that this constitutes the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s complete accomplishment of the foremost power of patience.
Furthermore, Māṇava,
if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is subjected by others to harsh speech, verbal abuse, slander, or humiliation, [he remains patient].
Whether with their own hands or bodies they are struck or beaten,
they are able to endure all manner of intolerable sufferings without any thought of retaliation.
Nor does he harbor any resentment. O Māṇava,
you should know that this constitutes the second power of patience fully accomplished by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Māṇava,
if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees immeasurable sentient beings who commit evil,
constantly practicing unwholesome deeds and ignorant of kindness and virtue.
They are unfilial toward their parents and do not love their kinsmen;
they are not compliant with their teachers and elders, nor do they respect śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
they distance themselves from virtuous friends and lack faith.
Although a bodhisattva sees such evil beings as these,
their mind is free from resentment and they do not seek out their faults; rather,
they constantly instruct and guide them so that they may dwell securely in wholesome dharmas.
Māṇava, you should know that this constitutes the third power of patience fully accomplished by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Māṇava:
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees sentient beings who do not believe in cause and effect, who are greedily attached to present pleasures,
whose natures are prone to anger, resentment, and strife,
and who delight in seeking out the faults of others.
Those who hold wrong views and are deluded, having turned their backs on the True Dharma,
should be met with compassion and guided toward joy;
thereafter, they should be established within the True Dharma.
Māṇava, you should know that this constitutes the fourth power of patience fully accomplished by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
You all should understand this.
If bodhisattvas dwell within this patience and practice in accordance with the Dharma,
they will further be able to give rise to the power of superior patience;
moreover, patience and the Dharma will always be naturally conjoined.
If one does not study the Dharma, one will be unable to practice patience.
Those who wish to abide in patience should apply themselves diligently to study.
Furthermore, māṇava:
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas achieve patience,
they will certainly attain various kinds of functional powers.
At times, they may even be oppressed by their bodies with various forms of suffering.
That is to say, regarding abusive speech, insults, imprisonment, flogging,
and the most unbearable, agonizing torments— within these,
the Bodhisattva gives rise to no thoughts of resentment and ultimately feels no fear.
Nor does one flee from it, but instead accepts it with a willing mind.
When patience is fully perfected,
one naturally attains eight kinds of superior and excellent meritorious qualities.
What are these eight? They are as follows:
once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has accomplished patience, in whatever place they are born and throughout all their physical experiences, [they encounter no harm].
Possessing great renown, they are loved and revered by all;
their praises spread far and wide, and they encounter spiritual friends.
Their companions, relatives, and kinsmen are all noble, eminent, and superior figures within the world.
Even all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas,
upon seeing this bodhisattva, gave rise to a sense of wonder and felt joy,
love, and delight, O māṇava.
This is the first supreme and superior meritorious deed of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in patience.
Furthermore, Māṇava,
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly practices acts of kindness and virtue toward all sentient beings.
Sometimes there are those who have been favored by a bodhisattva’s virtue,
yet because they do not recognize that kindness, they instead become his enemies;
they take no pleasure in hearing of or seeing the deeds performed by the bodhisattva.
Out of jealousy and malice toward the Bodhisattva’s superior power, great kindness, and various meritorious deeds,
they seek to harm him by means of all kinds of incantations, sorcery, malevolent spirits, poisons, and weapons.
Various evil deeds were plotted to slander and harm him;
yet because the Bodhisattva possessed this power of patience, he was ultimately never harmed. O Māṇava!
This is the second superior and excellent quality of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with patience.
Furthermore, māṇava,
once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has become endowed with this patience,
They will immediately attain immeasurable wisdom and eloquence,
becoming skillful in proclaiming various Dharma gates. Why is this?
When a bodhisattva has thus attained abiding in patience,
all sentient beings who engage in wholesome conduct in the world take the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, as their teacher.
Whether they be those training as arhats or other śrāvakas,
or those training as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—
such bodhisattvas, desiring to grasp great enlightenment, all go to where they are.
Having thus inquired about the meaning of this sūtra,
there further follows within this dhāraṇī, in its eighteenth section, the uninterrupted sequence of events concerning the celestial palaces.
One can enter that sūtra sequentially;
this is the sixth kind of analytical cultivation, which,
as explained above, is fully and definitively understood.
In this way, the bodhisattva is further able to clearly explain for others these three kinds of karmic treasuries of the dharani-gate,
and is also able to provide detailed explanations of their seventy-two varieties of phrasal gateways.
Māṇava, this is the third superior and excellent quality of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is endowed with patience.
Furthermore, Māṇava:
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having been endowed with this patience,
dwells in a great assembly and recites or expounds the sūtras,
if their mind becomes distracted.
Or, while distracted by other matters,
one may at times forget the methods, phrases, and sentences of the immeasurable teachings one has recited and mastered.
At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens descended to bestow upon the Bodhisattva what he had forgotten,
causing him to be without fear before that great assembly and to increase his eloquence.
That which was previously forgotten or erroneous becomes clearly manifest without omission. Māṇava,
this is the fourth superior merit and excellence of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is endowed with patience.
Furthermore, māṇava,
once the bodhisattva mahāsattva is established in patience,
he feels compassion for all sentient beings.
Their bodies constantly undergo immeasurable sufferings,
namely the heavy sufferings of the three evil realms— those of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts— and even further,
they undergo various kinds of human sufferings, sorrows, and lamentations.
By the power of patience, that bodhisattva has no fear within the cycle of birth and death, nor does he ever turn back to seek rest;
whatever they wish for or seek, they obtain according to their will.
Māṇava, this is the fifth superior and excellent quality of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with patience.
Furthermore, Māṇava:
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with this patience,
by the power of that patience, although they dwell within the sufferings of the three evil realms— the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts—
they do not give rise to alarm or fear.
They are not terrified by the eight difficult conditions,
nor do they feel anxiety or fear regarding the long suffering of birth and death;
for that bodhisattva, by virtue of the power of patience, [remains undaunted].
Even if a great mass of fire were to fill the entirety of space and one were situated within it, there would be no fear or terror;
nor would there ever be any occurrence of falling back or perishing. Why is this?
Because when this bodhisattva dwells securely in patience, he perceives neither his own body nor any place of abiding;
therefore, there is nothing to be feared, O māṇava.
This is the sixth superior and supreme meritorious quality of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with patience.
Furthermore, māṇava,
once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished patience,
Delighting in meritorious deeds, he constantly practices giving.
At the time of giving, he first relinquishes his bed and seat;
therefore, in all places where he is born in the future, [he shall possess such things].
They will always be born into the most eminent clans, great families, and positions of high honor.
Upon being born, they will immediately obtain four kinds of merit.
What are these four?
First, regarding food, drink, and material goods—
namely, grain, rice, utensils, and even clothing and precious jewels—
they lack nothing whatsoever.
Second, there are kinsmen and associates—
namely parents, down to slaves and servants—
who lack for nothing.
Third is the establishment of unhindered eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*).
This means that in whatever place one is born, body and mind are joyful and blissful,
and there is never any occurrence of opposition, oppression, or discomfort.
In all births, one constantly attains uninterrupted continuity of eloquence;
wherever one goes, one benefits sentient beings primarily through eloquent and wondrous speech.
Fourth, in whatever birth one takes, one is loved and respected by others.
That is to say, wherever they are born, their physical forms are upright and majestic;
among humans and devas, there are none who do not rejoice upon seeing or hearing them.
Although they have not yet left the household life, they will inevitably bring about great benefit for sentient beings.
He is always respected by sentient beings. Māṇava,
this is the seventh superior and excellent quality of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses patience.
Once the bodhisattva is endowed with these seven merits,
there will be no obstacles in the places where they practice—
whether it be among humans, devas, Brahmās, or Māras.
Even gods and ghosts cannot obstruct him.
Furthermore, O māṇava,
once a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with patience, [he attains this].
When they leave the household life,
they are able to renounce everything they possess:
their wives, children, family members, wealth, and precious treasures.
By the power of patience, they are no longer subject to defilement or attachment;
thus, other afflictions cannot obstruct them.
In this way, the bodhisattva becomes free from obstruction in all circumstances.
If one wishes to accomplish the Śrāvaka-yāna,
one will be able to realize and attain the fruit of Arhatship,
as well as meditative concentration, liberation, and unimpeded eloquence.
If one wishes to accomplish the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas,
whether during the lifetime of a Buddha or in a world without a Buddha after the True Dharma has vanished,
one attains the state of a Pratyekabuddha by contemplating causes and conditions.
If one wishes to accomplish the supreme vehicle— the complete and perfect fulfillment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) practiced by all Buddhas—
one will be able to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment (anuttara-bodhi).
Māṇava, this is the eighth superior and excellent meritorious quality of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is endowed with patience.
Chapter 18: Realizing Nirvāṇa. *Mahādharmolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, Chapter 18 on Realizing Nirvāṇa, Part One. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candana addressed the Tathāgata Emitting Light, saying:
"World-Honored One."
The Tathāgata has already explained the seventh method of contemplation regarding the meaning of this dhāraṇī sūtra; however,
since he has not yet explained the specific meaning of a single phrase within this dharma-gate, we are unable to fully comprehend it.
"Bhagavān,
you previously spoke of a dharma-gate called 'Entry into the Hundred Million.
It is regarding this dharma-gate that I now wish to ask a question."
If the Buddha, the Tathāgata, has silently granted his consent,
why does he not proclaim this wondrous Dharma-door of the treasury of skillful means and karmic activities consisting of these three types of verbal instruction?
World-Honored One!
Therefore, we wish to inquire about this seventh dharma-gate, the entrance into the number of billions.
If the Buddha would explain it,
it will enable this assembly of billions of bodhisattvas to discern and enter the profound state of fearlessness.
World-Honored One,
you should also, through skillful means, for the sake of the future benefit of these billions of bodhisattvas,
expound this seventh gateway of phrases in hundreds of thousands of billions of instances.
May we be led to enter sequentially into the stage of contemplating the meaning.
World-Honored One,
if you would deign to expound it for us.
"We, too, shall uphold the meaning of this Dharma-gate according to our respective capacities.
Ānanda, at that time,
the Tathāgata Emitting Light praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candana, saying:
Excellent, excellent,
māṇava! You now [inquire] regarding this profound dharma-gate.
He skillfully composes names;
likewise, he is well-versed in upholding the treasury of the meaning of verbal teachings. O Māṇava!
"O Māṇava, it is for the sake of these hundreds of millions of bodhisattvas that you now ask me about this matter."
"Do you now wish to hear the dharma-gate of entering into billions of methods?
The Bodhisattva Candana replied,
"So be it, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said, "Māṇava,
if a Buddha-Tathāgata were to speak of the meaning of this seventh contemplative phrase,
he would already encompass these billions of dharma-gates."
Māṇava, the Tathāgata,
the World-Honored One, through these three kinds of skillful means and verbal teachings,
reveals, elucidates, and proclaims them so as to bring joy to the multitude.
Thereupon, he knew that these hundreds of millions of dharma-gates could be entered in successive order.
At that time, Candana again asked the World-Honored One:
"How does one enter these hundreds of millions of dharma-gates?"
For what reason is it further called the "Dharma-gate of the Number of Billions"?
Furthermore, World-Honored One, I must know the point of entry.
I now ask about the destination into which these billions of dharma-gates enter;
I also wish to realize and know it.
If it can be awakened to and known, I shall certainly uphold it.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, I wish to further increase these billions of gateways for entry. As I understand it,
World-Honored One,
this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate.
For the sake of accomplishing the meaning of the retinue of patience,
World-Honored One,
I truly do not see a single bodhisattva within this great assembly who has not accomplished this profound gate of patience.
"World-Honored One,
it is because I have seen this matter that I ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about such a point of meaning.
World-Honored One," [he said].

Such a subject of meaning cannot truly be questioned by those who are indolent, lazy, attached to gain and offerings, lacking right mindfulness, delighting in excessive sleep, whose minds are constantly distracted, and who are addicted to the flavors of worldly affairs.
They, too, will be unable to hear, recite, receive, uphold, or contemplate it;
they will not even be able to practice and realize it according to the teaching, Ānanda.
When Candana had thus made his request,
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhāsa addressed Candana, saying: "Māṇava."
Therefore, you should now enter this dharma-gate of hundreds of millions.
Mindfully uphold it yourselves, and with a single mind, do not attend to other matters;
let your minds be undistracted and your bodies unmoving.
"You, Māṇava, should furthermore uphold this Dharma and Vinaya to eradicate the root of disputes.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha..."
In the past, while practicing the bodhisattva path through the long night of saṃsāra,
he underwent all manner of hardships and diligent sufferings for the sake of sentient beings;
when undergoing those sufferings, [he remained steadfast].
You should know that he has long since dwelt in the stage of patience;
therefore, O māṇava, he is courageous, diligent, and untiring.
If a person enters this Dharma-gate of the limit of exhaustion,
they should constantly and diligently study within it until the meaning of these words is fully exhausted.
Having accomplished the power of patience and being fully endowed with diligence,
one must never abandon this dharma-gate;
it is essential to first settle the mind before realizing and knowing it.
Candana spoke again:
"World-Honored One,
what is called the Tathāgata’s single-phrase Dharma-gate within this?"
We shall receive and uphold it.
Having upheld it, we wish to analyze its meaning among the teachings numbering in the hundreds of millions found within the sūtras,
World-Honored One.
We wish to hear this meaning from the Buddha:
by what skillful means does he teach the most supreme Dharma?
We shall enter therein.
Or perhaps one can discern all phenomena?
The Buddha said, "Māṇava."
You should realize these two meanings;
furthermore, you shall enter sequentially into the dharmas numbering in the hundreds of millions,
as well as the abodes of the phrases and meanings of the gateway to the ultimate limit.
If one can thus possess such discernment,
then those who have accomplished these merits and maintain pure precepts will be able to enter all those gates.
One should know the points of entry;
even down to each and every pore,
there is no obstruction whatsoever.
One should form this thought:
"I shall exhaust my eloquence to proclaim the Dharma in accordance with the truth.
How does one form this thought?
That is to say, he gives rise to a sense of self-respect and establishes a mind of majestic power,
surpassing the entire assembly of devas and humans,
like a lion king endowed with great sovereignty.
It is capable of subduing all wild beasts,
namely tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, and even the species of wild dogs, foxes, and polecats;
the Dharma Master is likewise so.
When preaching the Dharma, one should give rise to this thought:
"I shall always act as a guide for all sentient beings,
even against all celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, and various heterodox teachers."
I shall discipline and guide them all,
just as a lion subdues the jackals with its majesty;
having first aroused this resolve, I shall then preach the Dharma for them.
Furthermore, Māṇava,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits at the seat of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree,
by the power of his vow and wisdom, he presses the earth with his right palm.
He emitted a vast net of great light rays, numbering in the hundreds of millions,
which shone everywhere throughout the Buddha-worlds of the lower direction.
Among the sentient beings in those worlds, all who were capable of receiving the Dharma [were illuminated].
Having encountered this light, they are naturally able to awaken to and realize the Dharma.
Furthermore, wherever this light reaches throughout all worlds,
there are many immeasurable and diverse assemblies therein.
That is to say: whether it be the assembly of śramaṇas,
the assembly of brāhmaṇas,
or the assembly of followers of external paths.
Whether it be the host of celestial Māras or those emanated by Māra,
whether they question or answer.
Whether through exhortation or entreaty,
it was all due to the power of the Bodhisattva’s past original vows, his great oaths, his adornment of diligence, and his vigor; thus,
when he pressed the earth with his hand.
All that those multitudes had done was utterly dissipated and extinguished;
even if anything remained, it possessed no further majesty or splendor,
and they were unable to speak again, like those who are deaf and mute.
Māṇava, just as that Bodhisattva causes a net of light to emerge from every place where his hand touches the ground.
Thereupon, immeasurable billions of Dharma gates were manifested.
This constitutes the initial entry into the Dharma gate of the ultimate limit of exhaustion, complete and without deficiency.
I have now finished speaking.
Furthermore, māṇavas,
if you wish to enter this gate of the most pure limit of exhaustion,
it is called the "Ten Million Entrances" and it is also called the "Hundred Million Entrances."
One must first purify the profound mind,
contemplate and investigate to sever all webs of doubt,
and produce sublime sounds to achieve eloquence.
Only then can one enter. Māṇava,

one realizes and knows them in successive order;
it is likewise so, O Māṇava.
You should understand it in this way: how so?
Just as there is nothing whatsoever in any place.
It should be understood in this way, O māṇava:
all phenomena are like empty space.
In all places there is no obstruction and no limit;
likewise, it is so with the dharma-gates of its objective sphere.
It pervades all things, yet possesses no objective sphere.
However, this is not shared with those various non-Buddhists. Māṇava,
do you now wish to take all the characteristics of phenomena as your objective domain?
Māṇava, there is likewise no one capable of knowing the limits of the realm of space to explain them to others;
this space has such a name as this.
Such is his clan and lineage; such are his physical characteristics;
such are his features, whether tall or short, and so forth, O māṇava.
It is, for example, as if someone were to speak these words:
"I am now able to measure the void accurately;
such is its extent, such is its breadth."
Even regarding such categories as large and small, long and short,
or various forms and substances, that space ultimately cannot speak;
thus says that person.
"O Benevolent One,
from where have you obtained such wisdom that you wish to measure my length and shortness, my height and breadth, and my dimensions?"
O virtuous one, you should not now engage in recollection or conceptual discrimination regarding the measure of my space;
for the emptiness of my nature is fundamentally without limit.
In truth, it is immeasurable;
one should know that all such things are merely spoken of through conceptualization,
for originally no such thing exists.
Māṇava, by these causes and conditions,
you now wish to measure the depth and shallowness within the gateway of the three Dharma-piṭakas.
It is likewise so,
Māṇava. For this reason, from the very beginning, I have repeatedly explained this to you.
All dharmas are like empty space.
Do not give rise to doubt or confusion regarding this.
It is as worldly people say: "I doubt empty space."
Yet the nature of space is fundamentally beyond doubt;
who could possibly harbor any suspicion or confusion regarding it? O Māṇava!
These dharma-gates and the nature of space have,
from the beginning, no locus for the arising of names or language;
nor can any defilements or turbidities be found therein.
The celestial palaces cannot be apprehended;
even the syllable "A-ka-na" cannot be apprehended, and so on,
up to the dwelling places, which also cannot be apprehended.
Except for these verbal expressions within the dharmas of false conceptualization,
O māṇava, you should not be terrified by them, nor should you harbor thoughts of attachment or deviate from equanimity.
When teaching the dharma of the equality of space,
one should not cause others to give rise to a mind of attachment or thoughts of fear.
If they should give rise to a fearful mind or thoughts of attachment, [it will be detrimental].
One who gives rise to such matters based on this equality should be known as being profoundly ignorant;
they create obstacles for themselves and bring calamity upon themselves.
Such a foolish person will ultimately be unable to enter the treasury of the three vehicles' teachings and practices,
nor will they be able to attain unimpeded eloquence,
nor will they be able to proclaim the essential meanings of all dharmas.
Māṇava, that foolish person is fundamentally not within the sphere of the true meaning of all phenomena.
Since such a person cannot understand these characteristics of phenomena,
how could they possibly explain them or realize them through direct knowledge?
Such a person is a fool.
Consequently, their ignorance increases and they develop false pride.

Due to this ignorance and pride, even though they may recite and analyze words—having previously heard them from others or having formerly served preceptors and teachers—[they do not truly understand].
Furthermore, although they were granted instruction in the profound verses of the Dharma,
they were unable to receive and uphold them,
forgetting them immediately thereafter.
Even the worldly systems of writing and language are all erroneous and unable to record [it];
how then could they possibly comprehend the profound Dharma of the Buddha, O māṇava?
Even if all sentient beings were simultaneously to attain the fruit of Arhatship and the state of a Pratyekabuddha,
this profound Dharma would still not be within their sphere of comprehension;
how much less so for ordinary, ignorant people?
Māṇava, for this reason,
the Dharma-gate attained by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
is the most excellent and supreme among all sentient beings.
It is not of the world. Why is this? O Māṇava.
The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats,
and Samyaksaṃbuddhas alone have attained such a supreme and wondrous Dharmakāya;
therefore, they are the most honored and the most sublime among all sentient beings.
It is not of the mundane world, O Māṇava.
Furthermore, it is the Dharma-body attained by all Tathāgatas.
It must be attained through the practice of cultivation;
therefore, the Dharma of the Tathāgatas cannot be awakened to by other sentient beings.
This is obtained only by the Tathāgata, O māṇava.
Among these, all the Dharma-gates of the Buddhas—
You should listen well and, having heard it, reflect deeply upon it.
By practicing according to the Dharma, you will eventually realize it for yourself;
this wisdom is certain and free from doubt.
"You all should be fully endowed with deep faith;
with single-minded devotion, uphold this and reach the further shore, O māṇava."
There are bodhisattvas who, before attaining buddhahood,
desire to take up the path of the Buddha; they should diligently cultivate these dharmas, and only then,
sitting at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, will they realize and know them.
There may be some bodhisattvas who, by virtue of their sharp wisdom,
are able to understand clearly for themselves without depending on the explanations of others, O māṇava.
When that bodhisattva sits beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment,
he spontaneously awakens to all phenomena, and his mind is free from obstruction. Why is this?
Because in the past they contemplated the nature of all phenomena as quiescent and free from grasping;
because they made offerings to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas;
and because their pure brahmacarya was fully perfected.
Because he has accumulated immeasurable gateways of prajñā-wisdom,
and because he has cultivated great compassion and pity for sentient beings;
by these causes and conditions.
When a Bodhisattva in their final existence sits at the site of enlightenment,
the various gateways to the illumination of all dharmas that they previously heard and received naturally manifest before them,
without depending on the awakening of another.
Māṇava, you should diligently practice, study, abide in, and rely upon this fifth teaching.
Furthermore, Māṇava:
There is a dharma-gate named "Arising.
You should well uphold this first dharma-gate.
What is "arising"?
For example, just as a lotus flower grows from the mud yet is not defiled by it,
and if it were separated from the mud, it would have no place to grow;
so it is with the māṇava.
Within this teaching of the Dharma,
you should, with an undistracted and pure mind,
transcend verbal expression and enter the gateway of non-self.
Having realized this for oneself, one should proclaim this meaning extensively to others;
this will bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings,
causing them to distance themselves from evil states and abandon unwholesome thoughts.
If there are any doubts, they shall be eliminated;
this is what is called truly benefiting others.
One should never be separated from the three types of verbal instructions, the treasury of expedient activities, and the chapters and phrases of the Dharma-gates.

Furthermore, you should explain such phrases of the Dharma—true, pure, and pertaining to the three periods of past, future, and present—to others, severing all doubts and enabling them to realize Bodhi.
You all should receive and uphold this in accordance with the Dharma.
Māṇava, regarding the sixth section on the meaning of the Dharma-gates,
you have first entered the Dharma-gate of the palace.
One should also contemplate the correspondence with the letter A.
How does one contemplate it?
One enters the gateway of the teaching that reaches the limit of exhaustion through the sequential application of the method of the wooden board.
If one is separated from language, the meaning cannot be apprehended.
Just as one entering battle must don armor before defeating the enemy, so too,
having understood this, you should transcend the two extremes and realize the gate of luminous joy of mind.
One immediately enters that palace of nirvāṇa.
How can you know this Dharma-gate of the Radiance of Mental Joy?
In this state, there are no marks, nor can it be perceived or known through marks.
Since that is without marks, how can it be known?
One knows it just as the dharmas of suchness have no prior or posterior limits.
Furthermore, how is this known?
When realizing suchness as it truly is, one does not disrupt any activities of the three periods of time;
even their prior and posterior limits cannot be discerned.
O māṇava, you should realize what is called the limit of the three periods of time.
That which is called the past, future, and present is thus realized as being boundless. O Māṇava,
as for the palace gates I previously mentioned:
You should understand this:
because that which is not a palace is called a palace,
so it is with nirvāṇa as well.
Do not give rise to grasping or attachment therein.
That which is without grasping or attachment is called nirvāṇa, māṇava.
Furthermore, there is a seventh thematic gate.

You should know that when I was practicing the bodhisattva path within saṃsāra in the past, whatever actions I performed were like a magician constructing a palace to deceive others; I was just the same.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he skillfully expounds the Dharma so that they may realize and know it.
You should reflect upon how the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has expounded this gateway to the true Dharma for our sake.
Just as that illusionist and others are no different [from the illusions],
so it is, O māṇava;
this is the third gate of realization through the skillful means of well-cultivated meritorious deeds.
In this regard, the Tathāgata has taught and explained the deeds performed in the past for the sake of universally compassionating all sentient beings;
it is not solely for the benefit of you, this one individual.
"You all should practice this with diligent effort. Māṇava,
you should seek to realize such a dharma-gate of palaces and treasure-troves."
Māṇava, whatever exists within the treasuries of the world is for the most part all of the following:
coins, copper, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, amber, musaragalva, agate, conch shells, and jade.
Even though there may be various exquisite jewels, mani-gems, and rare treasures,
they are still merely worldly hoards;
the Tathāgata’s treasure-store is not like this.
All sentient beings are unable to see it;
because they do not see it, they give rise to much doubt and confusion,
and say to one another:
How is it that we now seek names and designations within a dharma that cannot be seen or known?
Since the Tathāgatagarbha is formless and invisible,
how can we now understand or realize it?
What kind of sentient beings give rise to this doubt?
Only those who are foolish and lack wisdom, O Māṇava.
O Māṇava, a person of wisdom within the Buddha-dharma should not engage in discrimination as to whether something is so or not.
The wise disciples of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,
do not give rise to doubt or confusion upon hearing the teaching of the profound Dharma;
furthermore, they should not engage in such conceptual discrimination as to ask from where these various dharmas have come.
However, these dharmas pervade all places;
since there is no location from which they could have come,
how much less could there be a place where they abide?
Māṇava, the disciples of the Tathāgata well understand the characteristics of phenomena;
they do not give rise to doubt or confusion regarding the most profound points.
Whether it be existence or non-existence,
there is likewise no one who harbors such thoughts or doubts;
how could there be any doubt?
Wherein is there doubt? Therefore,
O māṇava, do not give rise to further doubt regarding the characteristics of all phenomena.
For example, space is fundamentally free from doubt.
If that space were subject to doubt,
it could not be called unobstructed.
You must not harbor doubts regarding space.
If you say that space gives rise to doubt,
then there is the expedient dharma-gate of the treasury of the three karmas.
"O Māṇava, there is nothing whatsoever that can serve as a simile for this;
since you have already used space as a metaphor for this Dharma-gate."
Therefore, doubt has no place to abide.
You all should now examine this according to reality, O māṇava.
All ordinary beings and sentient persons are far removed from the true meaning of these dharmas and are unable to practice in accordance with the teachings as they should.
One should know that they rely upon perversions;
thus, these sentient beings [are deluded] regarding the profound meaning within this sequential dharma-gate of the threefold treasury of verbal teachings and karma.
There is no place of abiding, nor any point of entry. Why is this?
Because they possess much defilement and turbidity, their minds are distracted and wander through impurity; they lack all wholesome dharmas.
Therefore, Māṇava, those beings have no place of abiding within this Dharma from the very beginning.
Because they are defiled by the impurities of greed, hatred, and delusion,
their minds are distracted by afflictions and their faculty of faith is weak; thus,
although they hear the sound of the Dharma, they are unable to receive it.
Because of this, various afflictions increase and follow along, perfuming the mind;
thus, one accomplishes evil karma and the retribution of suffering blazes forth.

Chapter 20: The Characteristics of the Dharma Master’s Conduct The Great Dharma Torch Dhāraṇī Sūtra, Chapter Twenty: The Characteristics of the Dharma Master’s Conduct At that time, the assembly of those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas again addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Emitting Light, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!
How rare, World-Honored One!
You are most skillfully able to protect and uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas."
“World-Honored One, we no longer have any doubt or confusion regarding this profound Dharma.
However, for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings of the future,
we wish to proclaim the Tathāgata World-Honored One’s profound and wondrous scriptures, to shatter their doubts and confusions, and to cause them all to realize and know it.”
"Bhagavān,
what kind of sentient beings will there be in future ages who shall have no web of doubt regarding this Dharma-gate?"
Furthermore, what kind of sentient beings do not turn their backs on such a profound treasury of Dharma,
but are able to have deep faith and understanding, are able to receive and practice it, and are able to sever all doubts?
Furthermore, what kind of sentient beings will,
in future ages, delight in contentious debate and mutual refutation,
becoming submerged in doubt and regret regarding this Dharma-gate and unable to extricate themselves?
Ānanda, after the assembly of bodhisattvas had made this request,
the Tathāgata Prabhāsa then addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
Māṇava, in future ages there will be no sentient beings capable of believing and accepting such a Dharma-gate as this.
Why is this? Because those sentient beings of future ages will merely listen to and receive this Dharma for the sake of contentious debate.
They do not truly respect, believe, accept,
or practice it; sometimes, when hearing this Dharma-sound amidst the assembly,
their hearts find no joy, and they abandon it and depart.
By various skillful means,
they instruct other people who possess faith and reverence,
causing them to slander such sutras as these.
At that time, there were many hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings who sought awakening;
yet, being destroyed and reviled by wicked people,
they ultimately failed to cultivate such sūtras.
Seeing many sentient beings fallen into the net of doubt,
those evil persons were filled with great joy.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable sentient beings who were purely virtuous.
By the power of the Buddha, they joyfully accept and uphold [this teaching].
At that time, those sentient beings who lack merit should think:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have abandoned us and do not look upon us with compassion."
"In the past, I too should have heard those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach this Dharma-characteristic.
O Māṇava, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, out of great compassion, pity sentient beings."
Throughout the long night, he has proclaimed the profound Dharma-gate,
causing all sentient beings to practice in accordance with it, O Māṇava.
If sentient beings hear this profound Dharma and are able to give rise to faith and understanding, and contemplate it with right mindfulness,
such persons will be constantly approached by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to provide guidance and instruction.
If there are sentient beings who revile, disparage, abandon, and cast aside the profound Dharma,
you should know that such individuals will sink forever into the great darkness of the realm of doubt.
In the end, they will never be able to behold the realm of pure goodness.
Such sentient beings have no sign of entry into this Dharma-gate, O Māṇava.
How could the Tathāgata permit not teaching this Dharma?
For the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not harbor even a single thought of aversion or a desire for distance toward any sentient being.
Therefore, you should reflect well, observe with a single mind, and apply yourselves with diligent discernment; do not speak of this lightly.
Only when you know that sentient beings are capable of hearing this Dharma should you teach it.
You should all speak according to what you have heard;
if you are able to uphold it, you should likewise speak according to what you have upheld;
if you are capable of practicing it, you should likewise speak according to what you have practiced.
If the mind is joyful, one should express sympathetic joy;
if it brings great benefit to them,
the words should be clear and the meaning complete.
One should arouse right mindfulness during this section of the Dharma discourse;
only after having established right mindfulness may one proclaim it.
This applies when the Dharma master ascends the high seat.
One should not harm oneself or others.
One should reflect thus:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always act for the sake of all realms of sentient beings within the infinite worlds."
Abiding in great compassion, they give rise to a mind of pity;
recollecting the True Dharma,
they proclaim and explain it for the sake of all sentient beings.
This is the characteristic of suffering;
it is also the place where sentient beings dwell.
One should abandon it and exhaust this source of suffering.
When that Dharma teacher preaches the Dharma,
do not give rise to defiled attachment, and do not grasp at the characteristics of phenomena.
Toward sentient beings, do not conceive of "self" and "other."
If you hear pleasant words, do not become overly elated;
if you hear harsh speech, do not harbor resentment or aversion.
If others come to question you, do not give rise to a mind of anger, vexation, fear, or hatred.
If that Dharma master is free from anger and resentment,
he will have no faults or afflictions in any situation;
because he has no faults or afflictions, he will likewise have no doubts.
Because there is no doubt, all the teachings that ought to be expounded will manifest before him.
At that time, the Dharma-preacher should keep in mind these three kinds of profound dharma-gates of the treasury of karma.
In this manner, one successively attains the characteristics of all phenomena.
One should also recollect the meaning of these dharmas.
How does one recollect them?
Regarding the immeasurable and boundless profound phrases of the Dharma-gates that I have previously taught,
you should give rise to no fear and encounter no obstacles;
you should rely upon the mind and not grasp at names or sounds.
Furthermore, one should well understand that the nature of names and sounds is fundamentally pure,
and that the words and meanings of the teachings are without deficiency.
When that Dharma master preaches this Dharma, [one should listen with such understanding].
He is skilled in both the letter and the meaning, able to cause those among the great assembly who hear him to rejoice;
many receive and practice his teachings without opposition,
and many, having heard them, give rise to a heart of reverence.
Many people made offerings to him, and his good reputation spread far and wide;
with one voice, they praised and extolled the Dharma Master.
When that Dharma Master preached the Dharma, [the assembly gathered].
When all sentient beings hear the sounds and speech of this Dharma-preacher,
they all give rise to joy that fills their bodies and minds, O māṇava.
Therefore, when a Dharma Master wishes to preach the Dharma for others,
his mind shall not be distracted, his thoughts shall be free from defilement, and he shall not dwell on other matters;
he shall maintain a dignified physical demeanor, fully endowed with a majestic presence.
The throat and tongue are unobstructed, and his speech is subtle and refined;
his tone is harmonious and elegant, such that none in the world can equal it.
His voice is neither broken nor scattered, nor does it ever cease.
When uttering speech, the tongue does not protrude;
sounds are not emitted simultaneously from both the nose and mouth;
the teeth are white, even, and closely set, such that his discourse is clear and distinct.
The names, phrases, and sentences were complete without omission;
all those in the assembly who heard them delighted in listening.
Having heard them, they rejoiced and their merit increased.
In this way, such a Dharma teacher benefits both themselves and others.
If that Dharma teacher does not possess the aforementioned qualities, they will have only evil signs and various faults.
That is to say, their physical appearance is ill-proportioned and their conduct is frivolous and restless;
their teeth are yellow and uneven, their lips and mouth are coarse and vulgar,
their throats are hoarse and broken, and their tongues are impure.
Due to various causes and conditions such as wind, phlegm, saliva, tears, cold, heat,
and the suffering of chill, as well as bodily emaciation or the excessive use of medicine leading to obesity and injury.
It causes that Dharma master to be unable to achieve completeness;
his voice lacks clarity, his speech is indistinct,
his terminology is incorrect, and the meaning of the Dharma is not made clear.
When those who listen to the Dharma hear and see this, they all give rise to feelings of aversion.
Since they do not respect the person, they do not honor the Dharma.
Because they hold the Dharma in low esteem, even though they hear it with their ears, their minds do not believe or accept it.
Because of their lack of faith, they further give rise to slander,
thereby creating such causes and conditions for false views for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
Because those foolish people lack wisdom,
they are ultimately unable to engage in such reflection;
only those who possess wisdom are capable of doing so.
How does one reflect?
It is like a priceless jewel fallen into excrement;
when a wise person sees it, they immediately form this thought:
"This jewel is priceless; I ought to take it.
Once I have taken it, I shall wash it until it is radiant and pure, and I shall increase my protection and respect for it beyond the ordinary."
Among those in the world who saw it, there were none who did not love and delight in it;
they marveled at the jewel’s excellence and asked what its value was.
At that time, they perceived only the beauty of the jewel.
One never thinks of it while it is in the filth;
this is what is done by a wise person.
It is not like that fool who, seeing a true jewel in the midst of filth, discards it and does not take it.
Furthermore, Māṇava,
even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with wealth and treasures,
and someone were to take them and offer them to a Dharma-preacher, it would not be enough to be called much.
Why is this? The immeasurable Dharma-gates spoken by the Dharma Master possess profound and grave merit that is difficult to encounter.
"O Māṇava, all the treasures filling the world are not equal to even a small fraction of the merit of a Dharma teacher.
Any sentient beings who have faith and delight in this Dharma, and who honor, love, and respect it,"
He should constantly reflect in this way:
"Whatever this Dharma master now proclaims is no different from the golden words and instructions of the World-Honored One himself."
As for what is meant by "distinctive":
only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses the thirty-two marks and a golden-hued body;
with a Brahma-voice he proclaims the Dharma, endowed with perfect eloquence as the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
This is merely a distinction.
Although they are called "various marks," they are still common dharmas. Why is this so?
The Wheel-Turning Sage King also possesses various marks,
yet he cannot realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Because these are tainted and are not dharmas that lead out of birth and death,
O māṇava, you should therefore abandon the conceit of "I am."
One should give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings and,
with a mind intent on training and gathering them, further reflect:
"How shall I teach those sentient beings to distance themselves from the three poisons of affliction— greed, hatred, and delusion— and eliminate their pride?"
"Come and gather at my place to hear and receive the True Dharma.
Having heard and received it, teach it extensively to others,
so that many people may thoroughly penetrate the gateways of the Dharma."
Furthermore, he revealed and taught it to other sentient beings,
who, by practicing according to the instructions, increased their merit, O Māṇava.
If there are sentient beings who do not know how to go to where the Dharma master resides,
the Dharma master, for their benefit,
should at that time go personally to cities, towns, and villages.
Furthermore, those sentient beings already possessed faith;
seeing the Dharma Master personally presiding over the instruction,
they further gave rise to a sense of reverence and rarity.
Thereupon, they honored and sustained the Dharma Master with all kinds of gold, silver, rare treasures, and various articles of livelihood and pleasure,
causing many sentient beings to each plant roots of goodness.
Māṇava, for this reason,
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—
In another sutra, it is stated thus:
"If a person constantly preaches the Dharma,
and if a person constantly comes to listen."
These two kinds of persons both obtain immeasurable merit.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has further spoken thus:
"To make offerings to a Dharma teacher is to make offerings to all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
One obtains immeasurable merit. Why is this?
If there were no Dharma Master, there would be no one to preach it.
"If there were no teacher to explain it, who could understand this profound treasury of the Dharma?
Therefore, Māṇava, you should conceive of the Dharma-preacher as a Buddha and harbor no other thought."
Māṇavas, you should further conceive such a thought toward the Dharma-preacher:

"This Dharma-preacher is now able to preach this Dharma because he has already cultivated and made offerings to, and planted roots of goodness under, immeasurable and boundless billions of Tathāgatas in the past."
Regarding that teacher of the Dharma,
whether they be a monastic or a layperson,
one should practice and make offerings to them in these two ways.
The accumulation of their merit is equal and without distinction.
You should not give rise to discriminatory thoughts, thinking,
"This one is a renunciant" and "that one is a householder."
One should conceive a sense of rare wonder toward such a person;
wherever they may speak, they are able to cause the roots of goodness to grow.
One should simply rejoice in this and not create any obstacles.
Māṇava, there are sentient beings, whether monastics or laypeople,
who go to the place of a Dharma teacher for the purpose of hearing the Dharma.
At that time, you should conceive a sense of rare wonder and great compassion toward such a person;
you should not disparage them or fail to preach the Dharma for them.
I shall speak in accordance with the truth so that, having heard it, you may give rise to wholesome reflection and attain knowledge as it truly is.
Māṇava, for this reason, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has taught you this profound Dharma-gate and its subtle, wondrous phrases.
I wish for you all to remember and uphold this;

you should likewise, out of compassion for the sentient beings of the world, universally proclaim, reveal, analyze, and explain these subtle and secret teachings so that they may be easily understood.
Furthermore, māṇava,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having aroused great compassion,
protects the speaker of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Just as the Tathāgata, O Māṇava,
and all the Bodhisattvas do for the sake of sentient beings.
For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas,
they have constantly remained within the ocean of birth-and-death and afflictions,
undergoing various sufferings while performing deeds for the benefit of others.
Great compassion does not diminish, and wisdom is likewise so.
By these causes and conditions, one swiftly realizes bodhi,
continuing until the ultimate exhaustion of nirvana without remainder.
Thus it is, young brahmin.
Therefore, you should reflect upon this with your own minds;
contemplate only the meaning, and do not become attached to the words or the sounds.
If you do not understand what I have taught, do not give rise to slander.
Why is this, māṇava?
I have already cited various analogies for you to explain how these three gateways of the treasury of oral teachings encompass all phenomena.
I have also explained to you the sequence of the expedient means for entering into practice.
This is what should be practiced and this is what should not be practiced;
as well as the places of coming and going, and so forth—
I have also already explained the various skillful means and the true meaning, and so on.
I have also already explained the skillful means of practice regarding the three periods of time— past, future, and present.
I have also already explained that one should contemplate the pure and the impure,
up to the successive stages of entry from the *kalala* through the *mahā* and so forth.
Just as with those droplets of water, bubbles, and foam,
I have also already explained the matters concerning the coming and going of the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth— how they were originally non-existent and now exist—
and I have also already explained that all these [beings] born from a womb are designated by name and form (*nāmarūpa*) through skillful means and are impure.
I have also already explained the activities performed by the aggregates,

In this regard, you should apply yourselves with diligence to mindfulness,

"Manava, when listening and hearing, collect your mind and do not let it wander.
Today, the Tathagata has no other intention."
I desire only that you abide within this Dharma,
māṇava. If the Tathāgata,

Furthermore, Māṇava,

At that time, this trichiliocosm—

Furthermore, he bestowed upon them the prediction of non-retrogression, saying:
"O māṇavas, you should now emulate that woman."
One should give rise to such a mind of reverence and joy,

"You shall realize this Buddha-wisdom through successive stages.
You must apply yourself with diligence and not give rise to indolence or arrogance.
You should practice all the pāramitās in their proper order, bringing them all to fulfillment and perfection without deficiency."
Within this Dharma, you should swiftly realize and know it for yourselves. Māṇavas,
you should now contemplate the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma in this manner.
Even the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot exhaust it,
let alone other persons. Furthermore, O māṇava:
O Māṇava, if one could reach the very limits of space,
then the limits of this Dharma-gate could likewise be known.
Just as that space has no beginning or end,
so too it is with all phenomena;
the number of sentient beings cannot be known.

it cannot be described and cannot be seen.
It is not conditioned.
Furthermore, it is without form and without light, such that it cannot be realized or known.
Even the Tathāgatas, the World-Honored Buddhas, cannot exhaustively fathom this Tathāgatagarbha;
how much less can other sentient beings?
Why is this? Because that Tathāgatagarbha is ungraspable, O māṇava.
The treasury of the skillful means and karma of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas,
is pure and non-existent;
since it is non-existent, [it is thus].
Their quantity and such are all unattainable;
it is merely due to the causes and conditions of the ignorance of ordinary sentient beings that they give rise to delusive confusion regarding all phenomena.
Since it has been said that there are no dharmas,

This is merely that the Tathāgata has spoken expediently for the sake of all sentient beings in accordance with worldly conventions.
Māṇava, it is because the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, conform to the world.
O Māṇava, all conceptualizations regarding worldly truth are entirely unattainable;
for all sentient beings are submerged within the three realms.
In order to incite them toward renunciation,
he teaches the Dharma in accordance with their needs so that they may accept and practice it;
although they are ordinary worldlings, [they are thus guided].
One is able to feel weary of and take no pleasure in all conventional truths and conditioned phenomena;
having thus become weary,

What is the gateway of wisdom that enables one to receive it?
It is to know that all phenomena are like space;
having known them to be like space, one applies diligent contemplation.
That nature of space is primordially pure;
no defilements of affliction can stain it,
nor is there anyone who can grasp or hold it.
"O Māṇava, once he has applied himself with such diligence and reflected thus,

Māṇava, if one could attain the noble path by means of that which exists according to worldly convention and is conditioned,

Yet that ordinary person cannot become a Buddha.
Why is this? Because the nature of conditioned phenomena is subject to change.
These are phenomena subject to destruction and not ultimate phenomena;
their nature is weak and inferior, and they have no place of abiding.
For this reason, conditioned things of the conventional truth are not a place of refuge.
Even if one were to obtain a small measure of peace and happiness by taking refuge [in that way], it should not be accepted;
how much less so for that which is conditioned, impermanent, subject to destruction,
non-abiding from moment to moment, and not ultimate?
Therefore, you should awaken to this and not give rise to grasping or attachment.
Māṇavas, if you are attached to conditioned practices, [you will not escape saṃsāra].
Then you would be no different from ordinary laypeople;

Furthermore, who else would there be to provide you with offerings and service—honoring you with clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites?
Māṇava, for this reason,

They do not delight in any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);

Thus, one does not cling to the desire realm, nor is one reborn in the desire realm;

Fundamentally, it is not grasped from the beginning and ultimately does not arise.

He eradicates craving and exhausts the source of all suffering;

if there are people who, upon hearing this dhāraṇī sūtra,

Māṇava. Therefore,

Chapter Twenty-Two: The Merits of Upholding the Sūtra. From the *Mahādharmanirbhaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Two: The Merits of Upholding the Sūtra. At that time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
Again, he addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
if there are sentient beings who can themselves read, recite, receive, and uphold this Dharma..."
If one gives rise to a heart of compassion and expounds [this teaching] for others,
even if only a single phrase, causing them to receive and uphold it—
how much merit does such a person obtain, and in what roots of goodness do they abide?
One who can explain this Dharma without giving rise to doubt—
what kind of practices did such a person cultivate in the past, what vows did they make,
and how many Tathāgatas did they attend and make offerings to?
"From how many Buddhas has he heard such profound Dharma?
World-Honored One,
for whom does such a Dharma teacher proclaim such a profound Dharma?"
Furthermore, as for those sentient beings who listen to the Dharma,
what roots of goodness did they plant under how many Tathāgatas in the past,
such that in this present and future life they hear the exposition of this profound Dharma?
With a heart that delights in hearing and receiving [the teaching] and does not retreat or sink,
I desire to hear all such meanings as these.
I only pray, World-Honored One, [to explain them].
He explained it in detail.

Whether they be renunciants or householders,
upon hearing even a single phrase of this profound Dharma-gate of the Buddhas,
they are immediately able to read, recite, receive, and uphold it.
Arousing a heart of compassion,
they gather in sentient beings by proclaiming such a Dharma-gate— even if only a single phrase— to others,

yet there are no sentient beings capable of believing and accepting this;

Or, Māṇava, one may have heard this Dharma-gate from the presence of various Tathāgatas in the past and likewise be able to give rise to faith.
Listen attentively, you all.

If there is anyone who can read, recite, receive, and uphold even a single phrase of this gateway of dhāraṇīs and explain it for others,
the merit they obtain will be boundless.
It is immeasurable and incalculable;
I shall speak of it by way of a brief illustration, O Māṇava.
Even if a hundred billion universal wheel-turning monarchs were to perform meritorious deeds throughout all their births,

A hundred thousand millionth part would not equal one of them.
Māṇava, even if there were another ten billion Śakras, Lords of the Devas, and the merit they had cultivated—
Even a hundred thousand million parts of the roots of goodness prior to this do not equal one part.
O Māṇava, even if one were to surpass the merit performed by the Great Brahmā King by a hundred thousand billion times, it would still not compare.
Even a hundred thousand millionth part of the former roots of goodness would not equal one part of this.
Māṇava, let us set aside the previous matter for now.
Even if one were to further attain the merit of the three fruits beginning with *srotāpanna*,
it would still not be comparable;
this remains true even up to the merit possessed by *arhats* and *pratyekabuddhas*.

to the merit of upholding this sutra as I have previously described.
Compared to all the roots of goodness in the world,
even if one were to exhaust all thought to weigh and measure them,
there is nothing with which they can be compared; they are only equal to the merit of all qualities at the time of realizing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is no different from the roots of goodness obtained by the former Dharma Master. Why is this?
Because these two merits are both produced by means of this great *dhāraṇī* dharma-gate.
Therefore, none of the other Dharma-gates can be compared to this.
Māṇava, why should you listen to any other Dharma-gates?
One should uphold only this great dhāraṇī. Why is this?
Because there is not a single dharma that is not subsumed within this dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, there is not a single doubt that this dhāraṇī does not resolve;
yet, out of compassion for various sentient beings,
he employs skillful means to further expound other sūtras.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, having heard this Dharma-gate before the presence of various World-Honored Ones in past lives,

they now give rise to various discriminatory thoughts upon its being preached, O māṇava.
Māṇava, all the various dharmas and characteristics taught by the Tathāgata in his other sūtras are ultimately not apart from this Dharani-gate of the Threefold Teaching Treasury.
As previously stated in the analogy regarding the nature of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*):
it is all-pervasive, boundless, and immeasurable;

This dharma-gate of dhāraṇī is likewise without limit and immeasurable.

O Māṇava, can measure it.
That good son...
Or perhaps they have previously heard this gateway of dhāraṇīs in the presence of various Tathāgatas of the past;
because of that prior hearing, they now once again hear these profound Buddha-dharmas before me.
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
regarding the dharma-gate of dhāraṇīs spoken by the Tathāgata, there are three types of teaching and practice."
"World-Honored One, we have already understood.
We shall read, recite, receive, uphold, and practice according to what has been taught."
Having heard such a Dharma as this,
we have attained immeasurable joy, immeasurable exultation,
immeasurable happiness, and immeasurable benefit.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
has personally realized and known that which is beyond the reach of the wisdom of all sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
"Is there anyone at all who can know the limits and boundaries of the realm of this Dharma-gate of the Tripitaka?
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying, "No, māṇava."
This Dharma-gate of the Treasury of Karma of the Threefold Oral Teaching is such that no one can know its limits.
Even if all sentient beings were like those of great renown mentioned above— possessing sharp faculties and brilliant wisdom.
Whether for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas,
a hundred thousand kalpas, or even for immeasurable kalpas,
one could never know it nor measure it.

Chapter Twenty-Three: Confessing Faults on Behalf of Others. From the *Mahādharmapradīpa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candana rose from his seat.
Maintaining his dignified deportment, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Tathāgata Emitting Light,
saying: "World-Honored One!"
I now, in the presence of the World-Honored One,
sincerely repent for such evil beings as these,
on account of those evil beings who slander the Dharma.
Regarding even a single phrase of this dharani gateway,
one may give rise to a mind of slander;

"Even to the extent that one creates an obstacle for a single sentient being regarding a single phrase,
