I now act for the sake of those evil sentient beings— even those who exist throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds."
Having practiced perversions and slandered the True Dharma,
I now, for their sake, sincerely repent before the Buddha,
World-Honored One.
For the sake of those sentient beings,
who lack protection and refuge, who lack eyes,
who lack wisdom, and who are possessed of evil speech.
I now repent with utmost sincerity for their sake,
World-Honored One.
If there should be another person who repents in this manner before the World-Honored One, [they shall likewise be purified].
"What roots of goodness does he attain therein, and what merits does he acquire?
At that time, the Tathāgata Prabhāsa addressed the Bodhisattva Candana, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Māṇava, you have been able to perfume your mind with such skillful means as to question the Tathāgata in this way.
If a son of good family should sincerely repent before those evil beings who destroy the Dharma, [he shall be purified].
"You shall obtain an immeasurable mass of great merit, māṇava.
This mass of merit is difficult to measure."
I shall now briefly expound this through a parable,
so that these sentient beings may give rise to a heart of joy, O māṇava.
In this manner, all the worlds existing in the eastern direction,
and within them all sentient beings, have entirely become great donors;
likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
To all sentient beings throughout the ten directions,
they act as great donors for all of them,
constantly practicing generosity throughout immeasurable, boundless, unspeakable, and incalculable numbers of great kalpas.
This refers to gold, silver, various jewels, clothing, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, dwellings, and all kinds of requisites;
taking immeasurable and boundless sentient beings and gathering them all in one place to serve as the recipients of these gifts.
Māṇava, what do you think?
Can this accumulation of merit be called great?
Candana said,
"World-Honored One,
this mass of merit is truly vast and great."
Why is this? World-Honored One,
if there were a person who practiced the merit of giving for immeasurable eons, they would still not reach its limit.
How much more so, then, could one measure the limits of the mass of merit from the practice of *dāna* by immeasurable sentient beings throughout incalculable eons?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, māṇava.
Those immeasurable sentient beings..."
Although the immeasurable eons spent practicing immeasurable acts of giving and the resulting immeasurable masses of merit are beyond comprehension,
they still do not equal that of a son or daughter of good family who, amidst the aforementioned assembly of those who slander the Dharma, [acts as described].
Yet, the roots of goodness produced and the merit obtained from the sincere repentance of even a single person are immeasurable,
boundless, and beyond compare;
how much more so for the sincere repentance performed on behalf of immeasurable sentient beings!
Furthermore, māṇava,
setting aside all those evil sentient beings in this world who slander the Dharma,
suppose there were sentient beings in all the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions who reviled the True Dharma.
Māṇava, even among the multitudes who slander the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
it is sufficient for but a single person to repent with a sincere heart.
The mass of merit obtained and the roots of goodness produced would already be beyond limit;
how much more so when one sincerely repents for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions!
Such a mass of merit and roots of goodness sustains, gathers, and increases a multitude of virtuous qualities.
It is incalculable, immeasurable, and inconceivable.
Who could believe in such merit?
Only non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to believe it in small measure.
Then Candana again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"When those sons of good family practice in this manner, what do they seek to attain?
The Buddha said:
Candana, for the sake of bodhi,
that son of good family bears this heavy burden;
out of compassion for those sentient beings, he repents with a sincere heart.
By virtue of these roots of goodness,
one is further able to adorn the buddha-fields and ultimately attain such sovereign enjoyment.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, there was among the assembly an upāsaka named Candrottarā."
That upāsaka’s household was abundant in wealth and treasures;
he adorned his body and neck with pearl necklaces worth hundreds of thousands of billions of gold pieces,
and he possessed a wondrous jewel also worth hundreds of thousands of billions of gold pieces.
Then the upāsaka rose from his seat,
immediately untied his pearl necklace,
and offered it to the Tathāgata Emitting Light.
Furthermore, she offered exquisite jewels to the Bodhisattva Candana.
Having made this offering, Candralekhā’s profound respect and great joy increased even further.
He formed this thought:
"All my granaries and treasuries,
as well as all other means of subsistence, are fully provided."
At this time, one may offer pure gifts to the Tathāgata and Candanana.
Furthermore, one should think:
"Now, the noble Candanana..."
If, having known that I had conceived such a thought,
you were to speak of it to the World-Honored One,
and the World-Honored One heard it;
He immediately dispatched the Bodhisattva Candana to personally instruct me.
At that time, I received his teachings and followed them for the rest of my life,
personally training in those practices of the various bodhisattvas.
When the elder Candrottara gave rise to this thought,
the Bodhisattva Candana, having observed and known it through his knowledge of others' minds,
addressed the Tathāgata Prabhāsa: "O Tathāgata, please listen."
World-Honored One,
I now clearly see within this assembly the upāsaka Candrābha.
Again, he gave rise to a profound resolve and thought thus:
"I shall now, at this opportune time,
offer all that my household possesses to the World-Honored One with a pure mind."
"World-Honored One,
this upāsaka has been able to give rise to the great mind and possesses such wisdom and eloquence, as well as eloquence in giving and eloquence in relinquishment.
He wishes to invite the Tathāgata to speak on the matter of the mind set upon awakening."
However, because the Tathāgata’s virtue and morality are so lofty and his majestic spiritual power so sublime,
my heart is filled with shame and trepidation, and I do not dare to venture a request.
How excellent, World-Honored One!
"I have now come here on behalf of this upāsaka to request that the World-Honored One explain such matters.
At that time, the Tathāgata Emitting Light immediately addressed Candana, saying:
Excellent, excellent,
Candana! You have now perfected the knowledge of others' minds.
Māṇava, because he has long cultivated those roots of goodness throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas,
I also know the mind of this upāsaka.
However, for the sake of this assembly, let all these bodhisattvas set aside such thoughts and remain silent; furthermore,
let the entire multitude of bodhisattvas train in this Dharma according to the conduct of you, Candana.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candana addressed that householder, saying:
"Householder, do you truly have such a thought now?
The householder replied:
Venerable sir,
I truly have such a thought now; however,
it is solely out of a mind of reverence, a mind of respect, and a mind of aspiration.
I did not dare to consult the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One.
Now I see that the noble Bodhisattva Candana,
out of a heart of compassion, is indeed capable of such a thing.
For the sake of all sentient beings in the world who are without protection, without right mindfulness, and without a guide, I now,
before the World-Honored One, sincerely repent and take refuge in you as my protector and guide.
Having seen this, I immediately conceived a sense of great wonder and deep reverence for the noble Bodhisattva Candana,
for the noble Candana had never before encountered sentient beings who slandered the Dharma.
That you are able to perform this sincere repentance may be called excellent;
furthermore, you possess a heart of compassion for me.
I have made this request to the Tathāgata according to my own thoughts;
if you do not accept this sincere heart of mine,
then my vow shall remain unfulfilled.
If you, upholding my mind, were to question the Tathāgata,
I would immediately act in accordance with my vows and follow his instructions.
However, the noble Bodhisattva Candana has taken up this heavy burden for the sake of sentient beings in immeasurable and boundless worlds, and he sincerely repents.
Furthermore, you are able to ask me about this great matter of the heavy burden in such a manner.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Candana again addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Emitting Light, saying:
“World-Honored One,
the Tathāgata should also have heard this question posed by the upāsaka Candrottara.
The Buddha said:
Māṇava, I have now heard what Candrottarā has requested, Māṇava.
"What do you think?
Do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have any desire for personal benefit?
Candana replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata lacks nothing and has no desires. Why is this?"
I have heard that in the past, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, dwelt using but a single robe and a single meal;
they remained seated in one cross-legged posture for kalpas exceeding the sands of the Ganges,
and likewise for kalpas exceeding the sands of the Ganges.
Yet his body was not weakened or impaired, nor did he experience any fatigue;
it was solely for the sake of compassion toward all sentient beings. Why is this so?
Desiring to cause all sentient beings to dwell securely within the Dharma of reality as it is,
and further desiring to cause all sentient beings to fully attain the true Dharma,
the Tathāgata thus employs skillful means to manifest through parables and verbal discourse.
World-Honored One,
although the Tathāgata employs such various skillful means,
sentient beings do not even believe or accept them when they see them directly.
How much more so when, at a later time, they do not see the Tathāgata.
Then the Tathāgata Prabhāsa said to the Bodhisattva Candana:
"Furthermore, if there is someone who gives various precious objects as a gift..."
They were placed upon the knees of the Tathāgatas as they sat in the full lotus posture;
yet the Tathāgatas ultimately accepted nothing,
nor did their śrāvaka disciples receive these true precious objects.
Māṇava, you should properly instruct this upāsaka therein so that he may benefit his body and mind for a long night and dwell in peace and happiness.
As for the pearl necklaces, exquisite jewels, and other such things he has offered:
It is appropriate to return it to him;
you should merely instruct him so that he may practice the Dharma.
Such is the precious jewel of birth.
Although neither the Buddha-Tathāgata nor his śrāvaka disciples may take it, nor may they use it,
there is only the merit that increases through the act of giving.
For what reason?
It is because one causes all sentient beings to obtain benefit;
likewise, one should also instruct all sentient beings in this way.
At that time, having heard the holy teaching before the Tathāgata,
the upāsaka Candrottara took the arm of the bodhisattva Candana with his right hand and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Together with Candana Bodhisattva, he emerged from that assembly and returned to his home.
After spreading out a seat and sitting down,
this upāsaka immediately commanded his family members to open the storehouses.
He personally admonished him, saying:
"The various treasures within my storehouse should now all be brought out and placed before me;
I wish to examine their quality, whether fine or coarse, and also to know their total quantity."
Having understood this, I shall offer worship and make offerings to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
as well as to his assembly of disciples, the śrāvakas.
Then the householder’s wife said to the householder:
To be able to give rise to such a mind is truly to achieve great goodness.
Although I am ignorant, I have long contemplated this matter;
however, lacking the necessary skillful means, I did not have the leisure to inform you first.
"I have suddenly heard this auspicious command, which deeply comforts my original heart.
However, O Elder, this accumulation of jewels cannot be preserved forever."
According to my humble view,
this treasure store is difficult to rely upon;
one should instead entrust it solely to the field of merit of the Buddhas.
This merit is rare and shall never be lost.
Householder,
we should reflect in this way.
The precious and virtuous remains of my ancestors for seven generations have been buried underground and are ultimately cast away in vain;
all other wealth and possessions will likewise return to dust and soil.
"Venerable sir, if there is even a small amount remaining, who would use it?
This is a matter of great importance; you should act quickly and seize the opportunity."
Although I have today been fortunate enough to offer this to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
and have thereby shattered that heart of accumulated secret stinginess,
I privately reflect that it was truly somewhat late.
"O Householder,
such a person as he is difficult to encounter;
we ought to make offerings to him with a sincere heart."
If one hears the Dharma from him,
when the thought of the Dharma arises, it is not for the sake of any other worldly benefit.
Thereupon, the elder said to his wife:
I beheld the noble Bodhisattva Candana and heard his words; therefore,
I have conceived a spirit of reverence and a most rare and marvelous mind.
Furthermore, because this bodhisattva alone is able to sincerely repent on behalf of those sentient beings who slander the Dharma within those immeasurable and boundless worlds,
I see this and consequently give rise to a heart of increased reverence and a sense of the rare and marvelous toward him.

Furthermore, because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others have made great vows for the sake of all sentient beings to shoulder heavy burdens and constantly practice various difficult and arduous ascetic disciplines.
His wife again cautioned the elder, saying,
"O worthy one,
do not harbor such thoughts."
"You should quickly follow this Great Bodhisattva to the presence of the Tathāgata.
You must generate such a profound and sincere mind of reverence to make offerings to the Tathāgata;
since the beginning of time, no one has ever been able to initiate such a great offering."
At that time, the elder personally inspected all the storehouses within his home as well as the various treasures buried in the earth inherited from seven generations;
they all appeared before him, and though he calculated and weighed them, they could not be fully enumerated.
He immediately addressed the Bodhisattva Candana, saying, "Noble Candana,
I am now unable to do this for the sake of these riches."
They fall into hell and undergo various sufferings and afflictions,
just as those bees are able to produce sweet honey once the honey has first been perfected.
"If one eats what has not yet been digested, it will immediately harm one's own body.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Candana addressed the elder, saying: "Elder,"
"So it is, so it is. It is just as you have said,
householder."
Your ancestors accumulated these treasures through many years and lifetimes, not without diligent toil;
yet in the end, they were unable to give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion to practice generosity toward even a single sentient being.
In this life, one guards these objects with a mind of stinginess;
when one's life ends, one is reborn in the evil realms.
Having been born there, one possesses no virtuous thoughts.
Even if one were to wish to give rise to wholesome thoughts at that time,
how could one possibly fulfill such a desire when great suffering assails and oppresses them?
O Householder!
Even your own kinsmen cannot save you from this;
what need is there to mention other sentient beings? Ānanda!
At that time, having heard these instructions from the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candana,
the elder [prostrated] before the Tathāgata Emitting Light and the great assembly.
He made extensive offerings.
Having completed his offerings, he shaved his head and went forth as a renunciant in the presence of the Tathāgata,
practicing and making offerings to the World-Honored One for as long as he lived.
Those various treasures and riches were inexhaustible.
Thereupon, Candrottarā again addressed the Bodhisattva Candana, saying:
"Noble One," [she continued].
"From now on, what further means of making offerings to the Tathāgata do you know?
If I know them, I shall practice them all.
Candana replied:
"O Householder,
I truly do not know from where this accumulation of wealth and treasures arose in the past, nor where it will cease now. Why is that?"
Because there is no place from which they come and no place to which they go,
householder. It is,
for example, like bees that are born together.
He sequentially consumed honey from countless billions of jars and vessels.
These bees do not know from where this honey originates, where it has come from, or where it goes;
who could believe such a thing?
In the same way, O householder, is this treasury of wealth and jewels.
Impermanent and unstable, it is buried beneath the earth;
gradually reaching the gathering of waters, it ultimately returns to the great ocean,
O Householder.
You should reflect further upon this:
in my previous lives, my ancestors and forefathers were merely deceived by their own stinginess and malice.
Accumulating wealth only increases evil karma.
Alas! Where have my ancestors been reborn now?
What has been accomplished through all this arduous toil and management?
They merely pursue empty fame to seek victory over others;
with continuous envy and jealousy, they greedily savor their attachments.
Due to these karmic causes and conditions, they shall sink forever into the evil realms.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The Six Perfections. *The Great Dharma Torch Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Four, Part One. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"At that time, the Tathāgata Emitting Light addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Good Awakening, saying:"
"Māṇava, you should listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
I shall now explain the Dharma of the Bodhisattva for you."
If bodhisattvas maintain pure ethical discipline without deficiency or diminution,
they will certainly achieve the adornment of meaningful benefit;
such is the supreme maintenance of ethical discipline among all bodhisattvas abiding in right morality.
Ultimately pure, one enters the gateway of suchness;
in accordance with the knowledge of phenomena, there is neither "that" nor "this.
The mass of merit of the precepts is vast and boundless.
No one is able to know its limit;
even if all ordinary beings in the world, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
were to attempt it, none could know it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sujñāta addressed the Buddha Prabhāsa, saying:
"World-Honored One,
now is precisely the right time."
We only pray that the World-Honored One will,
for the sake of these hundreds of millions of bodhisattvas,
fully expound the true characteristics of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s precepts and conduct.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Sujāta, "Māṇava,
that which is called 'precepts' is named the inconceivable state."
The accomplishment of the merit of virtuous conduct is thus:
it is unshakable,
free from defilement, pure, and perfect.
It eternally exhausts all evils and has no place of abiding;
it is as vast as space and cannot be grasped or held.
Furthermore, O māṇava:
Such are the various pāramitās,
namely: the dāna-pāramitā and the śīla-pāramitā.
The perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā),
the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā),
and the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā,
the Dānapāramitā is foremost and supreme, without any diminution.
Or, within various states of existence and future births,
some may even reach the abode of the Heavenly Kings,
while others may experience decline.
In future births, they will be born into poverty and low station;
lacking food and clothing, they will sustain themselves by begging,
constantly wandering and coming and going within the stream of saṃsāra.
Because of poverty, one is unable to purify the dānapāramitā;
thus, the dānapāramitā naturally diminishes, O māṇava.
There are no bodhisattvas who remain exclusively in dhyāna;
only the Tathāgata enters once and does not emerge.
It is not that bodhisattvas are always in meditative concentration.
If one were always in meditative concentration, one would avoid and protect against birth and death.
However, when Bodhisattvas wish to take rebirth in those places of existence, they intentionally retain a small amount of defiled affliction;
it should be understood that at such times, they temporarily relinquish the faculty of wisdom.
Because that faculty of diligence has nothing whatsoever to relinquish,
it is not called "renouncing the bodhisattva path" while dwelling within those immeasurable cycles of birth and death.
This mind of greedy attachment is also characterized by both relinquishment and non-relinquishment;
at that time, although there is diligence, one does not attain awakening. Why is this?
Because the perfection of wisdom has not yet been fulfilled,
one must not abandon diligence when encountering places where birth occurs.
Thus it is, O māṇava.
Furthermore, there was no conjunction of two minds acting together. Māṇava,
I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Ratnāgni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
He appeared in the world,
O Māṇava; such was the retinue of that Buddha.
There were only twenty-four śrāvakas,
as well as six great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, māṇavas.
The sūtras recited by those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are called the *Jambūpāramitā*.
Those six bodhisattvas...
Each dwells within the practice of a single pāramitā.
The first bodhisattva praises the dāna-pāramitā and regards the dāna-pāramitā as supreme.
The second bodhisattva praises the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), regarding it as supreme.
The third bodhisattva praises the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Thus, they take the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as supreme.
Fourth, the Bodhisattva praises the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*),
and thus takes the perfection of vigor as supreme.
The fifth bodhisattva praises the dhyānapāramitā,
regarding the dhyānapāramitā itself as supreme.
The sixth bodhisattva praises the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, they take Prajñā as supreme;
with single-minded devotion, they practice the accumulation of the virtues of Prajñā,
without any other thoughts.
Māṇava, at that time,
the Buddha Ratnāgni, wishing to know the inclinations and aspirations of those bodhisattvas,
questioned them regarding their original practice.
Once those bodhisattvas had received the noble inquiry,
each answered according to the practice of their own mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One Ratnāgni thought to himself:
All these bodhisattvas have newly entered the path of practice with the aspiration for enlightenment.
I must now act in accordance with their intentions and must not oppose them. Why is this?
If one were to contravene his mind, one might even fall back or sink away.
Thereupon, he addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Do you all know these six pāramitās?"
The bodhisattvas said,
"World-Honored One,
we have already understood the six pāramitās. The Buddha then asked again:
"How do you all practice and uphold the six pāramitās?
Each of the bodhisattvas then spoke of the specific pāramitās they themselves had practiced.
Furthermore, O māṇava:
What is called the first bodhisattva’s joyful practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*)?
It refers to when that bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving,
[giving] everything they possess, even including their home.
Whenever anyone came to him with a request, he gave them everything they sought.
He bestowed nine thousand celestial maidens as gifts;
these women were so exquisite that it would be difficult to describe them all in detail.
I shall now briefly explain the price of that maiden.
It is equal to all the wealth and various goods found in this Jambudvīpa, namely:
natural treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, conch shells, beautiful jade, coral, pearls, and so forth.
Furthermore, all the elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, camels, mules, donkeys,
and other such four-footed livestock found throughout Jambudvīpa—
such diverse species as these.
Furthermore, among all the people of Jambudvīpa and other sentient beings—
whether they possess karma or lack it, whether they possess wealth or lack it—
all such things as these [are likewise].
Compared to the nine thousand women previously given as gifts,
they could not even equal the value of a single one;
yet that bodhisattva, because of his profound mind’s deep love for the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), [offered them].
Seeing people come to beg, he gave even these nine thousand beautiful women to them.
Furthermore, while that bodhisattva was still living at home, he possessed nine thousand white elephants and nine thousand priceless precious horses.
Thus, the mane, tail, and coat of this noble steed are all like the color of stone collyrium;
furthermore, they are also like those of the horse-king Kesarin,
and likewise like the precious horse of a wheel-turning monarch.
Raising his whip, he galloped once and crossed the great ocean;
such horses as these he gave entirely to others.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva possessed priceless, supreme jewels.
Furthermore, he completely filled nine thousand [vessels] and gave them all away as alms.
O Māṇava, the remaining items cannot be described in detail.
O māṇava, whenever he sees a petitioner,
he bestows gifts upon them all.
Having thus practiced such giving, that bodhisattva—
Thereupon, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Ratnāgni, he grew weary of the world and left the household life.
He diligently practiced until he fulfilled the dānapāramitā, O māṇava.
This is the first [practice] of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who delights in practicing the dānapāramitā.
Furthermore, māṇava,
what is called the second [practice] of a bodhisattva who delights in practicing the śīlapāramitā?
That is to say, when that bodhisattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā),
he constantly praises the observance of precepts;
furthermore, desiring to surpass those non-Buddhist seers who possess the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā), he fully cultivates those five supernormal powers.
Having attained the five supernormal powers within the Dharma of that Tathāgata Ratnāgni,
he left the household life and observed the precepts, possessing only three robes.
Following the Tathāgata’s instruction, he gave rise to a mind of boundless measure.
Having attained mastery of mind, one accomplishes the wisdom of a Tathāgata;
by generating the aggregate of ethical discipline, one obtains such a body,
even unto the full perfection of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
For this reason, at that time, that bodhisattva praised the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Fully maintaining the precepts,
he practiced equanimity, O māṇava.
This is the second way in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva delights in practicing and abiding within the śīla-pāramitā.
Furthermore, māṇava,
what is called the third way in which a bodhisattva delights in practicing the kṣānti-pāramitā?
That is to say, when that bodhisattva practices patience,
he may be born in a royal palace as a crown prince endowed with great power;
at a time of the kalpa-turbidity, there are sentient beings who frequently engage in unrighteous conduct.
They are unfilial toward their parents;
they do not respect śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas and lack right faith;
they defile and ruin householders and scatter the families of others; they constantly engage in theft and destroy the seals and marks of others.
They delight in contention and are stubborn and perverse, refusing to accept wholesome words.
When they see others committing evil, they either praise it or remain silent.
Failing to guard against verbal transgressions, they recklessly speak of right and wrong.
Killing, stealing, double-tongued speech, and false speech—
those who fully practice these ten unwholesome deeds and distance themselves from the ten wholesome deeds will gradually increase in number.
Every day, one thousand, two thousand, or even several thousand officials and law-enforcers were constantly catching and seizing [criminals].
As the prince passed by,
there were also various other wicked people among them.
Some tunnel through walls in violation of prohibitions;
some scale city walls and cross passes;
some abandon their posts and flee in rebellion.
Whether they have violated another's wife, defrauded another of their property,
or given false testimony regarding right and wrong—
when such offenders with many transgressions are apprehended by the authorities;
With all their limbs bound by shackles, fetters, stocks,
and manacles, they were led one after another before the prince;
in this manner, twenty years passed.
However, because that prince possessed compassion and patience,
he never from the beginning harbored any harsh, violent, or resentful thoughts,
nor did he ultimately carry out any acts of execution or slaughter.
He gave him gifts from his own private treasury alone;
thereafter, he reprimanded him according to the gravity of his offense and then released him.
He then instructed him, saying:
"You should know that because I have faith in the Buddha, I do not commit any evil deeds.
Furthermore, I have released you and will not subject you to harsh punishment.
I wish for you to remember this kindness, abandon evil, and cultivate goodness."
Māṇava, at that time the prince thought to himself:
"I am currently dwelling here among these sentient beings."
How is this different from the executioners of King Yama punishing and judging sinners?
Now that I am able to practice patience in accordance with the Dharma,
I should lead all sentient beings to the presence of the World-Honored One.
Although I have long practiced such a dharma of patience,
I must nevertheless never, at any time, inflict physical harm upon those sentient beings by executing them, imprisoning them in jail, or even binding and beating them.
At a later time, one should merely reprimand them and release them;
furthermore, one must not again behold or hear the evil words and deeds of such sentient beings who are ungrateful and devoid of righteousness.
"Therefore, you ought to request the Buddha to rescue them and cause them all to abide in the ultimate state.
O Māṇava, at that time, the prince, having reflected upon these matters, [acted accordingly].
He then proceeded to the abode of the Buddha Ratnāgni;
having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him with reverence, withdrew to stand aside, and related these matters in detail.
Māṇava, at that time,
the World-Honored One Ratnāgni heard the prince’s words and,
in accordance with the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), gave his seal of approval.
Thereupon, he praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You are a virtuous man."
That you are now able to practice such pāramitā of patience amidst this evil age and among a multitude of unrighteous people—
this is because that Buddha, the World-Honored One, previously expounded the pāramitā of patience for you when you were a prince.
Having heard this teaching, he did not return to his own palace for the rest of his life;
rather, within this patience, he became even more firm, O Māṇava.
This is the third way in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva delights in practicing and abiding within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

The Buddha then addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
Kauśika, you should now know that if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, [who...]
Practicing according to the true teaching of the Buddha-Tathāgata,
yet after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they manifest the characteristics of a *pudgala* and practice various heterodox dharmas.
While they abide in those characteristics of a *pudgala* and those heterodox practices, [they do not see the Tathāgata].
Or they may contemplate the objects of śamatha,
yet being unable to rely upon the Tathāgata’s true teaching,
they conceptually construct the marks of a *pudgala* within their own minds.

When delusive thoughts appear— whether by the hundreds, the thousands, or exceeding that number— one then takes pleasure in dwelling within these marks of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*) and employs them as the practice of *śamatha*.
They preach the Dharma for the sake of the world,
yet they do not rely on the matter of vipaśyanā as taught by the Tathāgata,
and are unable to discern the characteristics of a pudgala.
Nor do they rely on *vipaśyanā* as their clothing; rather,
those sentient beings merely use all kinds of robes, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions for the purpose of traveling,
wandering, and residing in villages and cities.
There may be those who possess all five supernormal powers,
or four, or three, down to those who do not possess even one or two;

"Now you are able to know where such a great assembly as this resides.

"World-Honored One," [he said].
"I know that this assembly is now all dwelling upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.

World-Honored One.

Chapter Forty: The Past Deeds of the Buddha Prabhāsa. From the *Mahādharanī-dharmolkā-sūtra*, Chapter Forty: The Past Deeds of the Buddha Prabhāsa. At that time, the Tathāgata Prabhāsa addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Uttaramati, saying:
Māṇava, I recall that in the distant past, at the beginning of a kalpa,
there was one named Durdharṣa.
Furthermore, the second kalpa was named Removal of Pleasure (Ratiharā).
After this kalpa had passed, there was yet another kalpa.
Thus, for three kalpas there was no Buddha at all.
During those kalpas, wherever any sentient beings were born,
they never once heard even a single sound of the Dharma.
How much more so for those who manage to practice according to the Dharma;
it is impossible that they could fail to cultivate [the path].
Those beings are born into a world where the Dharma has disappeared.
They exclusively engage in evil conduct;
they are unfilial toward their parents and do not serve their teachers or elders;
they show no respect for śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
They distance themselves from upholding the precepts and rely instead on unwholesome dharmas;
constantly delighting in negligence, they fall into the darkness of ignorance,
failing to distinguish right from wrong and knowing nothing of good and evil.
They do not distinguish between the honorable and the lowly,
nor do they harbor gratitude for their upbringing; they do not even know who is their father or who is their mother,
let alone what constitutes a brother or a sister.
Because they do not understand such dharmas as these,
each and every one enters the dark abyss of ignorance,
losing the eight roots of goodness and the dharmas conducive to joyful practice.
Falling into the profound and far-reaching sufferings of hell,
they will ultimately never realize who is the Buddha or what is the Dharma.
What is the Sangha?
Furthermore, during such eons, they do not recognize any roots of goodness.
There was a bodhisattva named Gandhottama who manifested his birth into a brahmin family.
Not long after his birth, both his parents passed away.
Thus the Bodhisattva’s body gradually grew,
and he brought his faculties to maturity, endowed with the power of diligence.
With his roots of goodness fully ripened, he left home to enter the homeless life.
Having gone forth, he practiced asceticism with diligent effort for forty years by a tree in a forest.
He ate only fruit and drank only water, having no other food.
As for the fruit he consumed, even if it was ripe on the tree, he would never take it first;
rather, it had to be the remains left over after being pecked at by jays, parrots, monkeys, and various other birds and beasts.
Although there are no insects that eat them, they ripen at certain times;
when the wind blows, they fall naturally, and only then are they gathered.
This is the season for eating them.
He vowed to eat only once every seven days;
during those seven days, he would never take a second meal.
Thus, even when the time for a meal arrived, the Bodhisattva [refrained].
Since there was no further fruit from his practice, he let the time pass in vain and had nothing to eat.
For forty-two years, whether eating or not eating,
he practiced dhyāna-concentration with long-term austerity and diligence.
By practicing meditative concentration, he attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Thus,
after forty-seven years had passed for this bodhisattva,
by means of his supernormal power, he employed the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which surpasses that of human eyes.
He observed all sentient beings in the world who do not uphold the precepts and possess no merit at all,
but instead exclusively commit evil deeds, being envious and slanderous.
They do not serve their parents nor do they respect śramaṇas;
throughout the long night, they blaze with the growth of manifold evils,
mutually threatening and harming one another more fiercely than enemies.
At that time, having seen such evil sentient beings, the Bodhisattva gave rise to great sorrow and compassion, and sighed thus:
"Alas! How lamentable!"
Alas, how lamentable!
These sentient beings have incurred a most grievous loss;
how could they possibly [remain] within this vast realm?
There is not a single sentient being who possesses even a fragment of a root of goodness,
much less one who possesses them in their entirety;
furthermore, they reflect in this way.
"Today, I should use my divine eye to observe this trichiliocosm in search of even a single sentient being who is fully endowed with roots of goodness.
If I were to see such a one, I would be greatly rejoiced."
Why is this? Because I have obtained such great benefit from him;
if one does not know his location, one should simply follow this [benefit].
They further instructed one another, causing the roots of goodness to grow.
At that time, having formed such a thought,

Māṇava, it is like a tree that produces both flowers and fruit during its flowering time, and produces only fruit during its fruiting time, Māṇava.
"What do you think?
If the flowering season of that tree has not yet arrived, could one obtain its flowers by seeking them?
"No, World-Honored One."
"If the time for the fruit has not yet arrived, can one obtain the fruit by seeking it?
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, māṇava. The Tathāgata is also like this."
"It is simply because the time for speaking has not yet arrived that I have not spoken, Māṇava.
What do you think?"
"Furthermore, just as that tree can be known to have its place of origin,
can its flowers and fruits also be known to have their place of origin?
No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is.
All that exists—the speaker and the spoken—has no place from which it comes."
Māṇava, suppose at some time someone were to dig up that tree,
pulling out its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves.
Furthermore, he used knives and axes to hack and chop it until it was shattered,
until not even as much as a jujube or a chestnut remained. O Māṇava!
"What do you think?
Once that tree has been thus dispersed,
would it be possible to find its original flowers or fruit?"
"No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
Since it has already been broken and scattered, not even the appearance of a tree can be seen; how then could there be flowers or fruit?"
The Buddha said, "So it is,
so it is, māṇava."
Since all phenomena are devoid of characteristics,
how can they be described?
Furthermore, O māṇava:
When any Dharma masters have ascended the Dharma seat,
they should first contemplate the gateway of the letter A,
and likewise keep in mind the Tathāgata’s treasury of the threefold teaching without ever letting it go.
When one thus contemplates these formations within that continuous application of mindfulness through the three doors,
and attends again and again while performing this task:
Up to the point where no contentious speech arises, O Māṇava,
when those Dharma-preachers wish to preach the Dharma.
Māṇava, you should maintain mindfulness of those six days of practice without abandoning them or taking rest;
in this way, all dharmas can be realized and known.
In that gateway of the syllable *ka*, the linguistic explanation proceeds in an uninterrupted succession; therein,
with the syllable *a* as the first, it is conjoined with wisdom,
and only when the twenty-one phrases are complete is the whole perfected.
Māṇava, as for what is called "instruction," it consists precisely of these twenty-one phrases in their proper sequence without confusion.
Māṇava, for this reason, the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, appear only rarely.
Why is this? At that time, there will be no such practice of the Dharma;
although there may be many people, in the end none will be able to practice in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, there were also immeasurable sentient beings who initially gave rise to hearts of love and admiration for this Dharma;
yet when it came to the actual practice, they mostly gave way to alarm and fear, ultimately gaining nothing at all.
Māṇava, if there should be another person who thinks thus:
"By practicing in this way, I shall attain the accomplishment of all Buddha-dharmas."
That constitutes attachment.
If this attachment were the Buddha-dharma,
why was it that in the past, at the beginning of the kalpa, human beings...
Regarding internal and external things, there is neither self nor what belongs to a self;
one does not cling to any phenomena and does not rely on contrived effort.
The fruition of retribution arises spontaneously, and the intended object is immediately attained.
Thereafter, they gradually gave rise to a competitive spirit and lost the natural fruit-retribution of various flavors, O māṇava.
For this reason, you should know that the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, never cling to the enlightenment of a Buddha.
You should not give rise to attachment toward it.
Those who are attached cannot experience happiness.
Why is this? For attachment is the root of all suffering.
Māṇava, you should observe the people of Uttarakuru;
although they share the same human body as those in the other three directions, their karmic retribution is the most supreme.
Although they may have lacked acts such as giving during their lives,
after their deaths they all attained rebirth in the celestial palaces of the desire realm, O māṇava.
You should know this:
unconditioned phenomena can lead to the experience of happiness for a long time,
whereas conditioned phenomena involve attachment to a self and what belongs to a self.
There is not a single unwholesome dharma that this person does not undergo. Māṇava,
as for these unwholesome dharmas:
That which is called all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) and the cycle of birth and death;
therefore, the Tathāgata constantly admonishes you not to be attached to any conditioned dharmas, O māṇava.

To neither create nor become attached to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is precisely what the Tathāgata has ultimately proclaimed as the practice of the five perfections (*pāramitā*), such as generosity. Therefore,
it is taught that in all circumstances one should mutually cultivate and train in these various perfections.
What is meant by "perfuming cultivation"?
Having practiced giving, one is then able to listen to the Dharma;
upon reaching the place where the Dharma is being taught, one is then able to inquire about it.
When they encounter a superior teaching during their inquiries, they immediately seek to study it.
If they come to know that all phenomena are without superiority,
without self, without grasping, without arising, and without emergence—
When one is able to know all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as they truly are,
at that time one attains true faith (*śraddhendriya*) toward all Tathāgatas;
furthermore, one is able to arouse diligent effort (*vīrya*).
How can one give rise to a mind of diligent effort?
Because there are such great skillful means,
one is then able to swiftly resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
May we always be able to practice within this Dharma and ultimately realize it for ourselves;
when hearing such an exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā, may we not give rise to fear or terror.
Māṇava, how can one be free from fear and terror therein?
It is because they maintain a perception of equanimity toward all things.
What is the perception of equanimity?
It refers to being without expectation regarding all phenomena and without a contentious mind. Why is this?
"Because of the perception of them as being like illusions and transformations, Māṇava;
this is the explanation that reveals the meaning."
In these various pāramitās, there is liberation,
because the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the purpose of severing disputes and because he does not give rise to contention or rivalry.
"Although birth is severed, it is not [absolutely] severed. 46.

Chapter on Conditioned Arising (*Pratītyasamutpāda-varga*). From the *Mahādharmapradīpa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, Chapter Forty-Six on Conditioned Arising. At that time, the bodhisattvas again addressed the Buddha Emitting Light, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is it called ‘causing birth to be uninterrupted yet not completely severed’?
The Buddha said:
If it is thus, then among the true explanations of all phenomena there is no room for doubt.
Because there is no room for doubt, one realizes this through such direct knowledge;
at that time, one causes [the continuity] to arise as neither interrupted nor non-interrupted.
By upholding this practice of the Dharma, one attains the further shore.
Even as I now speak thus without interruption,
sentient beings are still unable to understand it.
How much more so for one who is able to receive and uphold the Dharma?
O Māṇava, it is like the great ocean, which is always able to contain all the great rivers.
And although hundreds of thousands of streams and currents flow into it,
that great ocean is never filled.
All such sentient beings alike possess the three kinds of greed, flattery, and manifold evils;
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly proclaim for them all the Dharma gates, such as the Buddha-bodhi.
If he could not even receive it when it was never interrupted,
how much less so when it was interrupted at times and not spoken? O Māṇava!
For this reason, the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, have never ceased raining down the great Dharma rain. Why is this?
I do not wish for those future sentient beings— who are deluded, blind, and sightless— to fall into unwholesome paths. O Māṇava,
it is just as all the world knows there are days and nights because of the orbs of the sun and moon.
The wheel of the Dharma is likewise in all respects.
If there are Dharma masters who preach the Dharma for others,
and those people seek the Dharma, reciting and studying it until they have mastered it thoroughly.
Furthermore, they are able to universally expound the teachings to act as a lamp of light for the world;
for those sentient beings who are mired in the darkness of sleep and blindness and cannot sever the wheel-like net of birth and death,
they preach so that it may be severed.

Furthermore, for those sentient beings who are obstructed by envy, lack of faith, and being constantly shrouded, entangled, and bound by these three things, thereby falling into the evil destinies, [the Bodhisattva] kindles the great torch of the Dharma.
By means of this light, sentient beings perceive the Dharma.
If sentient beings have fallen into the evil realms, they shall immediately and swiftly emerge from them.
Having already abandoned those perilous and evil paths,
they each seek together the level and correct path.
Māṇava, as for the level and straight path,
it is that which can lead one to remain far removed from dangerous and evil paths.
This is the level and straight path. Māṇavas,
if you do not have faith in and practice according to such teachings, it will be difficult for you to attain liberation.
Those who are able to believe and practice shall open the gate of great benefit for all the world.
Having attained the Dharma, they shall in turn teach and instruct one another.
All sentient beings who hear this will act as witnesses;
and those sentient beings will each say to one another,
"The Tathāgata has taught the true Dharma for my sake."
Furthermore, he showed us his non-perverted teaching: "Māṇava,
you should thus apply yourself with diligence and without slackening, or else engage in right action."
Because right action is accomplished, one is far removed from dust and defilement and is free from attachment.
Because there is no attachment, one attains pure vision.
Because vision is pure, there is no longer any cold or heat.
Because all worldly affairs are accomplished through right and wholesome karma,
other sentient beings further engage in various heterodox teachings and unwholesome karmic actions that differ from this.
One should give rise to a mind of equanimity toward that person and should personally contemplate and cultivate the remedial dharmas.
Once one has attained the practice and study of such dharmas, [one will be liberated].
One will then be able, amidst those sixty-two kinds of evil and false views,
to attain true knowledge and vision, achieve the genuine Dharma,
and eliminate all obstacles to reality as it is.
Furthermore, Māṇava,
if a Dharma-preacher constantly expounds the essentials of the Dharma for hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings who possess the faculty of faith.
Or again, there may be someone who, for the sake of even one or two sentient beings who have broken the precepts, hold wrong views, or commit grave evils,
preaches the Dharma for as little as a single snap of the fingers;
regardless of whether those wicked people accept it or not.
The merit obtained by that Dharma-preacher surpasses the aforementioned mass of blessings, being immeasurable and boundless.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, in all future births, he shall always attain diligence and valor to make offerings to all Buddhas.
At that time, although there may be many kinds of beings, whether human or non-human, who feel fear in their hearts upon hearing the true Dharma,
you should simply continue to preach the true Dharma for them.
Māṇava, you should observe that all sentient beings are constantly possessed of such immeasurable evil desires, flattery, deception, and pride.
Enveloped and bound by the darkness of ignorance,
because of this envelopment and obscuration, one gives rise to great terror regarding these phenomena.
Due to this self-induced terror, one is unable to practice the Dharma.
Even if one were to speak hypothetically,
one would still be unable to cause others to accept and practice it;
or at times, one might recognize within oneself the obstacles posed by afflictions.
They said to one another,
"We now possess such manifold evils;
though we have heard the True Dharma, we do not abandon our various views."
"I must eliminate all such views.
How should they be eliminated?
I now know for myself that I must eliminate all views."
If one accepts various views and does not sever them,
one enters the dark forest of false views;
because of these false views, one is constantly bound, confined, and entangled within birth and death.
If I can sever the root of all views,
I shall naturally be liberated from the fetters of birth and death.
Māṇava, when the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, speaks for the sake of others,
no one who hears and receives it will ever give rise to fear.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata,
the World-Honored One, being himself free from fear,
possesses no deficiency whatsoever in the qualities of a Buddha.
When speaking to others, it is so that those who hear may increase their wholesome karma. O māṇava,
when hearing the Dharma...
"You all must not become attached to these dharmas;
you should simply be single-minded and give rise to no other thoughts.
[This is] the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
It is for this purpose, Māṇava, that the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones,
appear in the world; indeed, they have only this one concern.
It is for the sake of benefiting all the world and purifying the eye of the world,
by severing the obstacles of all non-paths, O māṇava.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, speak with but a single voice,
yet cause those sentient beings to understand it each according to their own kind;
this is the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s supernormal power.
Therefore, this is so. The Tathāgata expounds the meanings of all dharmas with a single voice;
he is able to attain immeasurable wisdom through a single meaning.
If one can, by means of a single wisdom, immediately shatter the roots of the sixty-two kinds of false views,
causing all sentient beings to be entirely free from all defilements and impurities.
If there is a place of supreme evil and extreme terror,
where sentient beings receive bodies and perform various karmic actions,
the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma therein to teach and transform them, thereby delivering and rescuing sentient beings.
Without ceasing, he instructs and admonishes sentient beings.
"If you do not commit such evil karma, you will never be born here," says the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One; there is no other way.
Please instruct me on how to sever the aggregates, bases, and elements of karmic activity—all of which are conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Rebirth is likewise so;
all conditioned formations and the assumption of bodies within the entire world are such.
I have instructed them all not to engage in such things;
for these various matters, I have constantly proclaimed that there is no heaven,
no human realm, and even no life or wealth.
All worldly activities are entirely non-existent.
If there were an agent, there would be rebirth.
What, then, is an agent?
All conditioned activities that are performed are themselves the taking of birth.
If one takes a subsequent birth, you should know that within this there is no sentient being who does not take birth.
You should all know that those who perform various conditioned activities are precisely those who take birth.
Furthermore, māṇava,
it is like a great nāga king who universally raises a vast cloud that covers everything.
A great rain poured down, thoroughly moistening the great earth.
It caused all trees and groves to flourish and grow luxuriantly,
and all the hundred grains and fruits were brought to full maturity.
All these sentient beings depend on this for their livelihood;
even the various animals likewise thrive thereby, O māṇava.
If female cows eat lush, succulent grass and drink clear, flowing water,
and are always kept well-fed and satiated, one can then obtain milk from them;
from milk comes curd, and from curd comes fresh butter.
From fresh butter comes clarified butter;
from clarified butter comes ghee.
Thus it is, young man.
You should not give rise to fear regarding all phenomena produced through dependent origination.
Nor should you say: "How can it be said that there are sentient beings, or that there are no sentient beings?"
"You should simply observe well the causal conditions of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
young brahmin.
It is like what a person sees in a dream while asleep— whether they have actually done it or not."
They are all events experienced during the time of waking.
Furthermore, just as a seed has no fixed characteristic,
if one examines its form and substance, it cannot be said that it is destroyed, nor can it be said that it is not destroyed.
Why is this? If one says that a sprout is definitely destroyed, it will not arise; if it is definitely not destroyed, it likewise does not emerge.
It is the same for all conditioned phenomena produced through causes and conditions.
They arise due to the conceptualization and discrimination of deluded thoughts; therein,
there is truly no one who can accomplish them,
nor is there anyone who sees them.
In this way, Māṇava,
the Tathāgata does not say that there definitely exists a sentient being,
nor does he say that there definitely does not exist a sentient being.
The Tathāgata teaches only that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and cease from causes and conditions.
How do phenomena arise and cease through causes and conditions?
It is said: because of this, that exists.
When that arises, this arises;
when that is absent, this is absent;
when that ceases, this ceases.
If all phenomena arise from conditions,
how can it be definitively stated that a *pudgala* exists?
For this reason:
The Tathāgata does not say that there definitely exists a sentient being;
nor does he say that the gods, humans, and those in other realms of existence cease to exist.
He says only this: one who cannot relinquish attachment to inverted conceptualizations that claim "there is a sentient being" falls into the deepest darkness of ignorance.
I only command that you abandon [them] and show them the correct path;
do not ever again take pleasure in such individuals (pudgala), O māṇava.
That true Dharma is indestructible;
even for the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, a mere blade of grass is not something they would wish to destroy,
much less cause the extinction of a *pudgala*.
If it were to perish and be destroyed,
such a thing is impossible. For this reason:
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always speak thus:
there is not a single dharma that can be accomplished;
yet, furthermore, it is not that dharmas produced by causes and conditions do not exist.
Yet it is not that there is no attachment or perversion. Māṇava,
there is not a single dharma that is apart from causes and conditions.
Because there are causes and conditions,
it is therefore said that there are the characteristics of a person (pudgala) and that there are things which manifest the world.
One should encourage them to understand wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, Māṇava,
the perception of objects therein is precisely the perception of a raft.
Because of the perception of the board, one knows the perceptions of all things. What is the thing?
What is the board?
What is called "things" refers to dwelling within the conceptualization of things through false discrimination,
thereby creating all future conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Māṇava, for what reason is it further called "a thing"?
Because through such conceptualization, one performs manifold activities.
Therefore, it is called a "thing" (vastu),
because its prior and posterior limits are unknowable,
just like the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala).
Furthermore, if there are persons who conceive the notion of a wind-wheel,
they should be understood as abiding within the notion of a plank.
Māṇava, just as that wind-wheel does not remain for even a single moment of thought,
so too it is with all sentient beings who ride upon the winds of karma.
After those sentient beings have performed their karmic actions,
they further engage in various formations and thus achieve them.
Having achieved them, they never once give rise to even a single thought of awakening.
"What we have done since the distant past was not good;
through conceptual discrimination of empty phenomena,
we have wandered in saṃsāra and transmigrated through birth and death without ever dwelling for even a moment, yet we were neither aware of this nor could we see its limit."
Not knowing its breadth or narrowness, nor recognizing its smallness or greatness,
they neither see nor perceive that they constantly dwell upon such a wind-wheel of karmic activity;
coming and going, revolving in circles, they are unable to escape on their own.
It is like one born blind who has never seen form;
if someone else were to come and question him, how could he possibly answer?
Or it is like a foolish guide who cannot reach his destination.
Suppose someone were to come and ask about the characteristics of the path;
since he does not know them, how could he possibly answer?
Even if he were to utter some words, they would certainly lack any rational basis.
O Māṇavas, it is likewise with all sentient beings who ride upon the wheel of conditioned formations;
they revolve without ceasing, neither perceiving nor knowing [their movement].
And when those sentient beings ride upon this wind-wheel as they come and go, [they remain unaware].
It has no beginning, middle, or end;
its limits cannot be found, and it is entirely unknown, unseen, and unthought of.
Furthermore, O māṇava.
At that time, the blind man thought to himself:
"I should now dwell upon this wind-circle;
I have the notion that it is possible to remain stationed within this wind-circle."
Having reflected thus,
from beginning to end his mindfulness increases moment by moment without interruption.
At a later time, that blind man may attain a temporary state of stability.
He then wished to descend from this wind-circle,
yet he did not descend, further thinking to himself:
"If I can now see this path, there will be a place for me to descend, and I shall find a place to stay."
Having already attained stability, I should remain at rest for a short while myself.
Later, that blind man again thought to himself:
"Whether I see or do not see today, I shall remain for only a brief time."
Having reflected thus, he attains a temporary stay.
Having stayed, he reflects, "Now I have attained a stay," whereupon a sense of pleasure arises and his exhaustion is removed.
Yet I still do not see the path by which one descends;
how does one descend from this wind-circle?
If I were to see it, I would know the place where the wind-circles come and go.
Māṇava, while that blind man was forming such a thought,
he encountered a skilled physician who was well-versed in treating the eyes.
Although he encountered him, his eyes did not see him.
At that time, the skilled physician,
out of compassion for the blind man and in order to treat his eyes, went immediately to his location.
He asked the blind man,
"Can your eyes see forms in this way?
The blind man replied:
"If my eyes are like this, how can I see forms?
If I were to see, I would know the correct path.
The skilled physician spoke these words.
"Furthermore, open your eyes so that I may examine you;
if you are curable, I shall treat you.
Having heard this, the blind man [did as instructed].
He immediately opened his eyes wide to show them to the skilled physician.
At that time, the physician, having thoroughly examined the disease within the man's eyes,
immediately understood the fundamental cause of the ailment.
According to what was required, he established a method of treatment—
whether by cauterization, acupuncture, scraping, or medicinal application—
and having thus prepared such prescriptions for treating the eyes, he acted accordingly.
He said to the blind man,
"I shall now explain for you an excellent method of treatment to remove your eye disease and enable you to see all forms."
"If you were to see it, would you not rejoice?

Then the blind man said to the skilled physician, "As for me, having been blind since birth, I fear I am beyond the reach of rescue; yet if I may be saved as the physician has instructed, what words can express my joy?"
The skilled physician spoke again:
"This matter is indeed difficult, yet it is within my power to accomplish.
You need only give rise to faith in me."
"This is my family trade; you need not doubt it.
If you wish to verify it, you should ask the people:
'How effective was his treatment for this ailment?'"
The blind man spoke again,
"Great Master, what do you intend to do here?
The physician replied to him:
"Do not grieve so much.
I have committed no transgression therein.
Just wait a short while, and I shall prepare the medicine."
The matter must be examined with great care; one must not act with haste or agitation.
If one acts with such urgency, the task may prove difficult to accomplish.
Having thus instructed him, that skilled physician—
He then mixed the eye medicine with that blind man.
Once the medicine was prepared, he placed it in the man's eyes, and his vision became slightly clear.
Having regained some clarity, he quickly returned from the physician’s place.
At that time, after the blind man had been treated with medicine for but a short while,
the cataracts in his eyes were entirely eliminated.
Because the cataracts were removed, his vision immediately became clear and bright.
Suddenly they beheld things they had never seen since birth;
they also saw those blind men riding upon that wind-wheel,
wandering and circulating back and forth, unable to stop themselves.
He sighed in lamentation, saying:
"Alas, how tragic!
These blind men have also long dwelt within this wind-circle."
The cycle of coming and going has never ceased;
from the beginning, no one has ever explained this matter to them,
nor has there been any teaching to treat or heal their blindness.
He then had this thought:
"How am I any different from these blind men?
Having encountered the Great King of Physicians, I have found him."
"Having been freed from congenital blindness, I have reached this day.
How could I alone receive such merit?
I shall now return from here and request the King of Physicians."
He causes all these blind people to receive healing.
At that time, the man further thinks to himself:
"For now, I shall first inform the blind people."
Having explained this great matter so that he first understood its essence,
he then guided him to seek out a great physician.
Having reflected thus, he immediately addressed the blind man.
"You all should pause for a moment;
I now wish to declare something to you.
Then the group of blind men replied to that person:
"I have no place to dwell.
That person asked again,
"In what place do you now dwell?"
The blind men spoke again:
"We cannot remain here today;
how could you possibly remain here alone?"
That person further said to the group of blind men:
"When you see later on, you will naturally know for yourselves who has a dwelling place and who has no dwelling place."
The blind men spoke again,
"How can you alone know enough to surpass the collective deliberations of our group?
That man replied:
In the past, I too was just like you;
because I lacked eyes, I rode upon that wind-wheel,
wandering and transmigrating without end.
People of the world mostly suffer from this affliction,
laboring through the long night upon the wheel of non-abiding;
yet I have fortunately encountered the King of Physicians.
The Great Master, out of compassion, removed the cataracts from my eyes. By reason of this,
I see thus, I know thus, and I speak thus.
Today you have sunk into this wind-wheel;
you do not see it, you do not know it, you are not aware of it, and you do not believe it.
If even one among you were to understand it together with the others, [you would all be saved].
"Stay here for even a brief moment;
I shall seek that King of Physicians for you.
Once the King of Physicians has brought his mind down [to you], you shall know and believe it yourself."
By following the teacher’s words, one will surely obtain great benefit.
At that time, among the assembly of blind people, there were those who possessed wisdom;
having heard these words, they immediately thought to themselves:
"We should now receive this person's instruction.
What harm could there be in staying for a short while?
If we must follow their teaching as instructed, our joy will be especially profound."
Even if it does not turn out as he said, I shall have no cause for regret.
Furthermore, by staying here for a short while, I shall gain much:
I will have the opportunity to associate with virtuous people, and I will also resolve my own doubts.
"For these reasons, I shall now resolutely remain here and no longer harbor any doubt.
At that time, the blind man possessed of wisdom, having thought thus,
immediately consulted with the other blind men regarding their advance or retreat.
He addressed the assembly, saying:
"I have long been weary and exhausted;
having suddenly received these kind words, I shall now pause for a while and will not depart."
Having spoken thus,
he then replied to the previously blind Jñānin:
"If you know the time, sir."
He acted for our sake according to what was appropriate.
At that time, the former blind man, though born blind,
having been granted his sight, became possessed of light.
He proceeded at will without further obstruction and immediately formed this thought:
"I have now granted permission to those immeasurable blind beings, who have spoken these words."
"I shall open the light of your eyes.
First, we must go before the feet of the Great Master to offer our profound thanks for his past virtues, and then report this matter."
First, wisdom begins to arise.
That Great King of Physicians has already gone before on the path;
having seen him from afar, wisdom gives rise to profound joy and immeasurable exultation.
He then thought to himself:
"This Great King of Physicians has first bestowed eyes upon me;
he has guided me toward the light and removed my suffering."
He bestows upon me immeasurable and boundless happiness;
he brings me joy and relieves my exhaustion.
I should now go quickly to his presence and prostrate at his feet.
One should make offerings through ascetic practice of the body, praise with wondrous words,
give rise to a mind of rare aspiration, and show respect and reverence;
whatever may be required, all such things should be presented as offerings.
Having thus recollected,
he went to that place and, in accordance with his prior intention,
bore her virtues, expressed his gratitude, and offered him the utmost reverent service.
Furthermore, wishing to make a request on behalf of those blind ones,
he gave rise once more to a rare, pure, and reverent mind,
and further aroused a profound sense of earnest compassion and deep mindfulness.
He addressed the Great King of Physicians, saying:
"I have previously received your grace, which bestowed upon me the clear eye;
you have further enabled me to attain the wisdom of all skillful means."
Today there are immeasurable and innumerable beings born blind who,
riding upon the wheel of non-abiding, undergo endless suffering.
We pray only that you, the Great Physician, [will save them].
To eliminate their congenital blindness, he bestowed upon them eye medicine,
causing them to rejoice no differently than if it were me.
At that time, the King of Physicians, out of compassion for the blind, [acted thus].
He then went in person to where those people were.
Having arrived there, he addressed them, saying:
"You blind men, you were born without eyes."
"Now, I truly wish to see the object.
Then the assembly of blind men said to the King of Physicians,
"O Great Master,"
"We have never seen such a thing before;
today we contemplate it, so what more need be said?
The King of Physicians asked again.
"What have you not seen since the past?
And what is it that you now wish to see?
He replied again:
"Great Master, from the past until now, regarding the path upon which I have traveled,
I have merely thought it was the Way; yet in truth, I have not seen whether this road is short or long, nor near or far."
They did not perceive any signs of a beginning, middle, or end.
The King of Physicians then said to that group of blind men:
"Furthermore, this path is not the correct path."
"What you have practiced since the past was not the Way.
The blind men spoke again,
"Nevertheless, we have already conceived the notion of a path within it."
The King of Physicians spoke again,
"You should not give rise to such a thought," and he then pointed to that blind man of wisdom, saying:
"You should know that this person was formerly just like you;
later, realizing it was not so, he abandoned it long ago.
He then addressed the group of blind men again:
"If you all believe today that this man was like you in the past, I shall then punish you.
Thus, I proceeded step by step to carry out the act of punishment.
Thereupon, the group of blind men said to the King of Physicians:
"Indeed, Great Master!
You yourself know the proper time; how could we dare not obey your command?
At that time, that King of Physicians—
They should again prepare this same eye medicine used previously;
it shall heal all blind people so that they all equally obtain such pure eyes.
Because their eyes are opened, they all cry out with great joy:
Alas! We have now attained great bliss.
Yet, from the past until now, we have wandered aimlessly upon a pathless road within the wheel of great darkness, O Māṇava.
"You all should know that the Great King of Physicians who treats the eyes therein is none other than the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
He is like that first blind physician who, by treating them first, caused them to receive pure vision."
These are those sons of good family who are Dharma-preachers;
as for the rest of the blind who have obtained pure eyes,
they are the various sentient beings who uphold this dharma-gate of the sutra.
Māṇava, for this reason, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
has extensively provided you with analogies to elucidate such points of meaning.
Māṇava, you should train therein as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
If anyone wishes to train as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, [they should do so here].
One should train in this way,
Māṇava; for this reason.
The Tathāgata, Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha has fully provided this analogy for you all in order to explain its meaning, O māṇava.
If you would train yourselves as the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,
you should train in these gateways to the characteristics of all phenomena.
Furthermore, you should first engage in such reflection:
How shall I now employ various skillful means to act as a great light for those sentient beings who are born blind in the darkness, opening their eyes?
Māṇava, this is the explanation of the first practice of great loving-kindness and great compassion.
If you see those sentient beings who are obscured and blind, [you should act accordingly].
Furthermore, one must apply such methods of treatment.
Once treated in this manner, he will perceive the Dharma for himself;
he does not follow others, nor does he practice anywhere—that is to say, the wind-circle.
Māṇava, these are the ordinary beings and all sentient beings who have not yet attained the True Dharma and lack a place of abiding.
