Chapter Forty-Seven: Resolute Belief and Understanding.

Chapter Forty-Eight: Avoiding Evil Friends; Chapter Forty-Nine: Discerning the Field and Praising Giving. Chapter Forty-Seven: Resolute Faith. At that time, those bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān,
when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are about to expound the Dharma for others,
they should first request the Buddha [to do so]."
"If others come to ask about the boundless Dharma-gates,
how shall I explain them for the sake of sentient beings?
Furthermore, whether sentient beings ask or do not ask,"
Furthermore, what is meant by "speaking again" and "furthermore speaking to others to some extent"?
I now ask this question;
I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain it for me.
World-Honored One,
if there should be someone who ascends the lion throne desiring to preach the Dharma,
by what skillful means therein should they definitively obtain this treasury of the Tathāgata’s karma and immeasurable eloquence?
Having never entered into these three teachings,
nor having anyone explain them to them,
they have neither read, recited, practiced, nor upheld them.
"How does one attain the spontaneous manifestation of fully endowed eloquence?
At that time, the Buddha Emitting Light addressed the bodhisattvas,
saying, "Māṇava."
There is no such expedient in the world;
it can only be obtained by reading, reciting, and upholding this sūtra within the Dharani-door of the Treasury of the Three Teachings and Karmas.
Or, at times, there may be someone who, through the majestic power bestowed by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and by means of the Dharma-power,
attains it, O Māṇava.
If there is such a dharani-dharma-gate,
it is precisely through the recitation of this sutra that one attains accomplishment, not by being apart from it.
If one hears from another, one understands it swiftly just as it was heard and does not forget it;
whatever speech or other teachings are spoken, once they have passed through the ear,
they shall never be forgotten for as long as one lives.
If there are those who have never heard [this teaching] before,
they will not understand it even when hearing it explained for the first time; therefore,
it should be explained in full detail for them.

Māṇava, it is impossible for a person who does not uphold these three teachings— the Tathāgata’s treasury of karma— and does not receive and maintain them as they were spoken, to be fully endowed with all forms of eloquence.
Māṇava, if any sentient beings fully receive and uphold this Dharma-gate,
they will naturally attain immeasurable eloquence.
You should now know this, O Guṇagañja māṇava:
if there is anyone who hears this spoken by the Buddha in person, or through the power of his empowerment.
If there are those who possess the faculty of faith and the power of wisdom,
and personally approach a Dharma Master to seek and inquire about the Dharma, O Māṇava.
One should know that all these have extensively accumulated the roots of goodness of the three vehicles.
If there are those who follow any one of the vehicles,
at that time the Dharma teacher should establish the Buddha-dharma for them accordingly.
How much more so for those who possess the three vehicles,
O Māṇava? Or perhaps there may be hundreds,
thousands, ten thousands, or millions of beings of various kinds.
At one time, they gathered together at the place of this Dharma Master.
Each of them asked about various Dharma gates, various meanings and phrases, and various syllables.
At that time, the Dharma Master [addressed] those immeasurable and diverse sentient beings.
Free from doubt and without fear,
they respond to questions with unimpeded eloquence,
explaining the gateways of the Dharma without obstruction.
Furthermore, māṇava,
it is as if there were a person who has been a thief since birth,
possessing great courage and the skillful means of a thief’s wisdom.
Even though he dwells in the midst of hundreds or thousands of people, he feels no fear or anxiety whatsoever. Why is this?
Because he has long since perfected the wisdom of a thief.
Māṇava, that Dharma-preacher is likewise: when he preaches the Dharma,
although he is situated in the midst of a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of beings.
He explains profound meanings and answers questions as they arise,
without any obstruction, causing everyone to rejoice until not even a single thought of fear arises.
Why is this? Because he has previously accomplished unimpeded eloquence.
Furthermore, māṇava:
Just as the Nāga King Anavatapta can rain down various streams to fill the four great oceans,
so too is it with this Māṇava;
that Dharma teacher who has mastered the Tripiṭaka and fulfills all needs is likewise.
Māṇava, it is also like the Nāga King Anavatapta, who possesses great skillful means and is able to produce river water that accords with the intentions and wishes of all sentient beings.
In this way, Māṇava, that Dharma-preacher,
having first accomplished the treasury of the three types of verbal instruction,
is able to provide skillful guidance for all beings.
It causes all sentient beings to sever their doubts;
that they all thoroughly penetrate and fulfill the ocean of their vows is likewise so.
At that time, the bodhisattvas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān,
are these three collections of skillful means and karmic teachings contained solely within this sūtra of the dhāraṇī gateway?"
Is it also found within other sūtras and various dharma-gates?
We now petition the World-Honored One,
desiring to understand this definitive meaning.
"World-Honored One,
we have all together reflected thus: the Tathāgata,
the World-Honored One, possesses great skillful means."
I fear that today you will not further explain the meaning for us, leaving us in doubt and unable to understand.
Why is this? Because the realm of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom is profound and far-reaching.
Therefore, World-Honored One, we have already conceived a sense of alarm and fear.
It is as if there were someone who, wishing to cross the great ocean by swimming with both arms, sought to reach the further shore.
You should know that such a person will surely lose their life. Why is this?
Because there is no one in the world who can cross the great ocean by the strength of their hands alone.
World-Honored One,
we are likewise.
Just like those foolish people who are unable to follow and place their trust in the Tathāgata.
Desiring to measure the Buddha’s wisdom with their own minds,
at that time the Tathāgata Prabhāsa addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "So it is, so it is."
Māṇava, if one can seek with diligence, how could there be anything not attained?
What you have just asked is truly appropriate for the occasion.
In this matter, do not harbor thoughts of weariness or indolence, nor give rise to fear. You should,
by means of unimpeded wisdom and eloquence,
clarify the principles and meanings, and correctly expound the words and letters.
Thoroughly cultivating the three types of action to transcend the world,
purely upholding the prohibitive precepts while contemplating with a single mind,
and accumulating true wisdom through courageous diligence.
Do not cast off the heavy burden, do not retreat from your original resolve to seek all-knowledge,
and sever the web of doubt regarding all dharma-gates;
thus be fully endowed with such skillful means.
Having consulted the Tathāgata many times and having also observed for himself, he thought:
"One should uphold the True Dharma by means of four methods;
one should listen to and receive what has not yet been heard from the presence of the Buddhas."
If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you are to protect and uphold the True Dharma,
then regarding those evil beings in the final age who revile and insult this sutra,
you should discipline them strictly according to the Dharma.
Until the end of your life, you must constantly seek and entreat [the deity];
you must not abandon [this practice] through negligence, indolence,
or laziness, O māṇava.
Among these teachings, you should regard this as a matter of great importance.
Whether in the presence of the Tathāgata or his disciples,
you should always inquire about and request such true Dharma.
Having already cultivated this for oneself, one further brings others to accomplishment.
Through this, one successively teaches and transforms immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing them to enter this Dharma-gate.
Furthermore, O māṇava:
If, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek the Dharma,
there is not a single sentient being in the world to whom they do not go. Why is this?
Desiring to cause all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm to enter ultimate nirvana,
for this reason, when a bodhisattva seeks the Dharma,
they constantly make this vow.
From this day forward, in whatever place I may be born,
may I always hear that which I have not yet heard, even if it be but a single verse, a single phrase, or a single word; for its sake,
I shall not begrudge my body or life, but shall offer up my head, eyes, limbs, and all my members.
How much more so for all external wealth and possessions that one would wish to cherish as a treasure and refuse to relinquish?
Furthermore, O māṇava:
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of seeking the Dharma,
go to any place where the Dharma may be found to seek it—
even at times visiting the homes of caṇḍālas.
At times, he would go to those abodes of rākṣasas,
even to places inhabited by birds and beasts;
having heard [of them], he would go to all such places to inquire and seek the Dharma.
At other times, they would insist that the Bodhisattva say:
"If you can remain in my house for a full thousand years,
I shall then preach the Dharma to you."
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva remained at that place for a full thousand years,
attending to and serving him with whatever he required.
Having heard the Dharma, one should report it back and then return.
Furthermore, O māṇava,
if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of seeking the Dharma...
If such diligence can serve even outcastes, down to rākṣasas, evil spirits, and animals, for a full thousand years,
how much more so could it not be applied toward sentient beings who abide in the roots of goodness of the True Dharma, and toward wise and great Dharma masters?
By hearing the true Dharma, one cuts off delusions and resolves doubts.
Furthermore, Māṇava,
such is the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Having heard the Dharma, his heart was filled with great joy,
and he thought of going to repay the kindness of the one who had preached it.
You should know that at that time, material wealth could not be used to repay the kindness of the Dharma-preacher.
For what reason?
O māṇava, it is because her kindness is so great.
Even toward the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones,
there is no skillful means by which one can repay their kindness. Why is this so?
Because it is weighty.
What is meant by "weighty"?
It refers to the gift of Dharma.
Now, among all forms of giving,
the gift of Dharma is the foremost, the most excellent, the most sublime,
the unsurpassed, and the supreme of the unsurpassed.
It is incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless;
it cannot be compared to that gift of material wealth. Why is this?
Because there is no grasping or attachment, O Māṇava,
as for the gift of material wealth:
This is the giving of afflictions that involve attachment to signs, characterized by the outflows of birth and death and conditioned existence.
As for the giving of the Dharma,
it is the giving of wisdom that is exclusively directed toward transcendence, free from outflows, unconditioned, unimpeded, and signless.
Furthermore, as for the gift of Dharma,
no one can disparage it nor can anyone praise it.
If there should be anyone who reviles or disparages this gift of Dharma, [it would be like disparaging space].
You should know that such a person slanders the Triple Gem. Māṇava,
you ought to reflect deeply upon this matter.
Having respectfully requested [the teaching], they heard it and practiced it;
having practiced it themselves, they expounded it widely for others.
Because it was proclaimed in its entirety, the Dharma endures for a long time.
It also causes the wholesome dharmas of the world to increase.
Furthermore, māṇava,
it is like a merchant who, with a small amount of goods and wealth, engages in trade to seek profit.
This person’s assets gradually increase over the years;
their storehouses become filled, and they provide relief to many people.
If they do not engage in trade, their wealth will not grow.
Later, encountering famine and losing his family and dependents,
O māṇava, that Dharma-preacher was just like this.
One should constantly proclaim [the Dharma] without ceasing or becoming lax. Why is this?
If one constantly proclaims the Dharma, the Dharma will abide, increase, and bring benefit to humans and devas.
One brings the roots of goodness to maturity and eliminates all evils.
If one does not proclaim and propagate the Dharma, it will decline and perish;
for the evil realms will flourish while the worlds of humans and devas will diminish.
Furthermore, māṇava, it is like a caravan leader who,
leading a large company of followers and equipped with weapons and ornaments,
carries various goods and wealth as he traverses dangerous and difficult terrains.
While on the road, they encountered other merchants.
At that time, the leader clearly instructed them to protect the weak and guard one another from front to back, organizing the ranks according to the Dharma.
O Māṇava, even when encountering bandits amidst perilous difficulties,
one's wealth and property shall not be lost, and one will pass through safely and in peace.
That Dharma-preacher is likewise so:
although he dwells amidst an immeasurable assembly of hundreds of thousands and fully proclaims such a gateway to the True Dharma,
within that great assembly there are many disciples of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One.
Being intelligent and of sharp wit, they skillfully understand its meaning, reciting, reading, and upholding it.
By the power of such recitation and retention, they encounter no obstacles,
even if confronted by outsiders who possess worldly wisdom and eloquence.
Hundreds of thousands of heterodox treatises,
various incantations and arts, diverse forms of eloquence,
and manifold challenges will find no ground upon which to manifest and shall naturally perish.
"How can they create such obstacles?
O māṇava, you should know this."
Within that assembly of hundreds of thousands,
although there were those with wrong views and those who were merely worldy scholars of eloquence, all those bhikṣus nevertheless...
Do not accept their words, nor perform their deeds.
Do not offer them support, nor draw near to them. Why is this?
Because they lack any increase, accomplishment, or beneficial matters, and possess only the diminution and destruction of virtue.
Chapter Forty-Eight: Avoiding Evil Friends. *Mahādharmolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, Chapter Forty-Eight: Avoiding Evil Friends. Furthermore, O Māṇava:
Suppose there were a household that prepared various kinds of exquisite and delicious meals, such as those enjoyed by a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) and unknown among ordinary humans;
such wonderful food would be the most supreme in flavor.
However, suppose there were a small amount of potent poison,
the size of a mustard seed.
Māṇava, what do you think?
Suppose there is a person who, being hungry and empty, seeks coarse food, and suddenly encounters poisoned delicacies; would they take them as food?
The bodhisattvas replied: "No."
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Māṇava."
"So it is, so it is. It is just as you have said.
If one praises and speaks of the deeds performed by those possessed of worldly wisdom and eloquence,"
Even if such a person recites or chants but a single verse or a single line,
they must not remain within the monastic community. Why is this?
Because they are not disciples of the Buddhas. Furthermore, māṇava,
it is as if there were a person who contracted the foul disease of leprosy.
Such a person shall not be allowed to enter among pure assemblies—
namely, the assemblies of kṣatriyas, brahmins, elders, or householders— and indeed,
they should not even stand for a moment within any such assembly.
How much more so when listening for a long time in a pure assembly.
Māṇava, the worldly sophists and heterodox persons are likewise thus.
Furthermore, you should not even be permitted to stand before the pure assembly for a moment,
much less sit for a long time or participate in their activities.
Moreover, O Māṇava:
For example, Māṇava, how could a jackal— vile, base, foul-smelling, with a body emaciated by scabies,
and feeding on excrement and filth— be permitted to dwell among a pride of lions?
The world’s refutation of such heterodox persons is likewise so:
these people are utterly evil and devoid of roots of goodness;
they shall never be able to dwell within the buddha-fields.
Even if they were established first, they should still be expelled. Why?

Because it would not allow sentient beings to learn such evil views, which would cause them to increase immeasurable evil karma throughout the long night, leading them to fall into the various evil destinies and undergo great suffering.
Furthermore, māṇava,
it would be better to form friendships with enemies such as caṇḍālas, butchers, and executioners,
than to dwell even for a moment with those who possess such false arguments and evil views.
Māṇava, it would be better for you to split your tongue with a sharp blade than to discourse on the Buddha-dharma with one who holds wrong views.
Māṇava, would you rather endure the suffering of hunger for a thousand years without eating than,
because of wrong views, accept the offerings of faith from others?
Māṇava, it would be better to lie upon a bed of upright iron spikes for a thousand years than to sit or lie down even for a moment with those who slander others with false arguments and evil views.
Māṇava, it would be better to walk for a thousand years over ground covered with ashes and fire than to grant a place for walking to one who possesses false arguments and evil views.
For what reason? O māṇava,
the suffering of treading upon fire for a thousand years lasts but a short time.
If one studies evil views, one will fall forever into the evil realms.
Why is this? O māṇava!
Ordinary people, being ignorant and of meager mental power, associate with evil factions and habitually accumulate their misdeeds.
Supporting one another in their wickedness, they destroy the Buddha-dharma;
having thus acted themselves, [they suffer the consequences].
Furthermore, he causes immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to learn and practice false views.
Moreover, māṇava, what do you think?
"If a person slanders the Buddha and reviles the Dharma and the Saṅgha,
will that person attain peace and happiness for a long night?
The bodhisattvas replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Māṇava."
For this reason, O māṇava,
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has earnestly proclaimed such Dharma teachings.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great compassion;
he has never abandoned even a single sentient being,
having forever severed all evil thoughts and being free from envy.
He is far removed from false speech and has no erroneous words,
O Māṇava; such is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
This is the speaker of truth; this is the speaker of reality.
Whatever dharma any sentient being wishes to receive—
He immediately employs skillful means to expound the teaching for them,
so that those immeasurable and boundless sentient beings may each attain understanding according to their own kind;
by attaining this intellectual understanding, they swiftly enter nirvana.
Māṇavas, if you see anyone proclaiming false arguments,
take care not to listen to them, nor should you pay them homage.
There is no need for sympathetic joy.
You should understand it in this way, māṇava.
You should know that even if one were to remain silent for hundreds of thousands of years,
without reading, reciting, receiving,
or upholding the sutras of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, [the merit would still be greater than that].
O Māṇava, do not dwell with those who engage in false debate,
nor read, recite, or even briefly listen to their compositions.
From this day forward, in all places,
you must carefully refrain from befriending those beings who act contrary to the Dharma;
do not dwell with them, nor draw near to them.
Why is this? If one associates with unrighteous and evil people and follows their activities,
that person will not attain peace and security for a long night.
Why is this? Because having understood it themselves, these people go on to teach others with unwholesome dharmas;
they constantly practice false dharmas in the past, future, and present.
Because you practice what is wrong, you wander through the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra. O māṇavas,
you should know that those who practice worldly dharmas have never seen or heard of the supramundane, superior dharma of the noble ones.
How much less could one who practices deviance attain realization?
Furthermore, Māṇava,
those evil sentient beings are incapable of acting as a pure field of merit for others to obtain the fruits of retribution.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, does not permit this;
he does not allow that evil and heterodox person to receive offerings from others,
nor does he permit other sentient beings to provide such an evil person with clothing, food, or various requisites.
Why is this? Because those deluded persons do not practice according to the Dharma and thus never abide within that which is in accordance with the Dharma;
they do not seek liberation and thus never abide within that which is liberation.
"O Māṇava, you should know that they are ignorant and blind; they do not practice my Dharma and abide in false teachings."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly say this:
"If sentient beings have not yet entered the True Dharma,
nor have they entered the Dharma of the Śrāvakas."
If one makes offerings [in such a manner], the karmic fruit will be diminished.

Chapter Forty-nine: Praising the Field of Merit and Commending Giving, from the *Mahādharmapradīpa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. Chapter Forty-nine: Praising the Field of Merit and Commending Giving. At that time, that Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
Māṇava, whether one makes offerings to a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) or even feeds a mere hungry dog, [the merit is equal].
According to their respective categories, all possess merit;
therefore, one should practice giving in all circumstances.
The distinctions in the resulting rewards correspond to the state of mind of the donor.
Māṇava, giving to one who maintains the precepts yields a distinct fruit;
giving to one who has broken the precepts also yields a distinct retribution.
The giver and the receiver differ in their respective conditions;
even down to the hungry dog that receives its retribution,
they are likewise different, O māṇava.
Therefore, all should diligently seek to abide in pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
up to and including all the powers and fearlessnesses.
One should seek all merits therein.
Furthermore, O Māṇava, for these reasons:
For the sake of accepting robes and food from various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,
has permitted four matters. What are these four?
That is to say, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not personally accept or store wealth, nor even food, drink, or medicinal decoctions for their own sake;
rather, whatever they require, they seek through lawful begging.
If they obtain offerings and listen to and receive the teachings of the Tathāgata,
this constitutes the first permitted matter for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, if all bodhisattva mahāsattvas constantly practice the teaching and transformation of all sentient beings.
They distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas and bring wholesome roots to maturity.
If they have any need, they seek and beg for it in accordance with the Dharma;
when they receive offerings, the Tathāgata permits them to accept them.
This constitutes the second matter for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to undertake.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, at all times,
constantly make offerings to the Tathāgatas and the stūpas of the Tathāgatas, they should seek whatever is required in accordance with the Dharma.
When offerings are received, the Tathāgata listens and accepts them;
this constitutes the third matter opened up for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly delight in reading, reciting, praising, and explaining the sūtras to reveal them to sentient beings.
If there is anything required, one should seek and beg for it according to the Dharma;
that the Tathāgata accepts offerings from others is permitted.
This constitutes the fourth matter opened up for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Māṇava, if there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to abide within these four kinds of dharmas,
you should know that their practice will increase throughout the long night and never suffer diminution.
Furthermore, they preach the Dharma of Bodhi for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing their roots of goodness to grow.
Having practiced in this manner, by whom could such Bodhisattvas receive offerings?
This refers to being worthy of receiving superior offerings from householders, lay devotees, brahmins, kings, and even universal monarchs (cakravartin).
What kind of offerings does one receive?
That is to say, dwellings, bedding, clothing, food and drink, medicinal decoctions for curing illness,
and even various kinds of wealth and requisites provided to meet all needs;
when a bodhisattva dwells in such deportment while receiving these offerings, their merit does not diminish.
Furthermore, māṇava,
if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others, having accomplished four kinds of practices in accordance with them,
obtain four fruits of retribution through these roots of goodness.
What are the four? First,
if that bodhisattva intends to dwell in the position of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) and practice the ten wholesome dharmas to transform sentient beings,
he immediately becomes a wheel-turning sage king for immeasurable thousands of lifetimes according to his wish.
Second, if that bodhisattva intends to manifest as the king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma and transform the thirty-three devas,
he shall immediately attain this according to his wish for immeasurable thousands of lifetimes.
Third, if that bodhisattva intends to leave home, renounce the world, cultivate the path, and realize the fruit of a śramaṇa,
he shall immediately attain the realization of the fruit of a śramaṇa according to his wish.
Fourth, if that bodhisattva desires to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), he shall do so.
By means of these roots of goodness, one eliminates perversions and dwells successively within all roots of goodness;
one shall certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Māṇava, these four dharmas constitute the supreme practice for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Those who are able to abide in this Dharma and are worthy of receiving offerings, as well as those who are able to give, both are said to be donning the great armor;
it should be understood in this way. Why is that?
Māṇava, among these,
one who is indolent, lacking in vigor,
or who has lost right mindfulness cannot [attain it].
Those who lack dignified deportment and delight in sleep,
who do not abandon indolence and laziness throughout the long night,
and who distance themselves from vigor while being ashamed to inquire of others.
Having accepted such offerings,
such a person would not even be fit to receive a single piece of rotten wood discarded in filth by another for six years.
For what reason? O māṇava,
if sentient beings do not abide in the True Dharma.
Within the three realms, there is not a single thing that can be extinguished.
For this reason, the Tathāgata,

the World-Honored One, does not proclaim or extensively expound such Dharma matters for those sentient beings who are thus foolish and hold false views, nor for those who do not abide in dignified deportment and do not rely upon the Buddha’s precepts.
Furthermore, Māṇava,
when all Bodhisattvas first seek the practice of the Dharma,
there are four matters that cause them to retreat from the mind that desires the Dharma.
What are the four? Māṇava,
if there is a bodhisattva who acts as an administrator for the assembly.
At times he would travel to villages and towns,
or go to royal capitals and enter royal palaces;
for the sake of sentient beings, he came and went, managing various affairs.
Yet, among that assembly, there was not a single bhikṣu who purely maintained the prohibitive precepts,
nor was there a single person who was courageous and diligent;
most were ignorant and did not understand the sūtras.
At that time, seeing that his many followers were practicing what was not the Dharma,
the Bodhisattva immediately withdrew from and abandoned his intention to seek the Dharma,
thinking: "How can I now dwell together with and live alongside such people to study this Dharma?"
Māṇava, you should observe that in this degenerate age, bhikṣus falsely assume the name of "monk" and cause others to provide for their protection;
yet those who manage monastic affairs have no heart of reverence or admiration for them.
For this reason, Māṇava,
those bodhisattvas cause such non-practicing sentient beings to quickly abandon their wholesome aspirations.
This is the first matter concerning the regression of the mind that seeks the Dharma for a beginner bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Furthermore, māṇava, if there is a bodhisattva who,
desiring to study the various meritorious practices of a bodhisattva, goes to another place to hear and receive the true Dharma.
Having arrived at that place, he first inquired about the practices of the bodhisattvas;
with diligent and courageous resolve, he acted according to what he had heard.
He observed that among that assembly, there was not a single bhikṣu capable of explaining the Dharma regarding the matters he had thus inquired about.
However, that bodhisattva, having doubts regarding the Dharma that no one could resolve,
immediately gave rise to slander and withdrew from his original resolve, O māṇava.
This is the second matter concerning the regression of the mind that seeks the Dharma for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is a beginner.
Furthermore, māṇava,
if all bodhisattvas keep in mind the relinquishing of worldly conditioned things.
That is to say, regarding such various requisites as clothing, food, and even medicinal decoctions,
one who wishes to train in the conduct of such bodhisattvas should go among the assembly of the Sangha.

He saw that the bhikṣus were sitting on high and large beds, greedily indulging in food and drink, and accumulating many impure goods; they constantly delighted in sleep, took pleasure in discussing worldly affairs, lacked the thought of wearying detachment, engaged in unwholesome reflections, followed the current of birth and death, and increased the activities of Māra.
At that time, having seen this matter, that bodhisattva withdraws and abandons his original resolve. Māṇava,
this is the third matter by which a beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva regresses from the mind seeking the Dharma.
Furthermore, māṇava,
if bodhisattvas wish to practice the supreme bliss and desire the dharma of the araṇya, [they should do so].
If one wishes to practice the cultivation of the samādhi of emptiness,
yet lacks such understanding and wisdom within oneself,
how can one properly practice the dharma of the araṇya?
Furthermore, regarding the mindfulness of the gate of the emptiness samādhi,
that bodhisattva reflects thus: "Today,
I should quickly go to the place where there are either those who have left the household life or those who remain in the household life."
He sought out and inquired about such practices as these.
Thinking that if there were someone capable of explaining this matter for him, he could then rely upon it in practice,
he went accordingly to all those who had gone forth and to all those living at home.
Having consulted those who could resolve his doubts, but finding none capable of doing so,
he thought again:
"I should now go among the assembly of bhikṣus and inquire about this matter."
Having reflected thus,
he went into the midst of the great assembly and saw the bhikṣus inquiring about this matter;
yet, not a single person in that assembly was able to provide instruction.
Not even a single person arose to rejoice in it.
When the Bodhisattva saw this, his original resolve was shattered.
Yet, those monks who were without practice—
I shall now explain such matters for you Bodhisattvas:
from this day forward, you should always accept these excellent couches and mats, various garments, and various fine foods.
The statement that the Buddha did not permit it was because he waited for an invitation from others.
O Māṇava, although those people instructed the Bodhisattva in such matters as these, [he did not accept].
Furthermore, I do not know how one should receive the Dharma:
how may one receive the food and clothing of others without harming oneself,
and having received these things, how may one attain purity?
They all do not know such matters as these, O Māṇava.
Those foolish people are possessed of what is contrary to the Dharma.
They destroy the conduct of a śramaṇa;
they are indolent, lazy, and impure, like a foul-smelling place.
These śramaṇas are withered grass, devoid of the nourishment of the precepts.
Constantly harboring greed, hatred, and delusion, how could they know such emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
Since they lack wisdom and understanding, how could they practice it?
Since they lack understanding and practice, how could they explain it?
Even if there were such a teaching, how could it eliminate doubt?
At that time, having seen this matter, that bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of slander and immediately regresses from the mind of wholesome aspiration for the Dharma.
Māṇava, this is the fourth matter concerning the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s regressive seeking for the Dharma.
Furthermore, Māṇava:
"Is there not such an evil person within this assembly?
The bodhisattvas replied,
"No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Māṇava,
such sentient beings calculate that it would be improper to accept this foul-smelling, discarded, and unwholesome food for seven days."
How much less could they receive pure and exquisite food?
This person originally lacks the physical characteristics and status of a bhikṣu who has left home and received full ordination;
by what cause, then, could they obtain the name of a member of the bhikṣu-saṃgha?
Furthermore, māṇava,

this sublime food of the devas was not originally prepared for those who practice unrighteousness, those who have violated the pure precepts, those who have fallen into various [wrong] views, or those who do not act according to the Dharma.
Māṇava, you should maintain right mindfulness;
you are now staying here on the summit of Mount Sumeru.
This food is the exquisite food of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
it is the most excellent, sublime, and supreme.
Even a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King among humans would not be able to obtain it.
How much less, O māṇava, could one who merely wears this saffron robe in name, yet is foul, impure,
and practices what is contrary to the Dharma, be worthy of receiving this divine *sūdhā* food?
For this reason, the Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has previously told you:
"Having eaten such sublime food as this, it shall cause the donor to obtain a great fruit and reward."
Māṇava, I have already explained and proclaimed in various places that a person who has broken the precepts cannot even receive from a faithful donor as much as the palm of a hand.
How much less could one possibly digest this sublime food of the devas? Why is this so?
Because for those who eat this food, no evils whatsoever exist.
That is to say, there shall be no urination, defecation, indigestion, hiccups, or labored breathing; indeed,
there shall be no afflictions such as fainting or mental confusion, O Māṇava.
Even if one were to accept those seven days of food while discarding all putrid and rotten meals, a person of pure and virtuous conduct could still cause the donor to obtain a great karmic fruit;
how much more so when accepting such celestial *sūdhā* food?
Such food as this does not exist in the world;
therefore, it cannot be compared by analogy to the coarse or rough textures found among human beings, O māṇava.
If those who have broken the precepts and lack right mindfulness should eat this food,
such persons will surely obtain great unwholesome fruit. Ānanda.
At that time, having heard these matters, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Emitting Light, saying: "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
Now, within this assembly, the community of bhikṣus is free from dust,
grime, gravel, pebbles, chaff, weeds, withered branches, and broken leaves; even down to their minor deficiencies,
they have no afflictions or manifold ailments that require various medicines.
"World-Honored One, this assembly of bhikṣus possesses only firm and pure observance of the precepts;
they have skillfully entered meditative concentration and are free from all fears."
Now, within this assembly, there are those who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna,
those who have attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin,
and those who have attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
There are arhats; there are pratyekabuddhas;
there are those who have resolved their minds upon the Mahāyāna.
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
as well as lions among men who are endowed with supernatural powers and have attained the further shore;
in this place there are also those who constantly practice the samādhi of emptiness.
The samādhi of signlessness,
the samādhi of wishlessness,
and furthermore, the constant practice of the most supreme and unsurpassed dānapāramitā.
The most supreme perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā),
the most supreme perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā),
and the most supreme perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).
The most excellent perfection of dhyāna,
the most excellent perfection of prajñā, and so forth,
including the constant practice of the powers and fearlessnesses.
"World-Honored One,
this pure assembly of bhikṣus has received such exquisite food from Śakra, Lord of the Devas."
I know that this assembly can accept all offerings from every quarter without being unable to digest them.
Why is this? Because if anyone in the entire world eats food that is unsuitable to them, they will immediately fall ill and suffer.
If even eating these [ordinary foods] can prevent illness,
how much more so in the case of this subtle and pure food,
wherein there is not even the need for excrement or urine?
How could those who eat this food experience the disease and suffering of old age?
It is impossible for them to fall ill. Ānanda!
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Emitting Light addressed the bodhisattvas,
saying: "Excellent, excellent, māṇava!"
Today you have been able to cause this Śakra, King of Devas, to give rise to joy in his heart.
Māṇava, there must now be beings within this assembly who have conceived such doubts.
By the Buddha’s majestic power, this great assembly has been caused to ascend to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha now [teaches] for the sake of this great assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
In order to decisively eliminate the net of doubt,
he thus expounds the True Dharma,
causing all to realize it through various parables.
Ānanda, when the Tathāgata Raśmipramokṣa spoke thus,
Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
if a person makes offerings to the disciples of the Buddhas,
or to Arhats who have exhausted their outflows.
Whether they be pratyekabuddhas,
or the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
or the buddhas, tathāgatas, arhats, and samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"Is it possible for such giving to be without distinction?
World-Honored One,
you have now spoken of the characteristic of a single dharma."
This reveals the meaning of the single liberation of all things.
Within this, how could there be any difference in giving?
I pray that you will fully explain this meaning.
"May these sentient beings attain freedom from doubt.
The Buddha said, "Kauśika,"
Do not give rise to doubt or uncertainty regarding this place where these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
preach the Dharma. Kausika,
I shall now demonstrate this meaning to you through various similes.
This shall cause all wise people to attain certain understanding.
Kauśika, when a person wishes to practice the giving of alms:
One should form this thought:
"By practicing such generosity as this,
I shall attain an immeasurable accumulation of merit and wisdom."
Furthermore, it shall cause the recipient to attain an immeasurable accumulation of merit and wisdom. Kausika,
you should now know this.
The Tathāgata has previously taught that once a single act of giving has been dedicated toward the immeasurable,
such a vow ensures that even when giving to animals or starving dogs,
one shall still obtain immeasurable karmic fruition.
How much more so for one who gives alms to a srotāpanna,
a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, or an arhat.
This applies to pratyekabuddhas and these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
how much more so for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
Kauśika, for this reason,
do not give rise to doubt or confusion.
Although one may offer only a small thing as a gift to the Tathāgata, one obtains immeasurable merit.
Because it is dedicated toward the immeasurable,
giving to the disciples of the Buddhas in this manner will likewise result in the attainment of an immeasurable mass of merit.
Do not harbor doubts,
Kauśika; this applies to the disciples of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Just as the great ocean is difficult to measure,
you should no longer question the Tathāgata in this manner.
All those who practice giving obtain immeasurable retribution—
whether they be śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
Kausika, or the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Within this, I shall cause you to sever your doubts.
Listen attentively, receive it with heedfulness, and reflect upon it well;
I shall speak for you.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain this for us."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, listened with single-minded attention.
All the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who were present in this assembly,
having heard the Buddha’s teaching, rose from their seats and joined their palms together.
He stood before that Buddha with reverence.
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhāsa addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika."
Now observe these Trāyastriṃśa gods—
the places where they received the retribution for karmic actions performed in the past,
as well as the causes and conditions of the roots of goodness they cultivated.
Do you all know this, Kauśika?
Among these gods of the Thirty-three now present...
"Is there anyone who knows for themselves whether they have performed wholesome deeds?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One, there is."
I now fully know the causes and conditions of the past virtuous karma created by these devas;
yet the sons of the gods themselves cannot know what they did in former times.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Kauśika, you should now observe among this assembly of devas which son of heaven possesses the least roots of goodness.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Śakra, Lord of Devas, observed with single-minded attention.
Among the assembly of devas, there was seen a certain son of heaven whose roots of goodness were the least;
yet in his past life, that son of heaven had been born among human beings.
At that time, the Buddha-Tathāgata had a disciple who was practicing for the fruit of Srotāpanna;
while begging for alms in sequence, he entered that house.
He happened upon that man sitting upright while eating.
Upon seeing him, the man immediately rose from his seat and pointed to the seat,
offering it to the one practicing for the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Having washed his hands and taken food, he offered him a single morsel.
The begging bhikṣu then accepted the food from that person;
having eaten, he remained there for one day.
However, this son of heaven possessed only such roots of goodness in the past:
rising respectfully from his seat, he offered a single morsel of food as an act of charity.

By virtue of these roots of goodness, after his life ended, he was born in this heavenly realm to receive this present retribution. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having seen those roots of goodness of the son of heaven, [reflected].
He then addressed that devaputra,
saying: "Good son,
you should now come before the World-Honored One."
He recounted the virtuous deeds he had cultivated in the past.
Then, having heard the command of Śakra,
that devaputra rose from the assembly.
He then went before the feet of Śakra,
King of Devas. Ānanda,
at that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, spoke again to that son of heaven, saying:
"Good son,
you are now before the Tathāgata,
personally recounting the karmic conditions of what you did in the past."
This causes the other devaputras to give rise to joy in their hearts;
they conceive a sense of reverence toward the Tathāgata and develop a mind of affection and respect. Ānanda!
Then that devaputra, having received the instruction of Śakra,
immediately stood before the Buddha and, for the sake of the various devas,
recounted for himself the roots of goodness he had cultivated in the past.
When the various devas heard that son of heaven recounting the roots of goodness he had performed in the past,
they spoke to one another and were filled with great joy, Ānanda.
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhāsa addressed Śakra,
the Lord of Devas, saying: "Kauśika, what do you think?"
Now, regarding all the palaces, various ornaments,
food and drink, and other garments possessed by this devaputra—
indeed, among all the articles he enjoys:
Even regarding a single, trivial object such as a leather sandal—
suppose all sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa were gathered together in one place;
would it be possible to weigh and calculate the price of that most humble sandal, or to know its value?
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Kauśika."
Setting aside all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa for a moment,
suppose furthermore that all sentient beings in the four continents possessed wisdom and were endowed with great skillful means.
They cannot even know the price of the lowest-quality leather sandals,
let alone know the value of other things. Why is this?
If even a portion of Jambūnada gold the size of a mustard seed were to have a marketable value,
then all the people of Jambudvīpa, along with all their wealth and possessions— whether bipeds, quadrupeds,
or those with many legs— [would not equal its worth].
All such values do not equal even a small fraction of it.
I shall provisionally describe its value through skillful means, yet in reality,
it is priceless, Kausika.
Observe now this single act of giving food:
even such a being as this attains such immeasurable karmic fruit;
how much more so for one who gives much!
Kauśika, you should know that by giving such gifts as these,
one will in turn obtain such immeasurable fruits of retribution.
Śakra spoke again:
"I know, World-Honored One,
all the fruits of retribution and adornments belonging to these sons of gods."
Even if all the people filling this trichiliocosm were to gather together, they would not be able to know it,
let alone those of the four continents.
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Emitting Light addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
Kauśika, what do you think?
Regarding all these articles of enjoyment belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa gods:
He took the smallest of the devaputras from the Yāma Heaven,
along with all their karmic rewards and requisites.
Furthermore, how did the matter of their ascending and descending proceed?
Śakra spoke again:
"World-Honored One,
if all the bodily ornaments among all the people in this trichiliocosm..."
From the bodily ornaments of the Four Great Kings up to the bodily ornaments of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven here—
having gathered all such bodily ornaments together.
Together with the lowest of the Suyāma devas,
that deva had originally no desire for the various objects before him;
how then could it be said that he took them up?
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
it is as if a Wheel-Turning Sage King were traveling throughout the four seas when suddenly someone offers him coarse rice.
"Your Majesty, you have never before accepted any discourse on eating food.

World-Honored One, it is likewise with that Suyāma, the lowest of the gods; he has no desire for any of the fruits of retribution or any ornaments found here in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, nor even among humans."
How much less would they covet and then consume [the offerings]? Why is this?
Because they themselves possess the subtle and exquisite fruits of retribution consisting of the five sensory pleasures.
"This is not due to personal desire.
The Buddha again addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika,"
What do you think?
Compare the palaces and the array of ornaments and requisites inhabited by the Tuṣita Heaven with those of the Yāma Heaven,
the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and the Cāturmahārājika Heaven.
As for all other devas and humans,
will the palaces they inhabit and the various articles of their enjoyment likewise become equal to those of the Tuṣita Heaven?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied,
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
Kauśika, in this manner they successively become increasingly superior;
the gods of the Brahma-abodes surpass those of the six heavens of the desire realm.
Up to Maheśvara, who surpasses all other gods,
Kauśika; by these causes and conditions, the distinctions in the fruits of giving are immeasurable.
I have now finished explaining this for you through a different interpretation.

At that time, the Tathāgata Emitting Light again addressed Śakra,
Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika,
there are certain extraordinary gifts that yield immeasurable retribution."
Just as the bodhisattva vehicle is immeasurable and boundless,
so too is this matter of the adornment of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
that is to say, hearing the true Dharma in the presence of the Tathāgata.
They shall attain such immeasurable roots of goodness.
When this sutra is preached, all doubts held by all sentient beings will be forever severed, Kauśika.
For this reason, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study the conduct practiced by all Buddhas.
Having heard this from the Buddha, you should practice according to what was taught. Kauśika,
do not give rise to doubt regarding such a matter that can be verified through realization.
"You must apply yourselves with diligent effort, single-mindedness, and courageous vigor,
without rest or weariness. Kausika, you must not allow even a single sentient being to give rise to envy within the void."
You all should likewise abandon jealousy yourselves.
This space is called a common dharma;
it cannot belong exclusively to a single sentient being nor to a single phenomenon alone.
All phenomena are like empty space;
one should maintain this through the adornment of all things.
A person of wisdom shall, within these teachings, personally and forever sever all doubts and delusions.
Kauśika, there is ultimately no one who, having known space, would again become deluded regarding space. Kauśika.
This Dharma gate is the foremost, the highest, the most excellent, the most sublime, and the deepest.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who can maintain continuous mental engagement with this Dharma gate, [they shall attain great merit].
Even if they give rise to a single thought of sympathetic joy,
you should feel profound庆幸 (gratitude and joy) regarding this and reflect thus:
"One should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva."
Because they have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past,
they are able to hear the exposition of such a Dharma-gate without being startled, without fear, without retreating, and without sinking.
Their giving of the Dharma is pure like space and enters into the category of space.
Alternatively, it is taught that through this skillful means of the analogy of space—
whether heard in its general or specific exposition— one will not give rise to fear or weariness;
by practicing in accordance with it, one perceives suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, Kauśika,
all those in the world— gods, humans, and asuras— are equal to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Even all the nāgas, spirits, and ghosts should love and respect [them];
they should all show them honor.
All should be honored with offerings;
all should be protected. Why is this?
Kauśika, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who remain within saṃsāra still possess immeasurable residual unwholesome dharmas.
However, one who is able to fully practice such profound patience—
while practicing this patience—
even if there were a great assembly of celestial Māras numbering immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas.
Using various forms and various modes of speech—
whether by startling, terrifying, deceiving, or enticing—
they cause this bodhisattva to retreat and lose their original resolve.
However, the Bodhisattva’s original resolve became even more firm;
his physical form remained serene and not a single hair moved. Kauśika!
For these reasons,
I shall provide you with various explanations through parables and skillful means;
you should contemplate them with single-minded attention and well-considered reflection.
One should know thus and train accordingly.
You should contemplate so as to accord with the true meaning,
in order to fulfill all the qualities of a Buddha.
Kauśika, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice this Dharma in such a manner,
even if their bodies were to fall from the summit of Mount Sumeru down to the great earth, [they would not be shaken].
He may even take up Mount Sumeru and hurl it back across the great earth;

That which was previously not yet expanded and not yet abandoned,

Chapter Fifty-one: Entrusting to Śakra Devānām Indra. *Mahādharmolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, Chapter Fifty-one: Entrusting to Śakra Devānām Indra. Ānanda!
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Emitting Light,

The Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika,
what do you consider to be the instruction herein?"

You should understand well that in this matter, what is called "instruction" is merely a name consisting of syllables. It is simply termed "instruction."
Although formless and invisible, by means of the skillful method of the wooden board, one can understand the locus of that person’s verbal instruction. Kauśika,
this letter-gateway *ka* is the sovereign of twenty-one phrases and syllables.

"How shall these twenty-one phrases be subsumed?
When you later explain them to others, [you should do so in this way]."
Internally, you should exercise self-restraint and not give rise to a distracted mind;
you ought to always maintain it correctly, Kauśika.
I have already explained for you through skillful means that gateway of the letter *ka*, which is in constant accord with the teachings of the devas.
You should explain it; you ought not to remain silent.
"What is the gateway of the letter *ka*?
What is the teaching of the devas? Ānanda."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Emitting Light, saying: "World-Honored One,
this present Dharma-gate of the letter 'Ka' accords with the teachings of the devas and continues without interruption."
This must be understood and known:
this gateway of the syllable *ka* is the sovereign of twenty-one phrases;

Just as with the teaching of the letter-gateway NA,
it stands at the very end;
those fourteen phrases are continuous within a single context.
World-Honored One,
furthermore, as for the syllable *ka*,
it is like the palaces inhabited by the Four Great Heavenly Kings.
The palaces where the King of the Trāyastriṃśa devas resides,
and the palaces where the Yāma devas reside;
among those who dwell therein, Śakra is the sovereign.
Thus, the gateway of the letter *ka* is surrounded by thirty-four phrases,
consisting of the preceding twenty-one phrases and the subsequent fourteen phrases combined together.
World-Honored One,
this is an illustrative skillful means for explaining how to know this realm.
Having thus explained it by way of skillful means, [he said:]
"Then one may be said to have entered among the ranks of those who speak the language of the devas.
World-Honored One,
I now provide this exposition for the sake of all other sentient beings."
"It is not so, World-Honored One.
This state is entirely the realm of wisdom of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas."
The Tathāgata himself knows,
O Bhagavān,
all the palatial abodes consisting of syllables and phrases beginning with the letter *ka*.
"World-Honored One, we shall come to know this matter through the expedient means of observing the wooden board.
World-Honored One,
it is as if the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens dwell upon the summit of Mount Sumeru."
In this regard, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial maidens.
Thus it is with the World-Honored One;
from the gate of the letter A, it extends through to the letter Ka.
This continues until the letter *na*;
within this, immeasurable sounds and languages can all be discussed and explained,
World-Honored One.
Surrounded by his retinue at the gateway of the letter Ka,
how could it be described,
World-Honored One?
It is like the Lake Anavatapta, from which all rivers flow;
their waters pour forth without ceasing until they fill those four oceans.
World-Honored One.
Suppose there were such a lake or ocean,
and someone were constantly to take water from it using the tip of a single hair split a hundred thousand times,

This matter may not be disregarded. Why is this?
World-Honored One.
Even if immeasurable great rivers were to flow forth once more,
that lake-ocean would still not suffer any depletion;
how much less could it ever be exhausted by drops from a single hair?
World-Honored One,
it is impossible to exhaustively cite all similes;
for though there be many metaphors, in the end none can truly compare.
"If it were possible to compare them, such a thing could not exist.
Thus it is, World-Honored One;
we gods stand before the World-Honored One."
"Even though you have provided many analogies and explanations,
O World-Honored One, what could possibly be obtained from drawing water with a hair?"
Having now received the Tathāgata’s inquiry,
we dare not deceive or flatter him, nor do we harbor any negligence or arrogance;

World-Honored One,
when the Tathāgata questions them,
other people of the world may act with deceit and flattery.
Or if other sentient beings should give rise to indolence or arrogance,
World-Honored One,
I would never dare [to do so].
Now, I have spoken only according to my own limited understanding and capacity.
World-Honored One,
Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Whatever vocal karma there may be— sounds and speech that proclaim, clarify,
and explain the principles and meanings of all phenomena—
whether among all those in the world, be they Brahmās, Māras, devas, or humans.
"World-Honored One, there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are able to fathom or know it."
World-Honored One, regarding all the skillful means, parables, and explanations of the Tathāgata,
no sentient beings are able to understand even a small portion of their underlying meaning.
"World-Honored One, I have never heard of nor seen anyone in the world who is able to understand and know the meaning of the Tathāgata’s skillful means through explanations by way of parables.
World-Honored One,
we have now personally heard this meaning before the Tathāgata."
They shall uphold and remember it, never daring to forget or lose it.

are able to understand the matters concerning the Buddha’s bodhi.
World-Honored One,

Even if the Tathāgata were to explain them fully for us, [we would not grasp them].
Those bhikṣus were unable to practice accordingly.
There were upāsakas, or gods and humans, dwelling in araṇya hermitages who,

World-Honored One,
this is the explanation through the analogy of the Great Expedient Means,
namely, the treasury of karma of the expedient means of the three teachings.
World-Honored One,
within this treasury, we do not possess even a single thought of practice,

I only pray that the World-Honored One will,
